THE STRANGERS' NOOK. fin rural churchyards in Scotland there is always a corner, near the gate. which is devoted to the reception of strangers, and is distinguished from the rest of the area by its total want of monuments. This spot is known ai " The Strangers' Nook."] Merrily sings th 6 lark o'erhead ; Drowsily the vagrant bee • Hums above the sileat dead, In the churchyard by the sea. Pinks and pansies by the wall Bend beneath the winds that pass; • Sea-birds sail and curfews call O'er the tender mantling grass. • Rich and poor all silent lie. With deadened ear and painless head; They cannot hear the plover's cry, From their moss-enamelled bed. And if those dead to us of earth Speak yet of family or fame, 'Tis all embraced, 'tween death and birth, Beneath the letters of each name! But what of those lone, grassy mounds Which lie beside the churchyard door, Encompassed by the sobbing sounds Of ocean's homeless, sullen roar? Have they who in them silent sleep No loved ones left beneath the sky? The wandering winds the secret keep, As through the rustling grass tney sigh! Here is a mound all wreathed with shells, Which fleck the grass like flakes of snow; No sacred, storied headstone tells The name of him who sleeps below. The wild storm, one fierce winter night, With booming voice smote all the bay; A sailor lad, at morning light, Upon the foom-fringed shingle lay! There, side by side—strange fate of life ! Beneath that grave o'ertopped with rue, Lies one who midst us closed her strife • With fate; her name we never knew! We found her dead one winter morn,— And oh ! her face was fair to see Now rests she, far from scathing scorn, Asleep in God's sweet charity! And others came, vet never went, But lingered round our cottage fires; Their warp and woof of life were blent With ours; they had no new desires. No need had we to tend them long; They meekly waited in their woe To find some voice or long-lost song To guide their souls when they would go! So there they rest from strife and sin; Nor need they reek where now they lie, Since God has folded each one in Safe from the heel of passers-by!
They went 'mid lonesomeness and tears, With isolation in each moan. Will they awake to shining spheres?— ! God knows best —they are His Own! r 'Sunday Magazine. ALEXANDER. LAMONT.

A. polite man is one who listens with interest to things he knows all about when they are told by a person who knows nothing about them. When one is tempted to write a clever and unkind thing, though it may be difficult to restrain it, it is al- ways better to leave it in thejnkstand. A fact is to a principle what a handle is to a blade—it gives it character and a purpose, and enables you to grasp it more firmly and wield it with greater Success. reAleMbed says there are but two things that can reach the summit of a pyramid, an eagle and a reptile; 80 it appears there are but two characters in this world that can gain the highest. parallel of notoriety, the good man and the villain, the saint and the devil; the one on the wings of genius and inspiration, the other on the belly of meanness and subtlety. EATING THE &WWIET.—An elderly couple from the country dined at the table d'hote the other day. Sitting opposite to them was a young man, who having taken a stsik of celery forthwith. commenced to eat it. The old lady looked at him a. moment with an air of disgust, and then, nudging her husband, said, in stage whisper," D'ye see that fellow there atin' tiler bokav?" A Cur OF TEA.—Chemically analysed, a cup of tea contains twenty different articles, to wit :—Volatile oil. chlorophyl, was, resin, gum, tannin, theine, extractine, apotheme. albumen, sulphur, phosphorus, chloride of potassium, oxyde of iron, carbonate, sulphate of lime, car- bonate of magnesia, manganese, and silica. The peculiar flavour of the tea is given by the volatile oil, and high chemical authority has declared that tea is not only an astringent and dilutent, but also that it possesses nutri- tive properties. EXTENUATING CIRCUMSTANCES. Augustus: "Ton honah, if this don't heat all, y' know. Funniest thing I evah saw, y' know." Miss Fulalie (wearily) : "What did you remark ?" "I was just glancing ovah the papah, y' know, while you were hunting for that music, and I saw ttint a Wisconsin woman had married a woman, don't v' know. Ain't it funny ?" " Were there not ex- tenuating circumstances ?" " Aw, how could there be, y' know?" "Perhaps all the men of her acquaintance were dudes." DEAD LErtsas.—Who of the 'soldiers does not remem- ber t'ne sadness of the mails whin came after the bat- tle—with its letters full of love and tenderness for those Who lay near by on the bloody ground? And, when the armies of the United States laid down, after the last agonising campaign. their arms, when their ranks were but the bare arms of that tree whose leaves bad fallen— how solemn it must have been to those who intercepted those far-coming missives, to see them superscribed with name, rank, and army—a name that had passed from earth, a rank passed into memory, an army dis- banded. At the Wilderness, a gallant young Mississip- pian had fallen, and at night, just before burying him, there came a letter from her he loved host. One of the group around his body, a minister whose tenderness was womanly, broke the silent tearfulness with which he saw the dead letter; he took it, laid it upon the breast of him whose heroic heart was still, and said, "Bury it with him. He will see it when he wakes." It was the sublimest sentence of his funeral service.—

Exchange. EDrTORIAL Pruswirrys.—Recently, Mr. Charles A. Dana addressed an assembly of editors at Milwaukee, and for- mulated a journalistic octologue. The eight editorial commandments, according to Mr. Dana, are :—(l) Get the news, and get all the news, and nothing but the news. (2) Copy nothing from another publication without per- fect credit. (3) Never print an interview without the knowledge and consent of the party interviewed. (4) Never print a paid advertisement as news matter. Let every advertisement appear as an advertisement. No sailing under false colours. (5) Never attack the weak or defenceless, either by argument, by invective, ot ridi- cule, unless there is some absolute public necessity for so doing. (6) Fight for your opinions, but don't believe they contain the whole truth or the only truth. (7) Sup. port your party, if you have one, but don't think all the good men are in it and all the bad men outside of it. (8) Above all, know and believe that humanity is advancing, and that there is progress in human life and human affairs, and that, as sure as God lives, the future will be greater and better than the present or the past. COSTLYHoSPITALITY—OId Nanny James never told her little story but once, and she told it in touching words. "I knew she'd cum loon that Thorsdav, Miss Hetenor," the old woman said. "An' she'd been that good an' kind to me 'at Ali thowght Ali'd mak bould te ask her te hey a cup o' tea, as Ah knowd she'd had a cup one day at them mucky Scarth's. So what did An do but gets oot two o' the cha,ney cups-are-saucers, at was my great-gran'mother's, beautiful old charley it is, though only four o' them left and the teapot stand. An' Ah puts oot all the three little old silver tea-spoons. An' then Ah went te Grainger's, an' bowght half-an-ounce o' best green, to put to my bit o' poor black; an' half a poond o' curran's, an' a bit o' lard—nobbut a quartern. An' All paid for 'em, sir, Ah paid for 'ern all, not wantin' te go debt, though I had te take the tenpenen Au Ushaffy gives for the bit o' meat te sarve me the week. Nu then te get a drop o' nice cream Ah took my mother's old calabash, 'at my ' father brought f m foreign parts sixty years. ago. Ah took it up to Mrs. Ossett at the farm, she'd offers admired it; an' she gave me the splen- didest big jug o' thick cream, you might ha' cut it wiv a knife, and the beautifullest little pat o' fresh golden butter you ever set eyes on. Are eh.but Ali was a prood arid woman that efthernoon! An' Miss Helenor cum, an' all just as Ah'd hoped an' expected. She admired everything, injoyed everything, her words fairly browt tears o' gladness inta my eyes. • • • But oh, sir! had to cry at t'other side o' my face afore the week was over. Al couldn't believe it tell 'twas forced upon me, 'at she'd spread it everywhere 'at All were a deceitful, extravagant old woman, livin' on the fat o' the land, an' all the while plainin' poverty ! Even—as you knaw yer oiln sel, sir—the evardians 'at alloos ma two-and-six- pence a week got le hear on it. 'Twos told to them 'at Miss Caldbergh had foond ma sittin' doon to my tea we ouch spice cakes on the table, such thick, rich cream, such pats o' fresh butter, such strong green tea as never ;none of 'em had seen at my lady's table! Oh, dear, Ah was put oot ! An' me wi' nobbut the tea leaves She'd left an' a bit o' dry bread te my dinner for all the week after. . . . Yet Ah've never spoke of it, never tell te-day. BETTING A BONNET.
BY BYGIL.

I don't like a woman who tries to take a man down so much. I know I wouldn't do it if I was a woman. Because I say this I don't want anyone to think that I have been taken down by a woman and am therefore speaking feelingly. Not but what I might be taken down often enough if I didn't keep my eyes wide open, and by one, toe, who once promised to love and— But what's the good of talking! Very likely if anything was to be said to her about her promises she would say that the question was put to her so suddenly she didn't know what she was saying. They call them the weaker sex. Why, any one of them has as much strength in her tongue as a man has in both legs and one arm. Weaker sex, forsooth! My opinion is that for dodgery and all sorts of—of cussedness, a woman is equal to two men any time; and I think that every woman ought to ' marry two men, so that when she was dodging one the other would get a rest. And when they've dodged you, how simple and heavenly they try to look. Now, don t I they? They've an idea they're very clever, no doubt; but one cannot help thinking that it will, sooner or later, be somebody else's turn, and that a day will come; only the day keeps coming to the wrong party—to the same party, in fact, every time. Now, don't let anyone think that I am spiteful about women, because I sin not. Oh, dear, no; anything but that. But my beat plan, I think, will be to tell what has caused me to talk in this strain, so here goes, even if I get laughed at, though there's nothing to laugh at, let me tell you that. If a woman taking advantage of a man's trusting nature is something to laugh at, why, let those laugh who are unfeeling enough. The other day, over dinner, the Missis asked me if I had noticed how shabby her bonnet had got, and if I didn't think she required a new one. Well, most hus- bands will, I have no doubt, have an idea what my answer would be. At any rate, it brought down upon my head such a flood of eloquence as ladies are capable of pouring forth when their wishes are not complied with. I refused to provide the needful. The result was a small scene, and the having my manly bosom loaded with a full-grown feeling of discomfort as I proceeded down to business. Somehow, whenever anything of the sort occurs at our house, the matter always ends in my having a number eleven consciousness that I am an ' unmitigated brute, whether I am in the right or wrong. I felt so on this occasion. Previous to the introduction of the bonnet discussion the Missis had asked me to order a little fish up for the tea as I was going to business. I called and ordered the fish, and, knowing that the MiS3i3 was fond of oysters, and thinking to mollify her, I ordered a score to be taken up with the fish. That they would not be eaten until I went home, and that I should get half of them, at the least, I hadn't a doubt, and I was right. Over tea I said, "I ordered you a score of oysters with the fish; did they come ?" 64 "Did you eat them ?" "No." _

'Why didn't you ?" I didn t want them just then, and I didn't think they were sent specially for me. Besides, they weren't opened. I said, in a kind of a oh-we'll-rectify-that tone of voice, "Indeed ! Well, never mind, I'll open them for you myself after tea." After tea I said," Now, bring your vinegar bottle and you shall have them on the half shell ; they are best that way," and I went into the scullery whore the oysters had been put. Now I didn't remember at the moment that I had never opened an oyster before, and it didn't occur to me that there might possibly be some difficulty in doing so. Having seen, I may say, thousands opened, I never dreamt that there would he any more difficulty in per- forming the operation than in splitting open a hot cake. The Missis followed me into the scullery with a vinegar bottle in one hand and an expectant, waiting look in the other. Having secured an ordinary table- knife, I picked up an oyster and examined it carefully to find an opening. There wasn't any; in fact. I never in all my life examined anything that had such a shut up look about it. Where I thought I should have in- serted the knife it came to an edge as sharp as the edge of the knife I was holding. It just seemed about as possible to open the knife with the oyster as tne oyster with the knife. I put it down and picked up another. It was twin brother to the first one. I dropped that one and picked up another, and I dare swear that the edge of the last one was actually sharper than the knife I held, for I felt it, critically, with my thumb. I was a little embarrassed, for the Missis was watching me, with one hand partly field out for the first oyster. I turned over the oyster I held, and I tapped it with the knife. It sounded very solid. It might have been a piece of flat stone, and [began to think that, perhaps, there pos- sibly might be oysters that were all solid shell. I turned it over again, and looked all round the outskirts. I heard a te-he behind me' and then a sweet voice said— " What are you looking for ?" I said, "Well, I am looking for tlis oyster's smiler, but I don't think it has got one." "Well, be quick and get it opened, and don't keep me standing here all day. My arm aches with holding this bottle" I said," Does it? Well, put it down on the table and fold your arms a bit." Now, for all that I was leaning over the slopstone, and the Missis was partly behind me, I knew very well that she was amused and smiling. People may not believe in thought-reading, but I'm not prepared to flatly deny it, at any rate not where my partner is concerned. I could feel that she was smiling. She has a nasty way of smiling at any little thing of that sort. But perhaps it pleases her, and it doesn't hurt me, at least, nothing to matter anything. I wish somebody would tell her of it though, because I think it a very bad, vulgar habit. After turning the oyster over a few times, and looking carefully all round the selvedge of it, I came to the con- clusion that I had been dodged by the dealer. I felt certain that he had palmed a lot on to me that he couldn't open himself. I thought [would try another, so I dropped the one I was holding and picked a fresh one up. When I examined this one, I was more than ever convinced that the dealer had imposed on me. There were a half-a-dozen or more places where I could put the point of the knife in; in fact, the edges of this one looked just like the edges of the leaves of a book. Without further ceremony, I at once popped the point of the knife amongst the leaves and began to wriggle it; and to work my elbows up and down as I had seen oyster dealers do, and I did it in their fussy style too. I wanted to let the Missis see that I was up to the trick of opening an oyster as well as anyone. But it didn't open. No; a few of the leaves broke off short and left my knife outside. Without a pause I jammed the knife in again, and again oscillated my elbows, this time with a good deal of determination. The result was some more leaves came off suddenly, and my forefinger banged against the edge of the oyster, which made it bleed—my finger I mean, not the oyster. Now, would anybody believe it? That woman actually burst out laughing—burst out laughing be- cause I had cut my finger. It couldn't be anything else. She kept laughing, too, every time I tried to get into that oyster, and when I had pared all the leaves off it, and had made it as sharp as the others at the edge, without opening it, she sat down on the bread-mug and held her sides and laughed until tears ran down her face. It did look bad behaviour to me, but I couldn't stop her, though I tried to de by looking at her with a voice of thunder. When she had calmed herself by °verbal:mein t the bread-mug and breaking it, and after she had picked herself up, and was rubbing her elbow, I said, "You're very clever, aren't you, and you fancy yourself a good deal, don't you? I should fancy you've an idea that you can give me points in opening oysters, haven't you ?" She said, "Oh, no, I don't think that, butT do think I could have opened one before now. You have been at it twenty minutes, and you are no nearer yet." Now I am almost certain that that was not true. . .

don't think I had been trying mere than a quarter of an hourkt the most. I said, "Now, look here, you say you think you could have had one open before now. just bet you anything that for every one you open I'll open two." Something seemed to strike her as soon as I said that, for her face went straight all of a sudden, and she looked serious. I never like to see her go like that,

div.head: EXAM
div.p: THE EXAM

because it generally means that some sort of an idea has come into her head, that somehow, as the saying is, enples her to go at me. But in this instance I felt that I was the top sawyer, for a capital idea had struck me. I daresay it will strike a good many people that I was unutterably stupid when I tell them that not until that moment did the idea come into my head, that the simplest way to open an oyster would be to put the point of the knife into the hinge of the oyster and break it, and the thing would be done at once; but it is a fact, and I admit it. She said quietly," What will you bet ?" " Anything," I said, triumphantly, for I felt that I had her this time. She said," Will you bet me that new bonnet we were talking about at dinner-time, that I don't open ten of those oysters as soon as you open the other ten ?" Yes," I said, "11l bet you a dozen bonnets if you like. But, look here, you don't watch me open my ten, you take your ten away into another room." I thought that if she saw me get into mine through the hinges she might get the wrinkle and run me a tight race. She said," Very well ; count me ten out; I'm ready." I counted her ten, but I dodged her a bit. I gave her ten of the worst I could find, putting amongst them the three I had first picked up. That I was a bit mean in not telling her of the trick of breaking the hinges I ad- mit, but then, you know, it might have cost me the price of a new bonnet if I had done so. When I- had counted her ten out and she had put them on a plate she said, "Now I will go into the kitchen, and when I have got !another plate to put them on when they are opened, and a knife to open them with, I will call out 'Ready,' and then you can start." I attended her to the scullery door, which I closed after her and, without waiting for the signal, I com- menced operations. By the time that she called out "Ready" I had cut the palm of my left hand and had twisted my knife all shapes trying to spring the hinge of the first oyster. I tried the hinge of every oyster in rapid succession, and then I came to the conclusion that I could get into a paving-stone as soon with a knife. They didn't spring worth a bodle. I wasted about five minutes in hinge springing, and then a real good idea came into my head. Underneath the slopstone there was a rubbing-stone. I got this stone and began to hammer the edge of one of the oysters, holding it on the slopstone while I struck it. This was a success. At the expiration of another five minutes I had opened one oyster, rinsed the grit off it, and put it on a clean plate. I was hammering the second oyster with the rubbing-stone when the scullery door opened and the Missis came in with a plate in her hand. I had just time to look round and exclaim " Get out !" when I saw that she had her ten oysters on the plate, without the shells, and nicely vinegared and peppered. With a hateful smile on her face that was very near wide enough to prevent her getting through the doorway, she said, "I think IM just about first, aren't I ?" Dropping the knife and oyster I was holding I turned round and counted the oysters she had on the plate. There were ten undoubtedly. Yes, it looked as if I had lost the bonnet. But a sudden suspicion crossed my mind that I might have been tricked some way, and I said, " Where are the shells ?" Holding a handkerchief up which she held in her other hand, she said, " Here." I gave in. There was no way out of it; but it was very humiliating. I wouldn't have cared so very much, though, if the Missis hadn't been so very annoying about it, but I could see that she was laughing in her "innards" all the time. She didn't waste any time over getting the bonnet, and before I went to bed I was asked to admire it, and had paid the amount of the bill, which she pre- sented. I don't knew why women should be so aggravating, but it is a positive fact that that woman actually made a laughing stock of me before my own sister the next day. My sister had come to have tea with us, and that woman actually showed her the bonnet, and told her 1 how she had won it. There's not a great deal of dif- ference in women, so. of course, my sister must needs laugh and praise her for having been so clever. Then she said, "But however did you manage to get them open so quickly ?" "Oh, I musn't tell you that; I may have to make another bet with him:' I said, "May you ? Well, you can rest assured that you will never bet me anything again as long as you live." Turning to my sister, she said, " Well, then, I'll tell you how I beat him." I said," Oh, yes, tell us all about how you beat him. Don't fail by any means to tell us how you beat him. It'll be a treat to everybody will getting to know how you beat him." She first of all told about me tryingto open the oysters, and then about making the bet, and then she said, " Well, you know, he shut the scullery door so that I shouldn't be able to see what he was doing. That was just what I wanted, and if he hadn't closed it I should have done so. Now I must tell you that our washer- woman was washing in the cellar, and I happened to know that she had a boiler full of boiling water. As soon as ever he shut the scullery door I popped the ten oysters into a handkerchief and went into the cellar with them. I held the oysters in the boiler—sticking to the handkerchief by the corners—until they opened, then I popped them into a bucket of cold water, and in ibout two minutes they were quite cold. In about three minutes after that I had them out of their shells, put on a clean plate, peppered and vinegared, and into the scullery, where my lord was sweating and bLeding over his second oyster.' Could woman's perfidy go any further? I jumped up off my seat, seized my hat, and bolted out of that house with the intention of never returning. I don't think I ever should have gone back either if it hadn't been that about eleven o'clock at night I began to think about the children, and

FUNERAL SERMON AT WARRINGTON. THE LATE MR. NOAH LEGGE. At Wycliffe Congregational Church, on Sunday evening, the pastor, tbe Rev. John Yonge, preached a sermon in memory of the late Mr. Noah Legge, to a crowded congregation, which included a large number of the workmen of White Cross Works. Ile selected as his text the words "What cloth the Lord require of thee, but to do justly. and to love mercy, and to walk hum- bly with thy God? "—Micah vi. part of the eighth verse. Mr. Yonge, in the course of his ser- mon, urged that religion was not a question of creeds and catechisms; it was a matter of character and conduct. In concluding he spoke of the late Mr. Legge in the following terms :—Many of you, doubt- less, have had far better opportunities of judging his character than have been possible to me. You have seen his life from day to day, and seen it where a man's character is always most intensely tested—in the realm of work and toil and business. Some of you, of course, have seen it even more closely and intimately, in the privacy of home and family life. I can only speak from testimony I have received, but I am bound. to say that all the good I hear of Mr. Legge is just what I should have anticipated from my own observation of him for some years past. Our friend's religious life found its be- ginning in connection with Wycliffe, at a time when the Rev. Mr. Jessop was the minister. Then, in a season of great personal sorrow, he found the help and comfort of religious faith and hope. From that/time he became a regular worshipper here, and whenever absent from home would always find his way night and morning to some similar place of worship. He allowed no one and no circumstances to hinder him in that. For several years now Mr. Legge was in the membership of this church, and regularly sat down with us at the Lord's Table. But in becoming a member, he did not —to use the ignorant cant phrase we sometimes hear— "seS up to be a saint." There was no affectation of any sort about him. I, at least, never saw any sign in him that he thought more highly of himself in any respect than was seemly, and certainly he had no spiritual pride about him. He believed and found that membership with Christ's Church was a help to him in his personal life, that it did him good to attend public worship and partake in the Lord's Supper. He felt that here he often , received real blessing, and sometimes in his quiet way he would acknowledge that he had profited. But what I am most concerned to say to-night is this—and I am as- sured that it is true—Mr. Legge did not reserve his re- ligion for Sundays and services ' • he took it with him in- to daily life and daily duty. It is quite possible that ac- cording to ideas and standards which some would main- tain,our friend might not escape criticism. He would be a remarkable man who should. . There is not one in thus church now who has not a weak point somewhere in his armour, through which an arrow might not pass. But our friend's endeavour was to be ruled byhis religion 'in all his relationships and in all places, and among all sorts of people. I believe he suc- ceeded in his endeavour, and that those who knew him most and best would be ready to say of him, "lie was a good man and a true." He was, as most of you know, a Staffordshire man, beginning to work at the early age of seven years, and spending his early life amid many dis- advantages and drawbacks. He came to this town some 25 or 28 years ago, holding a position as night manager at Hallam, until 19 years ago he accepted a more respon- sible post at Whitecross, where he remained until his death. His manner of life and conduct among his men was such as to win their confidence, and even affection. The large attendance of them at 'his funeral was signifi- cant of the place he held in their hearts. One of his principal features wat that of a kindly consideration for others. He was ruled in his dealings with his men by a kindly heart and a sterling integrity. He had a special care for strangers, never forgetting his own experiences as a workman, going to new places of employ. He was kind and forbearing, patient and helpful to men who were new to their work. He had a hopeful way of speech that inspired and cheered them. Indeed, lam told that his interest in his men was almost fatherly. He sought to promote their social, moral, and spiritual wel- fare He encouraged them to habits of thrift, did all he could to lead young men to begin to save, doing this sometimes by deeds which cost him denial and loss. He liked his men to try and get a house of their Own; an idea which led him to lend his efforts and influence to societies having that end in view. Personally, he was often their generous and sympathising helper. Many

div.head: NER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 1, 1888.
div.p: NER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 1, 1888.

were the seasonable gifts he' quietly bestowed in cases of necessity, and when work was scarce his heart was burdened with care for men and families who were feeling the pinch of want. Not that he ever talked about this. Not he. "He did good by stealth, and would have blushed to find it fame." It was kindness such as this that moved a man to say to me as I was leaving the side of his grave, "Oh, sir, there are many aching hearts here to-day." He loved mercy, and many an effort did he make to help a fallen brother to regain his footing. And morally he sought to benefit them. He encouraged them to be truthful. If he detected deceit he exposed it and reproved it. But straightforwardness and honesty always pleased him. He used to say to yowl.'6 men whose course seemed dark and difficult, • Keen on doing right, it will come right bye-and-bye." Spiritually he cared for his men; not, I fancy, that he talked religion to them, but he was pleased to see or hear of their atten- dance at public worship, and was wont, I believe, with his own hand, to distribute the notices of special servi- ces held in this church; and I have myself noticed at those services his pleased demeanour as, looking round, he recognised face after face of those who toiled with him in the week. Always, I am told, he was distin- guished by a love of right, and truth, and honourable dealing. He was strenuous in his endeavour to discharge faithfully his duty to his employers, while at the same time he stood true to the interests of the men. His was a position, as I judge, of no little difficulty. It must be far from easy to hold the balance evenly and calmly, more difficult in these days of companies and sharehol- ders than in the old day of principals and firms. There is a tendency to hardness and heartlessness in a business " company " which has to strive for a perpetual dividend which was not always so painfully manifest under the older arrangement. But our friend did his level best to serve "the company" and be true to his men; in and through it all, quietly seeking to be true to his Master in Heaven. I hold in my hand a little paper, found in his desk at the works after his death, bearing some printed " Counsels " which he evidently prized, and kept be- neath his eye : Do nothing rashly and thoughtlessly. Change cautiously and carefully. Meet all your duties cheerfully. Bear disappointments patiently. Speak mildly and amiably. Act manly, bravely, nobly. Live soberly and virtuously. Deal truly and honourably. Learn all you can improvingly. Earn all you can, and constantly. Save all you can prudentially. Give all you can liberally. Judge all mankind charitably. Love one another faithfully. Be friendly, kindly, and holy ; And then God will help you daily. These were the kind of counsels that guided him; and, as his life showed, with considerable power. We may think of him and remember him as one who exhibited a ' practical religion. I believe he said while lying ill, not long before he passed away, "I could never talk about religion ; but I have tried to put it into my life." Death overtook him very suddenly. At church here twice on Sunday, at work till tea-time on Monday, and dead on Thursday morning! That death did not find him un- prepared. He calmly assured his family that he was "not at all afraid to die." For he believed it was all right with him. He had striven to "do justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with his God." And so, trusting in Christ, he had the testimony of a peaceful conscience, and could meet death without a fear. My friends, we may rejoice in his death, because it has been gain to him. To us it need not be all loss. His family and friends cannot do other than sorrow that he is gone. The men who gladly worked under his guidance will mourn his departure, as the loss of a friend,and a helper, and a daily example. We here, at Wycliffe, will miss his fine presence, his regular attendance, his interested demeanour, his generous help, his earnest desire for our prosperity. But if his life of humble honest practical godliness help us to be godly; if the men who honour his memory will copy his example and try to tread in his steps; if his calm and peaceful death give us comfort and hope concerning our own, then our friend will not have lived or died in vain, and his death will not for any of us be all loss. Whither he has gone, sas we may confi- dently believe, may you and I presently follow. This assuredly we shall if "looking to Jesus ' we " do justly love mercy, and walk humbly with our God."
WARRINGTON LADS FOR THE GRIMSBY FISHERIES.

At the fortnightly meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians, held on Wednesday, it was re- ported by the Padgate Schools Committee that Mr. Mines, the superintendent of the schools, had taken six boys to Grimsby on the 24th August, on two months' trial as fisher lad apprentices to the Grims- by Ice and Fishing Company. An interesting re- port as to the conditions of service in the fisheries was also read by Mr. Mines, and from this report we give the following extracts :- SUGGESTIVE STATISTICS. Mr. Miran reported—" After delivering the boys up to the directors of the Grimsby Ice and Fishing Co., they were handed over to Mr. John Guzzlewell, a large smack owner, to whom the boys will be ap- prenticed until they are 21 years of age, providing ' they are satisfied after a trial of two months. I found it necessary to report to the Board of Trade the boys' arrival at Grimsby, and Mr. Wood, the Superintendent of Marine (who was very courteous and obliging) supplied me with some useful infor- mation and statistics regarding the welfare of fisher lad apprentices generally, from which it appears that of 400 lads apprenticed from the 18th June, 1880, to 21st November, 1881—a period of 17 months —2O boys died. Of these three died from natural causes, one from an accident. ashore, on fell from aloft, seven were accidentally drowned at sea, seven were washed overboard, in strong weather, and 10 were lost with their vessels. One hun- dred and thirty-eight boys absconded. Ninety-two had their indentures cancelled through various causes, 10 of which were cancelled through ill-health, weakness, or physical defect, 30 through no fault of the apprentice, and 52 lads were deemed incorrigible. Of the 141 boys who setved their term of apprenticeship, 93 had had their indentures endorsed character excellent, 27 good, and 21 unsatisfactory. The Board of Trade investigate all cases of complaint by the lads against their skippers or owners, also any complaints made against the boys by their skippers.

div.head: THEI VESSELS AND HOMES.
div.p: THEI VESSELS AND HOMES.

Through the kindness of Mr. Jeffs, one of the directors, I was permitted to inspect one or two vessels, on board which some of our boys would form part of the crew. Their food, clothing, and sleepinv accommodation when on board I thought satisfactory, more especially as it was under the supervision of the Board of Trade. Leaving the docks, I next visited the homes of the lads in other parts of the town. I found a matron or " mother " in charge of each house, whose duty it is to cook the boys' food, mend their clothes: and attend to their domestic comforts when ashore. I found their homes generally very clean and comfortable, and their food ample and good.

THE FISHER LADS' INSTITUTE. In the evening I visited the Fisher Lads' Institute. This is a Commodious building supported by voluntary contributions, and managed by a board of directors. The building is licensed by the Board of Trade as a place of recreation and amusement for fisher lads when ashore. Here the lads are permitted to spend their leisure time free of charge. Through the kindness of ' Mr. Miller, the superintendent, and Mr. Brusley, I was shown through the various departments, consisting of a reading room and library, a billiard room, a refresh- ment room, a gymnasium, a swimming bath, and a Board room, all of which were well furnished and in good order. There is a savings bank connected with the Institute, and during the year ending November 24, 1887, 403 deposits, amounting in the aggregate to £133 les 4d, were made by fisher lads, and the president of the Institute adds year by year five per cent per annum to the interest allowed by the Institution. A temper- ance register is kept by the superintendent, and last year 80 lads took the pledge, as against 47 in the year previous. •

• THE TERMS OF APPRENTICESHIP. I procured a form of apprenticeship indenture, from I which it appeared that a lad received a small amount of spending money, which is increased according to his promotion. In the first stage of his apprenticeship he acts as "cook," and receives sixpence per week, in the second Stage as " deck hand," receiving is per week, and in the third and last stage as third hand, when he receives Is (id weekly. In addition to this spending money, a lad, when acting as " codman," receives 2d per score of cod taken during a voyage to Iceland and the Faroe Isles ; also a share of salvage, liver cask and roe money, according to the custom of the port. He is supplied with five suits of clothes, three of which are for use at sea, one shore suit, and one best suit for Sunday wear when ashore." The report having been read, the CHAIRMAN (the Rev.. G. F. Roberts, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said the committee had been rather startled to find that such a large percentage of lads failed to realise what was hoped for them—only 141 boys out of 400 turning out as fit for the servibe they were intended for. The statistics, however, dated so far back as 1881, and might not show what was now taking place, and especially as the Local Government Board spoke highly of this service, which they would scarcely do on such statistics as those presented by Mr. Mines. , The boys were as yet, however, not hired out, but only on two months trial; and with that report of Mr. Mines before them the committee would make full inquiries before hiring them out permanently.—Mr. DARI3YSIIIRE thought the fact that the indentures of 30 of the lads had been cancelled through no' fault of their own did not speak very well. He, however, agreed with the chair- man, that the service might now 'be improved, but the committee did not think the information they had got so far was very satisfactory.—The minutes of the commit- tee were then adopted.
Iror all kinds of domestic sewing. Bagley and Wright s cotton I s the best.—Advt.

div.head: TIER BROTHER'S KEEPER.
div.p: TIER BROTHER'S KEEPER.
BY MRS. J. K. SPENDER, Author of "Mr. Nobody," "Parted Lives," "Both in the Wrong," "Recollections of a Country Doctor," "Trust Me," &c.
CHAPTER VIII. FORTUNE TURNS HER WHEEL.

Ursula in her simplicity had not the least suspicion how the atmosphere of unseemliness into which her father had constantly dragged her brother had already taken the bloom from the boy's delicate purity, or that this Paris life had not left Raymond as free and innocent as he had been before:

The girl did not differ from many other women in viewing her male relations through rose-coloured glasses. She had seen her father's delinquencies through the same tinted medium, and had all sorts of pretty fancies about that dead father. She stepped out on theroof with a cloud-like shawl over her head, after her guests had gone that evening and looked at the stars which shone in the sky over the city of Paris —stars not only innumerable in themselves, but suggestive of an invisible stellar multitude beyond. Ursula had no religion. That was not her fault. When Leonard Campion had made an excuse for get- ting rid of Peggy, that old woman's exuberant belief in fairies as well as saints had left few traces behind, and the gospel of humanism and mind-emancipation ,as preached by Ursula's father, had alternated with her liking in an artistic way for the solemn services of the Roman Church. At first, now and then, when her father had made jokes at the expense of her most cherished theories, the child had looked at him with that wistful devoted gaze so pitiful in the face of a girl when a man she loves and honours seems to be plunging into perilous depths of thought into which it isimpossible for her to follow. But by degrees she got used to it. For a time after his wife's death Leonard Cam- pion had worked in feverish fits, spending his money as soon as he hadmade it, and enjoying his ex- istence in the intervals of his money getting—enjoy- ing it to the "finger-tips." And if Ursula missed the softening shadow of a mother's tender influence, it must be remembered that that mother had been a constant invalid. The girl had a quickness of adaptibility which made her enjoy the Bohemian society, with the frolics, the "quips and cranks," the crackbrained vagaries, the childish mirth which had characterised the opinions of these Bohemians. Their strange pranks had not been strange to her; their toughness to the opinions of outsiders had never jarred upon her—how should they when she never knew that there was an outer world?—a world which would condemn her as a heretic, a freethinker, while she was flattering herself, poor child, that she was dabbling in progressive ideas. Nothing was left to her of this Bohemian society now but the little circle of eccentric young friends in Paris, constituting the members of that new Round Table which she, Raymond, and Louis Grandet were trying to found for the protection of oppressed youth. As she stood for a few minutes meditating and gazing up at the stars she tried to recall the fading images of the wandering life led with her father, when Leonard Campion had gone abroad again after the funeral of his wife, condemning himself, as Mrs. Maclurchan said, to exile, as if he knew that he were disgraced and bore a brand upon his brow. The artist took a different view of the matter. "We are peripatetic philosophers, Bohemian rovers," he used to say, with a grin, "carrying about our houses with us like snails, hating to be tied by the lecr to one place." How many Places had they really seen? He did not tell his children the names, and Ursula could not guess, as pictures rose before her of magic worlds, of sea, mountains, and sky. Mountains with awful inacessible peaks, and frowns that deepened at the approach of night with mystic eyes in the skies above them. _ _

_ She closed her eyes—she could see them now— deep purple at sunset with a lemon-coloured glow lbehind them. Or with swathes of grey and white cloud like Lazarus in his grave clothes, with lakes beneath them as inky as the waters of the Styx. Where had she seen these plains of dark and silent awater—with not a ripple on the sur- face after the sun had set—or with dark bands across the emerald greenness of a different tint from the grassy shore? Was it in Switzerland, the Engadine, or the Tyrol ?—she had not the least idea. The only places she could clearly define were Venice, not always sparkling with colour and sunshine, but sometimes a " gloomy labyrinth of water ways," and Monte Carlo, where there was gambling and riotous expenditure. When they had settled at Paris, where their father sent them to different schools, he began to break- fast and dine at restaurants,indulging in the intervals between his, meals in curocoa and absinthe. He never let his children see him at the times of his greatest degradation. But men of a queer, soddened appearance, with tallowy complexions, who talked much of Karl Marx, and of tyrants and capitalists, began to frequent the house. These were dull days for 'Ursula and Raymond, when they had to comfort themselves by sauntering sometimes to the Palais Royal, sometimes to the gardens of the Tuileries, tothe Champs Elvs6es, or to see the pictuies in the Louvre. The higl spirits of the girl's youth were scared away for a time. For the molten meublee had to be given up, and strange acquaintance to be made with grimy lodgings and dirty floors. There were no more café concerts, no more exciting card-playing for Leonard Campion. He lay canfined to his couch for long hours of pain and solitude. He would have been thankful for the lees of the cup of pleasure which he had once been so eager to dnnk, thankful for the mere rinsings. But even these were denied to the dying artist, who lay groaning in his martyrdom. After all it was but a poor martyrdom. He was a martyr to his love for the enjoyments of existence, to the lusts of the flesh, the temptations of the devil His physique, which had once been remarkably strong, had now become flaccid, like his 'character, and that had always had a limpness about it— an absence of backbone, a disbelief in eveything good, natural outcomes of such a life as his. "The Worn-out machinery is ready to be put back into its box," he said, with a bitter smile to Desnoyers, who came to visit him. "I ask nothing for myself. I have had my little day, but my children—angels could not remain angels with such surroundings." There was something, no doubt, a little hysterical and contemptible in this appeal to another man to look after his offspring, for whose sake he had never been able to cut oft his own self-indulgence; but the redeeming feature of Campian's character had been the fresh efforts in the way of work lie had positively made for the support of these children,when otherwise he would probably-have sunk forgotten years before to a dishonoured grave. The letter from his dead wife had not been quite wasted on him, though the mode of its delivery had been, perhaps, somewhat theatrical and morbid, and Mrs.Maclurchan would have declared that it was in the worst style of Frenchified art. But the woman who had planned the scene had known the man with whom she had to deal, and Leonard Campion in his worst excesses had respected the scruples of his wife. He had so managed that the eyes of his children were never shocked by seeing him in the state of degrada- tion to which he 'was sometimes reduced by his bestiality. Ursula had known that her father was liable to fits of delirium, but not that the delirium was produced by drink. She had been taken to his bedside when he was recovering from fits of unconsciousness pro- duced by noxious drugs, hut he had always ad- dressed her kindly as soon as lie recognised her. She thought of his memory very gently now, after this unusual effort of retrospection. She had en- shrined -her father's figure boldly enough in her imagination, and if it ever tottered in its niche she felt vexed with herself, and made a speedy effort to re-establish it. As to the future, she vaguely hoped that when kind old Monsieur Desnoyer ceased to help them, she and Raymond would be able to sup- port themselves—the one with painting, the other as an artificial flower maker. How, she scarcely knew ! Her mind went blank when she tried to plan the details. It seemed strange to her afterwards—for Ursula, like most women who had been brought up to believe in nothing, was superstitious—that this train of thought should have preceded a letter which reached her by the early post the very next morning. Any sort of letter was a very unusual inisAive to the six-storied attic in which Urs is and Raymond hid themselves; but this was a big letter, with an air of importance, if not of challenge, about it—a letter sealed with portentous red seals. There was a little discussion as to whether it should be opened at once, or conscientiously put on one side, and left for consideration later in the day, consider- ing it was so alarming in its dimensions and likely to make Raymond late at the Atelier. But curiosity prevailed, and the contents of the letter were such that no studio was visited that day. It contained several manuscripts—one a letter from a lawyer, another a copy, in legal handwriting, ' of a short will, and lastly, a letter in Mrs. Maclur chan's scrawling caligraphy. Ursula's instinct was ti

open the latter before she looked at the more per- plexing legal paper, as the lawyer's letter informed her that the lady was dead. No theory of her childhood respecting the Fairy grandmother was half so overpowering and surprising as the contents of this posthumous letter. Part of it ran thus: "I am • seventy-five years old—it is the age when most people require rest, and something tells me that the rest will soon come for me. You, Ursula, pust be of age; your brother a little more than twolrears younger. I have very important reasons for address- ing myself to you in preference to that brother, partly because I believe the day is coming when women will be no longer kept down, but will come into their natural birthright like men, so that the influence of women may regenerate and purify the race; and partly because you as a little child touched my heart as no one else could touch it. It would have been useless to try and help you while your father was living ; to do so would only have been to supply fresh fuel for those vices which were consuming him body and soul. Few women have more reason than 1 have to cease to believe in men. My grandmother was rich, and well descended; my grandfather did his best to dissipate her property. The ruin which he began ' my father might have completed, had not my mother ' been early widowed. In spite of these warnings I, her only child, married, as she did, a tyrant andruffian, with whom I quarrelled, and from whom the law granted me a merciful separation just before the birth of your mother. All my hopes centred in that daughter, for as my son (who was a few years older than she was) grew up, he did credit to the noble traditions of his family, wasting in his foolish extravagance the pro- perty which I still had left, and which would have been absolutely frittered away if it had been vested in him as the only son and first-born of my children. But, fortunately for us all, some foresight hit been exercised by others who came before us. "The property, which had been for many years in the line of female descent, did not necessarily pass to those who had already shewn their desire to deprive us of it. The conditions of Inheritance not being in the direct male descent enabled me again to leave it to my daughter—the , delicate little girl before whose birth I had suffered , so much. I sacrificed myself to her, and owing to my devoted care she grew up not only beautiful but fairly strong in health. -Still the same curse de- scended on me, still I was to suffer through the cruelty of men. My tears and entreaties availed me nothing, the advice which I attempted to give was only received with scorn. In a word, your poor mother deserted me for another scoundrel who, when hb found that he had Married a dowerless girl after all, deserted her in his turn, with as little affection for her as she had shewn for me—such was the speedy retribution she brought upon herself. After that your mother fell ill and died, as you already know, which simplified matters a little, and released her from a bondage worse than death. So long as your father lived I dared do nothing for you, nor would I ven- ture at my death to leave any money to your brother. I could not, in good conscience congratulate your mother on the birth of a boy, who might inherit the evil tendencies of two generations of men. I look upon him as doomed, but my only hope of averting such doom is to commend him to the • care of a sister to your care, and leave such property as I have left to you, with the proviso that you should return to England at once and take possession of St. Agatha's Manor. You seemed to admire the old house and the adjacent estate in your childhood--I must entreat you to do your best for it and the land still. "One other alternative must be explained; I have mentioned it in my will. I have already alluded to the fact that I too had a son, older than your mother. Public rumour declared that he was legally my heir, and, not content with one fiction, it trebled my fortune, with his consequent expectations from me. He chose 'to listen to public rumour rather than to me, and insisted on his right to keep up the reputation for hospitality on which his father had prided himself. Happily for himself ,he never married, but when I told him I did not choose to have my property squandered he left me in sudden anger and went to Australia. I have never heard from him since, and often my heart has yearned over him. If he had lived I should have written to him rather than to you, but though I have advertised for him and made constant inquiries, all my efforts to trace him have hitherto proved futile. Should it be possibla for this uncle of yours ever to return and put in a claim for the property, and should that claim be established, you must return the greater part of the property to him. He will be bound by an important clause left in my will to provide for you and your brother if he should still be living. Ido not think, however, that there is the slightest cause to be afraid of this. He was not all bad, and he may have reformea in the course of years. Yet his re-appearance would make your position difficult. Have courage to devote your efforts to your brother. Let him prove that there is one man who can live down evil report and. rise superior to the traditions of an unhappy family." The brother and sister looked at each other when they had finished reading this strange letter. Rey. mend stamped his foot impatiently. "It is the letter of a mad-woman, but we had bettei not say she was mad. Let us bum the rubbish ' or trample it beneath our feet," he said, with de- clamatory energy worthy of an acclimatised French- man, "it reflects on those to whom we owe our twine." T. lie bells of St. Medard rang out suddenly on the clear air, and,eith a quick revulsion of feeling Ursula burst into tears. Through the mists of years she seemed to see again a pale face and hear sad words which for the first time she understood. "No, Peggy, I must do as niy conscience bids me; the children are my own—the only precious: things I have in this world—and she—she must do as she likes with her property." "Do you really mean," she asked, when she re- covered herself a little, "that you would have me write to the English lawyer, and refuse.this turn of the Wheel of Fortune? Will it be any good if I do ?" "Refuse it I" exclaimed the boy. "Oh, Epictetus !" His first dramatic impulse had gone. For it had been merely a dramatic impulse, and he was beginning to have a vision of all the advantages to be ensured by money. "It seems odd it should be left to you; but you are like most girls—you women like power." "Why shouldn't women like power as well as Disraeli?" she asked (Disraeli being then Prime Minister, and the first name that occurred to her). "Prime Ministers have a name." "I'll make a name." "You don't want to make yourself a name. What have women to do with names?" "I'll wait till the name comes to me," she said good-humouredly (they wee used to this sort of banter one with the other). "I couldn't be happy if I were not of use in the world, and now I'll have some chance." Her eyes glittered. "It is you who shall have the name. lam only a common-place creature, but you shall study and work. for it" The idea did not seem to take. He shook his head. His only desire had been for such knowledge as could help him to secure the good things in life ; he had never thought of valuing knowledge or doing any- thine for its own sake. "1 thought you wanted to do something, and that I was to help you," she said, a little disappointed. "I shall be able to help you finely now." " Thet is the worst of it. Seems to me our 'careers' must give way to the larger designs of Providence," rejoined the lad with an alacrity which was not quite natural. It seemed as if he were hiding some regret from his sister. Raymond, you are hardly glad," she said, with quick intelligence, "but this money will be for you. .It is a mere farce pretending to leave it to me. I : always wanted to shew them that you were worth something—and—and to be of some use myself. It's all that makes life dear to me," said the girl, still musing. He knew it was her way, and did not even ask her why she should care so much about him, but made an effort to rouse himself, and appear thoroughly pleased. For to set to work when they had come into money would be too -horribly disgusting. The thing to do was to have a spree on the strength of it instead of adjourning to their work. They knew all the places within a certain radius of Paris, and could take the train to any part of the suburbs to discuss the strange thing that had happened to them, and decide what sten to take next beneath the pure air of heaven. Ursula could buy a new trimming for her hat ; and as for Raymond, he could go at 'once to a barber and have his hair cropped. He wore it at present thick and long, thrown back from his fore- head so as to give him something of a leonine aspect, and, as he remarked, it was necessary to thin the plantation. Afterwards they returned to a tea a l' Anglaise, for they were extravagant that day, as well as capricious and excited. Raymond deprecated the possible dulness of prolonged sojourn at St. Agatha's, and suggested Homburg for the water cure, with a recollection of rouge-et-noir. And Ursula, whose temper was on the surface, and who was too quick, to be always smooth, reproached him with the wickedness of hankering after gaming tables. This quick discovery of his motive silenced him. It was as if all their ideas had to be melted down
ii

and re-cast, for the dash ot tionemianism which WO so congenial to them could not be consistent with their grandmother's letter. Both in their secret hearts owed a grudge to the grandmother, and by' the next morning even the idea of the fortune began to pall upon them like a novel opened with expecta- tion, which becomes a nuisance when looked at a second time. "There's Louis Grandet," said Raymond, slowly, when Ursula talked of setting off in a few days for England. tought of

div.p: :now we nev,

'Well, but you marrying." Raymond whistled. "That was when you could not do it, but now lirrx can you tell? He may get an inkling of all this. And as for you, don't you boast of the hardness of your heart. You are just the sort of girl to rush from one extreme to another. One day we shall have you head over ears in love," The girl was half inclined to accuse her brother Of being coarse. "How can you talk so—when you have never cared for anyone yourself? Are we not, both of us, much better as we are ? " The lad did not whistle again. He looked out of thewindow at the roofs of the houses sparkling in the sunshine, "They say it is always foggy in England." Neither had liked to speak of the insinuations Di Mrs. Maclurchan's letter. But it is doubtful if th° fortune were making either of them happier. (To be continued.)

THE COUNTY COUNCIL. The Chairman remarked that on the previous day thert was laid before the Runcorn bench of magistrates a letter from the Clerk of the Peace at Chester respectlai the Local Government Act. The Runcorn Union was present one district, but this district would have to divided inte electoral districts, and in accordance with resolution passed by the magistrates at the July Quarn Sessions the Runcorn Bench desired the Runcorn Bli,r`' Sanitary Authority to frame a scheme for sub-diviot the Union. He gave notice that at the next meeting should move the appointment of a committee for ta'' purposes of this order. THE NUISANCE INSPECTOR AND THE AGENT TO NORTON ESTATE. 112ECE REJECTION OF THE FISHERIES TREATY: PRESIDENT CLEVELAND'S MESSAGE. WASHINGTON, SATUBDAY.—In the Senate, yesterday, Mr. Hale declared the President's message was a des- perate attempt to recover lost ground, Mr. Sherman concurred, but urged that reciprocal rights should be in. slated upon. Primal:m.l,sta, Sotrnay.--Mr. J. G. Blaine made an important speech at Lewiston on Saturday evening. The City Hall was packed with 3,000 people. Mr. Blaine, referring to "”nsident Cleveland's message on retaliation. said: '" Wi; ;di due respect to the President, I must say that, considering all the circumstances, it is the mos! extraordinary document ever sent from the White House tn the capitol. Why should the railways of the Hnited States, that annually transport 50,000,000 dole. worth of Canadian goods in transit, be deprived of their business and 'endure large loss on account of the sudden Whim of the President? Why should thetransit from Detroit to TtuTfttio and New York over both American and'Oartadian tines of rail be suspended when it has no 'relation 'whttever to the .fishery 'question? Having for three :years offered to waive the 'rights of the fishermen and thenational dignity at the same time, the 'President desires now to cross to the other side of the question -.lncl out-Herod Herod in his demands for redress." 'ln reply to a suggestion that he should 'give an e:c• Vression of his views on the subject of the rejection of 'the American Fisheries Treaty, Mr. Chamberlain has 'telegraphed to a correspondent as follows: "I do not 'Propose to make any continent on the attion of the 'Senate, which has been long foreseen."

STANLEY'S AFRICAN EXPEDITION. Nur. DE LoiLIMA. AUG. 22.—1 t is announced from the 'Upper Congo that Major Barttelot left the camp at Zamburga on May 10th, with the object of joining Mr. Stanley. It was Major liarttelot's intention to follow Stanley's march step by step. Up to the end of June the camp at Zamburga had heard no news of Stanley. SPANISH FORTIFICATIONS. MADRID. SIINDAY.—'Since the beginning of the reign of the late King Alphcrnso the Spanish 'Government has been slowly spending several millions sterling on the fortifications of the Pyrennean frontier provinces of Catalonia, Aragon, Navarre, and Guipur.coa. Forts and redoubts commanding all the passts and railways are, being constructed. Large citadels are being built at Pamplona, San Sebastian, Confranc, and several towns whose present defences could no longer withstand modern artillery. These fortifications, with the network of railways converging from the interior of Spain towards the northern provinces. would permit of the Madrid Government easily concestrating 150,000 men to Oppose an invasion or to play an important part in any European war by a demonstration on. the Pyrenees Queen Christina has just presided at the military cere- mony of hoisting the Royal ensign on the first fortress completed. This is built on San Marcos Mount, between San Sebastian and the French frontier.

GREAT FIRE AT HAMBURG : SIX PERSONS BURNED TO DEATH. BERLIN, MONDAY —The large shipyard Arid wharf of Messrs. Blehm and Voss, at Hamburg, was the scene late last night of a disastrous fire, which almost destroyed the whole of the premises. The damage is very great. Fully a quarter of a mile of houses at Steinwood are in ashes. Six persons were burnt to death, and many others were injured. The damage is estimated at severa' million marks.

SEVERE FIGHTING IN EGYPT. MORE THAN 100 DERVISHES KILLED. A Cairo correspondent says :—A determined, attack 'was made on Wednesday by the dervishes upon the Fort of Khormoussa, which they captured. Troops were at once sent from Wady Haifa. After severe fighting they recaptured the fort. The loss of the enemy was more than 100 men. The Egyptians lost 16 men killed and two officers and 27 men wounded. The force of the dervishes is estimated at 600 men. TRAGEDY IN AMERICA.—EIGHT PERSONS STABBED_ TO DEATH. . ,

The steamer Arizona, which arrived at Queenstown on Wednesday with American despatches, brought particu- lars of a terrible tragedy which occurred at Prairie Centre, Ottawa, Illinois, on the 19th inst., res.ulting in the death of eight -young men. A ball was being held in a house at Prairie Centre, when at midnight two Young men fought about a partner. The men present took sides. Knives were, freely used, and eight persons were stabbed to death.

HEIRESS. °star litoellet, a Grerman, was charged on remand at tow-street, on Monday, with the abduction cif a young American heiress, named Eliza Elias, from Gertnany.—Mr. Mead' prosecuted, and Mr. St. John Wontner defended.— Mr. lindenneyer, of the New York bar, deposed that he was the legal adviser to the young lady's deceased 'father, who left he: about £40,000. In Jul last witness went to Cassel, in Germany, and had interviews with The prisoner with reference to Miss Elias. Prisoner 'called on witness, and said he wanted to marry Miss Elias, and asked what "the trouble" was. Witness said, "A great many. In the first place, the air is only 16, and none of her guardians will consent to her marriage at so early an age." Prisoner asked witness if he had seen her lately. Be replied that he had net seen her since she was a child. 'Prisoner said she was unusually well grown. Witness told the prisoner that the girl's mother objeated. and that. since he (witness) had been to Cassel he had made 111qt:ries, and found that prisoner was engaged to anothergirl, and had had illegitimate children by other women. Another reason was that he had taken Miss Elias Trona her home without her mother's consent, Pri- sorter 'ltt first said he did not know where she was, but ' afterwards admitted that be knew. He declined to say where. but asked if he did so whet witness would do to- wards forwarding the marriage. Witness said if he as- certained that she wished to marry the prisoner he would sen/ther to school until she was 18, when he would ask her-again. The prisoner made an appointment to meet witrias at Frankfort, but did not do so, and witness pro- ceeded to London, where he made inquiries, with the resalt that a warrant was granted, and the prisoner was arrested at Queenstown. 1113 was travelling with another person's passport. Witness asked wily he persisted in fatting that he was not Moeller. He replied that he bid net think anyone would be able to identify him. Witnest- 'observed that he had passed as Mr. Bulliman, and the lady as his wife. Witness asked if they were married, -and the prisoner replied in the negative. He said he had come to England to get rnarried.—lt having been staved ' that the German Government Untended applying for the prisoner's extradition, Mr. Bridge ordered -a further re- ' mend.
MURDER OF A FATHER, AND SUICIDE:

A HORRIBLE TRAGEDY. A shocking affair at Surbiton on Sunday night has caused great excitement. At No. 13 in St. James's-road resided Major Hare, a retired army officer, and a gentle- man highly respected in the locality. It appears that his second son, Gordon Hare, had for some years past caused considerable trouble and anxiety to 'his 'parents. who on more than one occasion had in consequence of his bad habits, furnished him with funds to leave the country. He invariably came back after a lapse bf time. and caused disturbances at his father's residence. About eighteen months or two years ago, upon returning from Australia, his conduct was so violent towards`his father that the latter was reluctantly compelled to charge him before the Kingston county justices, and the son went to prison in default of finding sureties for good be- haviour. On Sunday evening, in the absence of‘tbe major, who was at church, the son in unestion unexpectedly called at No 13, and asked to see his father. TIP was refused admission—so it is said—by his mother, and went away. A few minutes before eight o'clock he returned to the house, and stood on the steps leading to the front door, apparently waiting for the approach of 'Major Hare. As soon as the latter entered the front gate two revolver shots were heard, shortly followed by a third. rlnspectin Thurnby and Police-constable Butcher were ..quickly the spot, and a shocking sight met their 'view. Major Hare was found just inside the gate, whilst the son was lying across the steps. 'rho father was dead and the son, who had placed the revolver in his own mouth and discharged it showed some signs of life, and 'was promptly removed by the police to the Surbiton Cottage Hospital, directly opposite. Dr. Coleman, of Surbiton, was sum- moned. The father was about 63, and the•son about 35. The son had openly threatened his father, and when he left prison on the occasion referred to above he declared that he would shoot his father because of the proceedings he had taken. As the dreadful news spread, a large , number of persons gathered in the neighbourhood, and watched .the villa near which the tragedy had' been enacted, and much sympathy was expressed for the re- ls'tiveg of the deceased major. On Tueirlay, Mr. Hicks held an inquest-Mettle Cottage Hospital, Surbiton, concerning the deaths Of Thos. Hare, retired major, and Gordon Horace Hare, the victims of the tragedy which occurred at 13, St. .lames-road,' Sur- biton, on Sunday evening. The jury, after hearing the evidence, which was of a sad nature, found -that` Major Hare was wilfully murdered by Gordon Hare,who after- wards committed suicide whilst in a state .of unsound mind.

SHOCKING BALLOON DISASTER--A VETERAN AERONAUT RILLED.—,OTHER -PER- SONS INJURED. . On Monday evening, about six o'cloek. Mr.. Simmonds. the well-known aeronaut, while descending in'hiS balloon at Wickham Bishops, near Witham, Essex, met with an accident which resulted fatally a few `hours later. Mr. Simnaonds was accompanied by two gentlemen, named Myers and Field, the latter of whom received a compound fracture of the thigh, and the former, although rendered unconscious for a time, escaping apparently,-withcut any serious injury. On each Monday for some weeks past balloon ascents have been made by Mr. Simmorids from the grounds of the Irish Exhibition at 'Olympia, and recently a determination has been expressedto complete an aerial journey to Vienna, a fee of five guineas being asked from those who wished to accompany Mr. Sim- mends in his attempts to reach that city. Mr.-Sim- mends has on more than one previous ()cession successfully crossed to the Continent, and singUlarly enough, in these journeys he has almost always selected as his starting-point Maldon, only three Miles from the Place where on Tuesday he met with the accident resulting in his death. In March, 1882, be started from Maldon with Col. Brine, and then, owing to the -collapse of his balloon, narrowly escaped drowning in mid-Channel, being rescued with his companion by a passing vessel. Laser in the same year he successfully crossed from Maldon to Arms, and in the following year, accompanied by Sir Claude oe Crespigny, he, again starting from Malden, succeeded in descending safely ftt Oudekerk, near Flushing. In 1883, also, he crossed "with Mr. Stna le from Hastings to Cape La Hogue. Another balloon trip taken by Sir Claude de Crespigny, whose residence is also close to the scene of on Tuseday's mishap, with Mr. simmonds was unfortunately attended by an accident, Sir Claude breaking his leg in the descent. The ascent on Monday was made shortly after four e'clock. There was a strong south-west wind blowing, and it appears to have been a most enjoyable trip until the aeronaut decided to descend. • The locality was everything that could be desired for descending, and .verything seemed all right until the grappling irons cauht in one of three elm ties, and Mr. Simmonds endeavoured to come to earth outside then. The bal- loon unfortunately came down with a hump, land in , going up again struck a tree violently. The Silk burst with a loud report and became detached from the car, which again came to the ground with such terrible force as to smash it almost to atoms Several persons who witnessed the unfortunate descent were lulckly on the spot. Mr Gutteridge, surgeon, of !dat- ion, soon arrived and pronounced Mr Simmonds's ease hopeless, the base of the brain being fractured. As pre- - viously stated. Mr. Field sustained a broken thigh, hut Mr. Myers escaped with a severe shaking. Mr.. iimmonds lingered unconscious until nine o'clock, when the doctors pronounced life to be extinct, the cause of death being concussion of .the brain. This was the 11-95th ascent made by the deceased ieronaut, and his experience extended over a period of 30 years. Four of his ascents were made in the United States, six in India, and one in Egypt. Five times Mr. ,iiturnonds crossed the Channel. Of his Channel journeys two .were to France, one to Holland, and one was across the Irish Channel from Preston to Dublin. Amongst ->ther,journeya which Mr. Sim moods made was one from i3wansea to Simonsbath, in Devonshire, which was the place of his birth: and the deceased was fond of men- tioning this fact, which he regarded as a happy augury of his career in the profession he had chosen. Mr. Pullman, secretary of the Balloon Society, in an interview with a representative of the Central News. on Tuesday, said • I filled Mr. Simmorids' balloon for him on Monday, and was present at the start. I put the car on myself,and saw that the proper amount of ballast and sun- dries were•put in. I also worked the valve, and saw that it was in proper order. The grapnel irons and ropes were of the very best material; and I did not consider that any risk was run. Sirnmonds told me, before starting, that he intended to cross the North Sea. So far as the accident is considered, I do not think it would nave happened if Simmonds had had a basket- ear, which would have rebounded from the tree. I was one of the deceased's pupils, and have made a number of ascents with him, without any casualty. A telegram from Maiden states that Messrs. Myers and Field are both lying at the King's Head inn. where they were removed after the acci- dent. They are progressing as favourably as can be expected. The disaster has caused considerable excite- ment in the locality, and the wisdom of attempting to descend in the neighbourhood of large trees is much questioned.

A GLOOMY OUTLOOK FOR AGRICULTURISTS.—Heavy rain took :place on Tuesday in the midland, eastern, and southern counties, doing immense damage to crops. The prospects for agriculturists were gloomy, but after yes- terday's deluge they appear to be in many districts hopeless. In Derbyshire quantities of hay have been swept away, the river Derwent rising several feet in a few minutes. Harvesting operations, which had been begun in parts of Lincolnshire and other eastern dis- tricts, are completely stopped.

THE LIVERPOOL CORPORATION WATERWORKS DISPUTE. —HEAVY DmeacFs.—The most celebrated dispute in the engineering world has just been decided by arbitration. Mr. Hawkesley, the famous engineer, who undertook for the Liverpool Corporation to carry out the Vyrawy water scheme, at a cost of one million, had a dispute with the Corporation, in consequence of the interference of their local engineer. For a breach of his contract he has just recovered £35,000, the amount of his claim for re- muneration, based on payment by commtission. The arbitrator was Mr, Bosanquet,
