div.head: DOUBLE EXECUTION AT DTTIMING-
div.p: DOUBLE EXECUTION AT DTTIMING-
II A M.

The twcrtrien, Jones and Daniels, who were sentenced to deathat the recent Birmingham assises—the former for the murder of a child of -a married woman, with whom he had been living at Aston ; and 'the latter for the murder of a girl named 'Hastings, whom he had been courting, at Birmingham—ware executed, on 'Tuesday morning,- at eight o'clock. at the borough gaol. "Berry was the executioner. The scene of 'the exeeetion and theMcaffold were exactly the same ms those ,itt the first execution at Winsen 'Green, three 'years. ago. Thi scaffold was erected in EL smell outbuilding, in the'front of thesouthern wing of the gaol, andmot more than SD yards from the cells which the men had occupied. The platform was on the level of the ground, in the.centre cif a small brick-walled apartment. Since theircoridemnna- tionAhe culprits had paid great attention to the minis- trations of the prison chaplain, and had expressed con- trition for their crimes. They received fareviell visits from their friends on Saturday. The chaplain remained with the men until they retired trerest at-a late 'hour on Monday. Both slept well, rose before-six-a.m.. yester- day, and washed and dressed themselves. They partook heartily of breakfast of bacon and eggs. The chaplain visited them again before seven o'clock,andrematned to the close. They were fully 'resigned 'to their fate. Shortly before eight o'clock Berry visited the cells, and pinioned both men. They walked firmly,,and without the slightest assistance, to-the scaffold; and :death was almost instantaneous, Jones's 'body twitching convul- sively for a few moments. Jones weighed'9Bt. 121 b., and was allowed a drop of fift. 6in., and Daniels, 'being lOst. 2113., had a 6ft. drop. Thera was a large crowd outside.

div.head: WATERLOO BALL.
div.p: THE WATERLOO BALL.

Sir William Fraser writes to 7he Times to may that he has identified the room in which the ball was given at Brussels by the Duchess of Richmond the night before the battle of Quarte Bras. Sir William,says "Some time before leaving England 1 conversed-with a lady who danced with my father at the ball, and whO has, as you will see from her name, which '1 enclose. theliest means of knowing where it took place. This Iddy, giving me at the same time a list of those Who were 'invited, told me that Lord Byron's allusion .to -"that high hall" :vas "nonsense," She added that the billtook place, not in the Duke of Richmond's 'house; but. in a coach- maker's depot, a low-roofed room at' the • rear of it, the street being named Rue •dc la Illanchisserie. I made many inquiries in England and in Brus,sels. No one knew anything of the place,tut all agreed that the scene of the ball had been frequently sought without success, and that it no longer existed. 'I atlast ascertained that the site of the Duke of Richmond's house was now covered by a large hospital in .the Rue des Cendres. I visited the hospital, and. one Of the nursing sisters politely pointed out a wing Which 'bad formed part of the Duke's house. T ergamined •the gardeM behind this wing; neither in this nor in the building itself was there any trace of a ball-room. '1 Observed above the wall of the hospital the roof of ahigh building, and inquired what it was. The si.ster replied that it was the brewery of the Rue de la Blanchisserie. 'TWalked round to this street, and was informed by the proprietor of the brewery that he knew nothing on the subject. After some conversation I asked if 'he could tell me of whom big father purchasedlthe property ;he replied of a coach- builder named Van. ASCI9. I inquired if the coachbuilder had a depot. "Yes, a very large, one; it is. now my granary." Re then took me up to the first floor and I found myself in the room, the ,remembrance ,of which will live so long as the English language. It is 120 ft. long, 54ft. broad, and about I.3ft. high, the floor smooth enough to be danced on .to-night. This room,answers precisely to the description given to me. 'lt is imme- diately in the rear of the Duke of Richmond's ',house, it is in the street named, it belonged in 1815 to a coach- builder, and it is capable of hrilding at least 400 persons. Ido not think further proof . can be required. I have the permission of the proprietor to give his name, V. Vaginderachter, Brasseur, Rue de la Blanchisserie, 40 at 42. Be most courteously added that he wouldvbe glad to show the room to visitors."

div.head: END OF THE RACE TO EDINBURGH.
div.p: THE END OF THE RACE TO EDINBURGH.

As we ventured to anticipate -some time back, this week is to see the last, for the present at all events, of the race to Edinburgh. From -Saturday next the ~extra expresses will be withdrawn 'br both cornpanies, and the journey will in future be performed in 8i hours, -or at what, after the experience of the iast few weeks, must, we suppose, be called the moderato-and reasonable speed bf 47 miles an hour, lunch and ell other stoppages in- cltided. But in return for this two other accelerations are premised. The tip train from Perth, now leasing at II 45 cm., will leave at 8 30, form a connection 'with the 10 o'clock express from Glasgow, and arrive in London at seven o'clock, a whole hour eatiler than at present. The 10 o'Cleel up train from Edinburgh will run in the same time as the cor- responding down train—will arrive, that is, at Eustom at 630 instead of 7. But a glance at "Bradshaw" Will show that the important LiverpoOl and Manchester e:: - press arrives at that time at present. And the method in which these rival claims have been adjusted is ncrt a little interesting. The layerpool portion of this express has grown so heavy that it is now to be given a train all to itself. This will leave Liverpool 'fiva minutes earlier than at present, and reach 'Euston ten-minutes earlier- -6 20 instead of 6 30. 'lle Manchester-portion, which is much lighter, will start, as at present. at 2 15, but at Crewe it will join not the 'Liverpool but the Edinburgh: carriages—another light train—and so arrive in London' at its ordinary hour. One remark is obvious. A corn-, pany that ventures to propose to join theteenly-competi-j, tive Manchester traffic on to an express-that starts more than 200 miles further down the line has given hostagesi. to fortune in the matter of punctuality: but as these + Scotch expresses this summer have rumwith the clock- work regularity of the old mail coaches, no doubt the authorities have grown confident. Moreover, as no pas- sengers are admitted at intermediate stations, no sudden ' inrush of mountainous luggage can occur to cause un- expected delay. For the present. then, .it appears that the East Coast have accepted their rivals ao their equals to Edinburgh. Perhaps they are only reserving their energies for the next round, but perhaps also they have been partly influenced by the fact that, if they claimed -to be allowed to be a quarter of an . hour faster, it could be but little use to them. For the fast Manchester ex- press is due into King's Cross at 6 15 pen., and while to push it on one side would be most undesirable. to attach it-to the 10 o'clock up from Scotland wouldise simply impossible.—Timat.

div.head: ATLANTIC RACE.
div.p: THE ATLANTIC RACE.

The victory in the race which was not a racebetween the Cunard liner the I.lm bria and the Inman steamer the City of New York rests with the older boat. The two steamers left New York on Saturday week within an hour and twenty minutes of each other. The 'Umbria reached Queenstown oirSaturday morning, covering the distance of 2,883 miles in 6 days, 10 hours, awl 25 minutes. The City of New York did not arrive until yesterday, having made the passage of 2,811 miles from Sandy Hook to Itoche's Point in 7 days, 12 hours, and 23 minutes. On the whole the weather was good; and it is ,evident from the log of the Umbria that she was run at a high speed throughout. On five successive days she ran respectively 433 miles, 445, 441, 438, and 436 miles. On the other hand, the City of New York was run at a lower speed than on her outward passage, and, according to her log, the highest speed attained-in one day was '376 miles. And yet, remarks the Leeds Mercury, the victory of the Umbria is not so decisive as it appears to be. In her outward passage the new steamer ran 446 miles in one day, and exceeded 420 miles on four successive days. Taking a single day's record, she has beaten the highest speed made by the Umbria on her homeward passage, and that under circumstances when her engines were not fully tested. As to the homeward passage of the City of New York, it is evident she was kept within her power. In fact, her port engines were stopped three times, and her starboard engines twice, showing that the object of those in Command was to test her experimentally, to see how she would behave under certain conditions. She has, so far, behaved well ; and it would certainly he prematare to conclude that she has been beaten. Tde race, in truth, has yet to be run.

Ferguson, of St. Leotards, accompanied by Mr. Bull and aboatman,went, sailing from Hastings on Thurscluy, when a squall cap- sized the yacht, and Mr. Ferguson and the boatman were drowned. GREAT FLOODS IN SOL7II WALES. MOTO disastrous floods are reported from South Wales. At Builth, the Wye rose 20 feet, flooding the market buildings and the lower part of the town, and stopping railway traffic. At Llangammarch the suspension bridge was carried away and an hotel was flooded out, the furniture in the lower rooms being washed away. The suspension bridge at Llanynys was also carried away. Cattle have been f.h•owned, and the damage to crops is enormous.

AremarkableattaCk by a somnambulist is reported from Pontypridd. A compositor named Jones was going home at-night-when he was met by another man, named O'Leary, who hit him a tremendous blow beneath the chin, knocking him down, and then walked away. The man was brought before the local justices, and he de- clared he was a somnambulist, and only came to himself in the police cell. He remembered nothing of the occur- rence. The magistrates, Leheving the man's story, die- missed the ease. THE BOATING ACCIDENT 'AT DOOGLAS.—ANOTHER BODY RECOVIMED.—On dunday afternoon a body was washed ashore at Pcrrt Soderick. The features were so decom- I posed as tote unrecognisable, but from the clothing the corpse is supposed to be that of George Fletcher, Moss Side, Manchester, drowned on July 2'i by the upsetting of a rowing boat off Douglas Head. thf the two others, Henry Kelly and John Davy, drowned at the same time. SIIICIDIVIN DESPERATION.—A painful impression has ' been produced in New York br a melancholy occurrence in the Central Park, where the lifeless body of a young lady was 'found, and examination has shown that death resulted from poisoning by morphine. She has been identified as Christian Baird, daughter of Mr. J elm Baird, of the Register Office, Edinburgh. It seems that the young lady came' here as a governess, and, being out of employment, committed suicide in desperation. FRIGHThIfI, DRAT'H ON BOARD A WARSHIP. A tragic death has if,ust been . reported from H.M.S. Carysfort, in the Mediterranean. Two seamen were undergoing punishment in the cells, and the corporal of the guard should have visited them each hour, to -see that all was right. He went at two a.m., and found one prisoner dead, and*the other insensible. The two cells in question are situated in the hotest part of the ship, close to the engine, ond below all decks. Death was due to suffocation. It is stated that considerable developments of the London arreMorthLWestern Railway Company's under- taking are proposed on the Dee and on the line from Chester to'Holyheal Mostyn has been visited by high officials of the company with a view to estimating the suitability of the -place for tho formation there of a railway port; the accommodation at Chester is being greatly extended ;”and an additional double line of rails to Holyhead' from that city is in contemplation.

DARING HIGHWAY ROBBERY.—About midnight on Saturday a milkseller named Goliath was driving home with another man, when they were suddenly attacked by five men near Sundorne Castle, Shrewsbury. The men demanded their money, a considerable sum beingin the possession Of Goliath, but he managed to make his escape, and, -runtiing towards the town, obtained assist- ance. On this return -the other man, Perkin, was found lying on the.road "insensible. 'Be was conveyed to tha Infirmary, where' he lies in a precarious condition. The highwaymen ,escaped. MURDER AND SUICIDE AT PORTSMOUTH. Thomas Jones, pensioner from the 'Royal Marine Artillery, living in St. Marfs-street,Tortsmouth, murdered his wife iwin afterwards cut his own throat in the back room of hic house on Saturdaynight. Jones, who was a barber, had been seperated ,from his wife for some time, but the latter returned home on Saturday night. and the neigh- boors heard a'quarrel. Everything being quiet the Col- , lowing morning.,„,the police were fetched, and forced the 'door, finding Jones and his,wife with their throats ter- -ribly gashed and dead. SCHOOL 6. —Cardinal Manning, preaching on Sunday at the Roman Catholic Cherch, in Maiden4lame, Covent-garden, said that they had lately heard a great deal about free schools; but whilst it was stated that the remission of fees in the 'Board Schools of the Metropolis was en an average 11 percent., not less than 20 percent. of the children at- tending the Catholic Schools in his diocese had their school fees remitted on the ground of inability to pay even the small weekly sum charged for the purpose. After all, a god home was the best school, and he earnestly besought parents and guardians to set an ex- ample of sober, honest, and virtuous lives to the little ones of their households, and do all in their power to preserve them from the perils and ,contaminating in- fluences of the busy streets and thoroughfares of Londm. Miss °VALERO]) ON TRE DESTRUCTION OF GRAIN.— Mies writes to Cheshire agriculturists re- specting the very general and severe attacks on erain cropsin the•county by myriads of insects. So fearful is theinroad that the crop deficiency is estimated at 33 per cent. Misq Ormerod save the insects on the wheat are plant lice, which do mischief in all stages by drawing away the sap with their suckers, and also •by the great number of holes that these suckers make. In their young state these grain plant lice more especially attack the upperpart of the blade, which accounts for the dis- colours:lion produced as the plant hardens. They take what is soft,enough for them to live 'upon. It is espe- cially with•regard to attacks of this sort that it is im- portant not to allow the martens and the swallows to be driven away, as isso much the case in some districts, by the sparrows. The martens and swallows clear myriads of insects ,constantly, and if they are allowed to be driven away we shall suffer woefully.

A ROMANTie AFFAIR.—A correspondent writes that very romantic incident is reported from Chiswick, from which it appears that about two years ago, the wife of an hotel-keeper. Tesidelt in that part of the metropolis, and mother of four young children, suddenly dis- appearci from her home, and about the same time a gen- tleman, of welt-to-do alrcumstances, and believed to have become acquainted with the landlady over the hotel bar, was missing Also, it being surmised, which afterwards proved tote true, that they had eloped to- gether. The husband, finding that his fair partner did not return, sought a divorce from his faithless spouse, end succeeded in cititaininFthe usual decree nisi. After the lapse of two years, during which interval the gentle- man died, leaving tlierunaway wife his fortune, by will, it is said, of £14,000., she revisits her husband, with her old Lleve returned, and the money to recommend her, and asks his forg -reness for her past misconduct, which he grants, ard r ceives her back into her former home, the barrier to their residing, together, owing to the legal pro- ceedings taken after her hasty departure, being only sur- mounted by re-marriage. JUDGE FIDGETER AND TRAVELLING DRaYEas.—Since Judge Hughes has been a County Gault Judge he has had considerable difficulty in dealing with debts con- tracted by women through travelling drapers, commonly known as " Scotchmen." In a case before him at Stock- port, where a wife owned to getting goods unknown to her husband from a " cotchman," and then pawning the articles for drink, his Honour observed that he had been in communication with several County Court judges in reference to this class of debt. He found that it was usual in some circuits for the draper to give . . . . .

. - notice to the husband when the wife was served with goods, and he wished that practice obtained in his circuit. It might be a convenience for working people to get goods in this way, but it gave unscrupulous women an opportunity of getting their husbands into . . . ,

debt. A case that had gene to the House cf Lords gave him discretion in the matter, and in this case he should not make an order for the husband to pay. Judgment would be against the draper, but no costs would be allowed. These drapers must give husbands notice of their trading with the wives.

div.head: DEATH OF SIR JOHN ROSE.
div.p: DEATH OF SIR JOHN ROSE.

1 Sir John Rose, formerly Finance Minister of Canada. died suddenly, on Saturday, while in the act of firing at a stag in the Otilre of Portland's deer forest in Caithness. Mr. C. F. Cornish writes as follows :—The sad death of Sir John Rose, while in the act of firing at a stag, is not so strange as may at first appear. The intense nervous excitement which often arises when the moment comes for taking aim at a deer or chamois is well known to hunters of big game. By the Americans it is called " buck fever," a phrase said to have been originally Ger. man. It is more particularly likely to happen when, after a long day's stalking or driving, a deer suddenly appears within easy range. In some cases it induces partial paralysis, which lasts so long as the animal remains motionless and unaware of the presence of an enemy. A well-known foreign sportsman, when waiting for deer in a drive in a Bavarian forest. saw one at some distance in the brushwood. While he paused before firing to make sure that it was a stag and not a hind there appeared, without warning or sound, within fifty yards of him, a very large stag. He eagerly raised his rifle to cover the quarry; but the moment he did so the tag became invisible, or at least he could not see it. He lowered his gun. There stood the deer asbefere. Again he raised the rifle: but his hand shook, the sight travelled all over the stag's body, and he was obliged to desist. Then the sta.' moved away. Instantly he became himself again, and fired quickly, but missed his mark. A simi- lar experience was related by a noted athlete, an old Eton cricketer and football-player, who was shooting "moufflon." After he had been climbing the mountains all day without success a ram suddenly appeared from behind a rock close to him, and though he felt 'cool enough his hand shook so that it was impossible to aim at the animal.

div.head: DEATH OF A LANCASHIRE ANTIQUARY.
div.p: DEATH OF A LANCASHIRE ANTIQUARY.

We regret to announce that on Thursday week, after a long illness, Mr. John Eglington Bailey, F.S.A., of Stret- ford, died at the age of 48, leaving a widow and four children. Mr. Bailey was a native of Warwickshire, but , came to Lancashire with his family whilst still a child, and received the rudiments of his education at Boteler's 'Grammar School, Warrington. He was destined for a !commercial career, and entered the service of Messrs. Ralli Brothers in their Manchester House, where he occu- pied a position of trust and responsibility until the breakdown of his health a couple of years ago. Whilst diligent in business, Mr. Bailey had also a passion for literature and archreology. He was a skilful and en- thusiastic phonographer, and was one of the founders of the Phonographic Union, which held its meetings in an upper I'ODM of the Mechanics' Institution. Here he rde- livered a lecture on that wise and witty Thomas Fuller, which was published in the Popular Lecturer, and be- came the nucleus of an important contribution to biographical literature. Mr. Bailey was thorough in all that he did, and several summer holidays were devoted to searching out and visiting the various places identi- fied with the career of the author of the "Worthies of England." When in 87 the "Life of Thomas Fuller, D.D.," was issued, it at once gave Mr. Bailey an acknow- ledged position in the ranks of literature, and took its place as a standard biography. After this he turned his attention to local antiquities. He edited in 1877 the "School Candidates," a curieus tract by Dr. Henry Clarke, the mathematician, of whom he wrote an excel- lent biography. He also prepared for the press a very pretty 'reprint of "Manchester al Mondo," to which he prefixed an excellent introduction. This appeared in 1880, and in the same year he started the Palatine Note Book, which continued for several years, and is a store- house of archreological information as to the past history of Lancashire and Cheshire. He was much in request as an antiquarian lecturer, and his "Old Stret- ford," ." Memorials of Gorton," and othsr pamphlets thus came into existence. He contributed to the pro- ceedings of tne Manchester Literary Club, the Lanca- shire and Cheshire Antiquarian Society, the Historic Society of 'Lancashire and Cheshire, and various other local societies. He was for several years honorary secretary of the Chetham Society, and only relinquished the positionin consequence of an illness by which he was prostrated. This was the result of an overtaxed brain and nervous system. A long holiday passed at Hastings, 'Eastbourne, and the Isle of Wight failed to restore him; but after a time he regained some of his former elasticity, and began to interest himself once more in literature. During the present year there was apparently considerable improvement, but a relapse followed, and the end came on Thursday. Besides the works we have mentioned, Mr. Bailey had made exten- sive collections for a history of English shorthand. His collection of the literature on this subject was pro- bably the completest that has ever been brought to- gether. The other contents of his large and valuable library included a lengthy series of Puritan divinity and books on general history, local typography, and English literature. He was a Fellow of the Society of Antiquaries. An incessant student, it may be feared that his devotion was sometimes excessive. All his spare hours were spent in literary pursuits, and he has often carried his work long into the night, when he ought to Lave been enjoying the repose which tired nature demands. Mr. Bailey married in 1866 the second daughter of Mr. Samuel Mills, of Ardwick, who, with four children, as we have said, survives him.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Work hse on Wednesday "morning. Present—the Rev. G. F. Roberts (chairman), Messrs. Isherwood, Darbyshire,Noisey, Jolley, T, zones, Ratcliffe, Hum- phreys, Clarke, W. Houghton, J.klloughton, Bilshall, Harrison, and' Jones • J. C. Sutton (clerk). S. Sut- ton (assistant elerk)C. 11. Ward (workhouse mas- ter), and IL M., Mines. ME HOUSE COMbIITTEE.—THE PROI/55ED EXTENSION OF
THE 'WORKHOUSE.

The House Committee recorded that Mr. Voisey had moved, and Mr.isherwood had seconded a motion to the .effect that the committee recommend that the plans then submitted byllr. Owen as full -plans of the ptp- posed workhouse mtension be accepted And forwarded icr the acceptance and approval of the, Local Govern-: Board. Mr. Ratcliffe moved, and Mr. Hibbert seconded an amendment to the effect that they do not proceed with the extension of the Workhouse till they see what was the result of the settlement of the boun- I &ay question. On being, put to the vote four voted for Mr. Ratcliffe's amendment and three for the motion, the amendment being carried.—Mr. RATCLIFFE now moved the, confumation of the minutes, and Mr. CLAILIEE secon- ded this proposal.—Mr. VOISEY contended that inasmuch as the Board had already determined that the extensions were to be made and had %instructed Mr. Owen to complete his plans, all the committee had to do was to consider whether the plans when submitted by Mr. Owen were in accordance with the resolution of the Board; but a Sec- tion of the House Committee., consisting of a large con- tingent from Newton and Earlestown, thought their business was to determine whether that extension ought to be proceeded with. It seemed to him that if the reso- lution of the Board was to be rescinded it must be rescinded by the Board itself.—Mr. RATCLIFFE said he had objected to the extensions of the Workhouse from the very commencement, and things had lately changed very considerably. Formerly they thought they should have the Union intact, but now it appeared that they were going to lose the Cheshire townships, which would be a serious item. The loss of these townships would mean about am a year. Then again, they had only at present about 312 inmates in the Workhouse, whereas they had had as many as 440 or 450. He thought the time had not yet come for the extension. He believed that during the last two winters many persons had been brought to the Workhouse through the Ship Canal, but now that the canal was in full operation these people had gone out. He suggested that the plans stand over for Six months.—The CsultnainN moved that the minutes of the House Committee be not confirmed, and that further consideration of the plans be deferred for three mcnths. —Mr. VOISEY seconded this proposal.—Mr. RATCLIFFE proposed that they be left over for four months, and Mr. J. HOUGHTON seconded this proposal, which was ulti- mately agreed to unanimously.
SCHOOL FEES.
The School Fees Committee recommended that fees had beeen allowed in 59 cases, 48 of which were old and 11 new cases.—On the motion of Mr. JOLLEY, seconded by Mr. IlamusoN, the minutes ware adopted.
VACCINATION AT EARLESTOWN.

Mr. CLARKE asked if the expenses of the Newton vac- cination officer would come before the Board that day? —The CLERK said they would not.—Mr. CLARKE said there had been a vaccination case up five times at New- ton Sessions, and then dismissed, and he was wondering who Would have to pay the expenses. The name of the man who had been summoned was Richardson, and he had a child that was under a doctor or institute at Man- chester. The case was adjourned for various reasons four different times, and at last it was dismissed.—Mr. HARRISON : Do you know what it was dismissed for ? Mr. CLARKE: It was dismissed because the child was not fit for vaccination.—The CLERK said that when an officer in the discharge of his duty institutes a prosecution clearly the expenses could not fall on the officer.—Mr. DARBYSIIIRE : The expenses would fall on the Union.— The CLERK: Yes, of course.—Mr. CLARKE said he be- lieved that Mr. Sutton had told the officer to take the case before the magistrates, and let them decide.—The CLERK said that was very likely the case. He should probably say, let the case go before the magistrates, and if the magistrates found that there was a fair answer let them dismiss it.—The matter then dropped.
THE HALF-YEARLY CONTRACTS,

It was decided that the advertisement for the half-yearly tenders for supply of goois to the workhouse Sze., should be advertised in all the local papers.—Mr. DARBY- SHIRE suggested that only tenders for English beef and mutton should be accepted, and it was agreed that the words "English-killed should be inserted in the tenders for meat.
P4DGATE SCHOOLS. The School Committee reported that the doctor had certified the health of the children at Padgate Schoels to be good. The committee also mentioned that six boys
had been sent to Grimsby on trial as fisher lads. Further reference • to this matter will be found in another column.—The minutes were confirmed.

A RTIQIITEST. A letter waOrea,d from Dr. Peacocke, inedical officer for one of the Warrington districts, asking for leave of absence from his district on account of his being about to be married. He nominated Dr. Braid as his deputy during his absence.—Mr, HARRISON: Nobody can refuse that. (Laughter.)—The application was granted.

THE BOUNDARIES QUESTION.—PROPOSED DEPUTATIONS. The Crxiix said, in reference to the boundary question, that he had mentioned at ths last meeting that the tak- ing of the Cheshire townships from the Union would mean a clear loss of about £BOO a year. That would, however, only be the actual present sum for the main- tenance of the poor, but the sum would grow. He did not hesitate to say that it might involve them in an ultimate payment of 3d in the £. (Hear, hear.) He noticed also that the Stockport Union were similarly dis- satisfied with themselves. The proposed separation of the townships was a serious blow at the Lancashire town- ships, and it behoved those townships to do their utmost Ito prevent the Union from being interfered with in the way proposed.. He could not very well advise what was best to be done, but he gathered from what had been said by Mr. Harrison that something was being done by the Warrington Corporation, and he (the clerk) should advise that Board to concur with it and give it their sup- port.—Mr. HARRISON said he might say that that Board would be invited to co-operate with the Town Council, and it was hoped that a deputation from that Board and the Town Council would proceed to London to make representation against what he did not hesitate to say' was a monstrous proposal. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. RAT-. CLIFFS suggested that the deputation should include , representatives from other bodies in the Union.—The CHAIRMAN was quite sure that any action taken by the Town Council would meet with the very hearty support of that Board.—Mr. W. HotuaTon suggested that the ' clerk might write to the overseers of the various town- ships asking them to lay the matter before the rate- payers, who, as a body, were ignorant of the change that was proposed.—The CLERK thought they might also enter into communication with the clerk to the Stockport Union. He suggested that a resolution might be passed to the effect that in the event of the Local Go- vernment Board, or the Boundary Commissioners, as the case might be, agreeing to receive a deputation from the Corporation of Warrington that Board appoint a deputation to co-operate with them.—Mr. HARRISON moved, and Mr. JOL.. LEY seconded, that a resolution to that effect be passed.—Mr. DARLITSHIRE said he believed that the rea- son why some of the inhabitants of the Cheshire town- ships wanted to be separated was that they would have less rates to pay. He had been at a great deal of troxble to obtain the amounts in the pound paid in severaltown- ships of the Runcorn Union, and he found that the rate for the half-year in that Union had been fixed at is id in the £, while in his own township ef Grappenhall it was only lid in the L. It wanted someone to enlighten the ratepayers on that particular point.—Mr. HAnrusonsaid there had evidently been some influence used in a very mysterious way, and they were endeavouring to get to know by whom that influence was used. They were en- deavouring to get to know who the deputation was, for • it was evident there had been a deputation without the other side being heard.—The annx could only say that from the very first there had been reprints of every- thing that had taken place at that Board, aud he sent ' the reprints to magistrates and others concerned. Every- thing so far as the Board was concerned had been done openly and publicly, and if there had been any meeting with the Commissioners or any other authority on that subject, and unknown to the Corporation, the Board of Guardians and the rate- payers, then, he said, there had been a grievous wrong done to them. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. W. Houoirros said he had been speaking to an influential ratepayer of Grappenhall, and he was full of repentance already. (Laughter.)—Mr HARRISON thought it was mostly a matter of sentiment—some people wanted to be considered Cheshire gentlemen.—The CHAIRMAN: I did not know that Lancashire played second fiddle to Cheshire.—The Cumx said that even some of the magistrates had not been properly considered in that matter. Taking the cases of Mr. John Rylands, Mr. Bleckley, and Mr. Z. Armitage he said that if the separation of the townships took place these gentlemen would not be permitted to be ex-officio Guardians of that Board, and could not serve en the committees to which they had given so much service. The works of Messrs. Rylands Bros., in War- rington, were assessed at £1,478.; Messrs. Armitage and Rigby's, £2,422; and The Pearson and Knowles Co., with which Mr. Bleckley was prominently connected, £4,041 10s. Taking Messrs. Rylands alone, their assess- ment for Thelwall was £740, and when they paid on this assessment their rates went in relief of their rates for the parish of Warrington. But if Thelwall be added to the Runcorn Union then Messrs. Rylands would have to pay a higher rate for Warrington. The gentlemen he had mentioned would, ho hoped, co-operate with that Board in the matter.—The resolution proposed by Mr. Har- rison was then agreed to, and the matter dropped. The relief cases were next taken.
MR. BRUNNER, M.P., ON FOREIGN WORKMEN AND TRADE UNIONISM.

Speaking at a public meeting held at Winsford on Monday evening, Mr. J. T. Brunner, MT., referred to the proceedings of the Immigration and Emigra- tion Committee, and to the statement made by Mr. John Falk that he (Mr. Brunner) was a large em- ployer of foreign labour. He found that out of '2.000 workmen at Brunner, Mond, and Company's works there were only six foreigners, and these had come from Mr. Falk's. (Laughter.) He had never in his life sent to a foreign country for a foreign workman, and he would take care that he never did. (Applause.) The reason was that Englishmen did better work and very much more of it than any other nation of workmen. (Loud applause.) His firm paid one and a half times as much wages, per day as was paid in Belgium, France, Austria, Germany, or Russia for the manufacture of the same kind of stuff, and yet the wages per ton on the stuff came to less, and this because an English- man was worth one-and-a-haif times as much an any of the foreign workmen whose countries he had •named. The solid vote to which Mr. Falk also alluded in his evidence before the Commission, and whichzonstituted the votes of two persons, would be struck off the register in deference to his (Mr. Brunnees) instructions to his agent. He would re- commend working-men to make strong their trade unions. He aid not argue that a trade union should be used asa weapon against employers; but on the other bandit should be used as a means of mutual self help. ("Hear, hear," and applause.) If they in Winsford had not got a strong union, they would suffer by it. The union which it was proposed to form amongst the employers of labour in the salt district of Cheshire would be a very strong trade union. He held that if a trade union was right under one set of circumstances it was probably right under another set of circumstances. The stronger trade unions were made the more peace and the fewer quarrels would there be between the employers and the employed. (Aptilause.)

WTAREINGTON UNlON.—Persons willing to CONTRACT for the supply of any of the undermentioned articles from Michaelmas to Lady Day next, to be delivered free of expense at the Warrington Union Workhouse, or at the Indus- trial Schools, Pallgate, at such times and in such quantities as the Board of Guardians shall direct, are requested to send in TENDERS, properly sealed, endorsed, and free of expense, addressed to the Clerk to the Guardians, before four o'clock p.m. on Tuesday, the 11th day of September instant. The following are the articles for which tenders are required : Groceries and Provisions Shoes and Clogs Beef and Mutton Glazing . 1 Joints for Officers Brushes Milk Coffins Flour and Meal %Best Oakinn Rope for picking Loaves of Bread Best Penmaenmawr Stone Beer and Porter for breaking purposes Straw and Potatoes Leather Drapery, &c. Wood for cutting into Fire- Cord and Twill wood Coal and Slack Carbolic Soap Eal thenware Samples of any of the above may he seen on application to the Master of the Workhouse, The Coal and Slack supplied must be to the satisfaction of the House and Schools Csunmit- tee The Pit and quality of Coal must be named in the Tender. Fornas of tender and full particulars as to the prob- able quantities of each article required may be obtained at the Clerk's Office.

The Guardians also invite TENDERS for PRINTING and STATIONERY, from Michaelmas, 1838, to Michaelmas, 1889. All goods under this head must be equal to sample to be seen at the Clerk's Office, where also forms of Tender, ar.c., may be obtained. Goods required from Poor Law Publishers will be obtained through the Stationery contractor. , Each tender must be made upon the prescribed form, and properly enclosed and endorsed with the name of the article tendered for. Each contractor must be prepared (if required) to enter into security for the due performance of his con- tract. 'The Guardians do not bind themselves to accept the lowest or any tender. All contract accounts will be paid quarterly.—Ny order, • JAMBS CLOWNS SUTTON, • Clerk to the Guardians. Bewsey Chambers, Warrington, August 30th. 1888.

THE EXAMINER,

tutes, and a male companion, were charged with assaulting and robbing a man in Cockhedge-lane at a late hour on the night of Thursday, June 28th, 1888. In this case one only of the prisoners was sent to gaol. The Gun Inn is not in Cockhedge- lane ; but it came out that all the lot—and a bad lot they seem to have been—had been drinking together, at the Gun Inn, on the night of the rob- bery. The Gun Inn is therefore, to say the least of it, tainted by its associates; it is not a house of which smug Respectability that goes to church and gives to churches, has any reason to be proud; it is not a house of which the license should have been renewed by the magistrates on Monday last; it is not a house that has earned a title to be en- larged or rebuilt. It were better that it should be closed, or razed to the ground. We hold that the magistrates have neglected their duty by renewing the licenses of houses of the Gun Inn type; there ought to be a reduction—a large reduction—of licensed houses in the borough; and if the Licen- sing Committee grant any new licenses, at the Ses- sions which are to be held on Monday next, they will bring further discredit alike upon the town and upon themselves.

THE insurance of children's lives is a subject which is likely to engage the attention of the Select Committee which is now inquiring into the affairs of Friendly Societies. An opinion is gaining ground in some quarters that a large number of the children of the poor are neglected, and to a certain extent sacrificed, because of the consider- able sum, in case of insurance, which is to be ob- tained at their death. There have, no doubt, been instances in which the prospect of funeral money has proved a temptation; but we believe that under the present law, restricting, as it does, the amount of insurance, they are exceedingly rare. A few weeks ago Mr. JUSTICE DAY had a case of this kind •before him, at Salisbury Assizes ; and it led him to make a strong comment on in- surance societies. "Through the instrumentality," he said, "of one of those pests of society—those deadly societies which insure children—the pri- soners found theinselves in the position of making a profit by the death of the children. They in- sured the children in one of these societies which seemed to be instituted for the destruction of life, for the •perpetration of murder." Mr. JUSTICE DAY is a judge who goes to extremes in the ex- pression of his opinion, and his language has a ten- dency, therefore, to discount itself. We regard societies which insure either adults or children as saviours rather than as pests of society, for they encourage habits of thrift and independence, and are the means of saving the rates hundreds of thoussnds of pounds per year. Insurance societies are deserving of blessing rather. than ban. They are good in themselves, but, like other good things, they may be abused. In the present state of the law, it is illegal to insure a child, under five years of age, for more than £6 ; or for more than £lO if between five and ten years of age. There is reason to believe, however, that the law is often broken, and it might be worth while to consider whether something could not be done to secure its better enforcement. The poorer class of parents know little, as a rule, about Acts of Parliament ; they insure in one society for a certain sum, and, pes- tered as they often are with insurance agents, they are induced to enter their children in a second so- ciety. They pay altogether what they be- lieve entitles them to a larger sum than £6 at death. If the child lives on to be over five years old, or over ten, they may get that larger sum; but it frequently happens by death taking place during the first five years that parents are disappointed. They find, when they counted on receiving £lO, or it may be £l5, that they can obtain £6 only—£3 from one society, and £3 from tha other. In this case the second 'payments have proved to be money thrown away. This causes so much heart-burning and bad feel- ing that an insurance society will occasionally wink at the fact that, say, £5 has been already received, and pay another £5 in contravention of the law. The remedy for this is to inflict a severe penalty upon the guilty society, for the parents, as a rule, act in ignorance. They, however, ought to know what the law is in this respect, and act within it. If they choose to violate it for the sake of a large sum at the death of a child, and then 'wilfully neglect that child, scarcely any punish- ment can be too severe for them. It has been I suggested that the law should be amended with a view to Insurance Societies taking charge of chil- dren's funerals at a fixed sum, no money being permitted to be paid to parents or guardians; but we have no sympathy with such grand- motherly legislation. It would be an insult to nine-tenths of the people who insure their chil- dren. The other tenth, wanting a little money when there is a death in the family for something beyond bare funeral expenses, would most likely cease to insure if such an extraordinary proposal were enforced. Tho law as to the insurance of chil- dren may be capable of amendment; but it cannot be amended in that direction ; and we are inclined to think the subject requires much more ventila- tion before the law can with advantage be altered in any direction.

I SHOCKING PARAFFIN LAMP FATALITY.—EIIen Birchalu, 23 years of age, wife of a day-wage man employed at Collins Green Colliery, andlivingat 501, Ashton's Green- ' lane, met with her death under shocking circumstances on Sunday. The sad occurrence is a painful Warning against a common practice of blowing out paraffinH lamps., The deceased had been in the habit of having a paraffin lamp burning all night, and did so on the Satin day night. At six o'clock on Sunday morning she got up and blew down the chimney of the lamp. An explo- sion took place, and the flames set her .night-dress on fire. Her husband at once jumped out of bed and extinguished the flames, but no before she been seriously burned about the body and arms. The husband was also badly burned. Dr. Casey was sent for, but notwithstanding every attention the poor woman died about; three o'clock in the afternoon.—An inquest on the body was held on Tuesday, when the jury returned a verdict of "Acci- dental death."

"TOUCH AND GU." Another child—a little girl—has died through illnbss brought on by eating ice cream. "Sweets to the sweet" by all means, but not when their effects are deadly.

The bad weather has caused an increase in the price of wheat; and now we have an announce- ment of a rise in the price of coal. When the Two F.'s—Food and Fuel—go up everybody has every need to practice economy.

General Boulanger was down, but he is up again. The French must have an idol—even if its face be of brass and its feet of clay. And there is always a large section of the dissatisfied, who are like the Irishman in America. He didn't know which side he was on, except that he was " agin the Government." —ls there not too much fuss being made over the failure (through disloyalty, or inability) of the Cork Band to, play the National Anthem at the Irish Exhibition? Look at the incident as we may, it is no credit to English government of Ireland that such a thing should be possible. There is a cause for the milk in the cocoa-nut even when the milk is sour.

Sullivan must look to his laurels—if he has any. ' A hard hitter has been found in Wales; he is a somnambulist, who, meeting a printer out late, "hit him a tremendous blow beneath the chin and knocked him down." Now, if he could do that, en passant, and whilst asleep, what would he do when he was awake and in deadly earnest ? Sulli- van would be nowhere—or floored.

Sir Arthur Sullivan—there is more than one famous Sullivan—has had to protest against the way in which his "Golden Legend has. been placed on the programme of the Birmingham Musical Festival,,without as much as "By your leave." The Committee may think it well that he lets them off with a protest; he might have sued them for a gross breach of the law. To put it mildly, Sir Arthur has not been well used.

The Guardians, at Runcorn, are at last waking up to the fact that it is hardly the thing to pay £4O a year to Church cletyraen to minister to Protestant paupers, and to expect a Warrington priest to travel a long distance and attend the Catholics for nothing. They have resolved that the matter should be considered; let us hope that it will end in the priest receiving a "con- sideration."

Another woman has fallen a victim to the use of paraffin lamps. Ellen Birchall, aged 23, and living at St. Helens, was blowing out a paraffin lamp on Sunday morning, when an explosion took place, and she was so badly burned that she died the same day. The number of deaths under simi- lar circumstances is appalling. It is time for the Legislature to step in and prohibit the sale of lamps that are not "Safety Lamps." An inquest was held at Haydock, on Tuesday, on the body of a miner who lost his life in pre- paring to fire a shot. .de was using an iron drill instead of a wood rammer when the explosion occurred. The Government Inspector very pro- perly suggested that employers should prosecute men who endangered life by breaking rules. One prosecution, he remarked, would do more good than a hundred fines. It is a case of being cruel only to be kind.

The other day, at Rotherhithe, a quarrel about a shilling between husband and wife ended in the woman having a fatal fall downstairs. There is a story told of a Scotchman who was attacked by highwaymen, and made a desperate reeistance. When he was overpowered, it was found that the only money he had on him was " saxpence." "Egad!" said one of the footpads as he looked to his injuries, "if Sandy had had a shilling on him, he would have killed the lot of us." Dr. Oliver Wendell Holmes, good, kind, brilliant soul, entered upon his eightieth year on Wednes- day. He has survived so many of those who welcomed his "Autocrat of the Breakfast Table," that one is reminded of the last verse in his charm- ing poem of "The Last Leaf"— And if I should lire to be The last leaf upon the tree, In the spring .. 1
