Speaking at the Daresbury Licensing Sessions, on Tuesday, on behalf of the Warrington and District Licensed Victuallers' Association, Mr. Jenkins, solicitor, said I am reminded by Mr. Joseph Taylor, the president of the association, and who is now in court, that we will do all we can to assist the clergy and all teachers of religion. We will also assist in the education of the young, and in any good work we can in keeping with the holding of a license." We don't know whether Mr. Jenkins' winked at the Bench when he made this statement, or whether he laughed a little laugh in his sleeve, but it seems to us that he has sud- denly blossomed into a humourist of the first order.

Let the reader give his imagination rein with the idea of the licensed victuallers doing all they can "to assist the clergy and all teachers of reli- gion I" "Picture it ! Think of it, dissolute man !" and reform thyself, for the millennium is at hand. Instead of "Sunday opening" meaning, as nf yore, the supply of "liquid fire and distilled damna- tion," it will mean that the bar parlour will be converted by " teachers " into a Bible class, while the dancing room will be used by the " clergy" for preaching purposes. The lion and the lamb are about to lie down together, and sin shall be no more.

Mr. Robert Davies is not a politician ; he drops into politics, as Silas iWegg dropped into poetry, occasionally only—or he would not, at the Prim- rose League gathering on Saturday last, have revived the ancient error as to the primrose and Lord Beaconsfield, that it was "his favourite flower." When the Queen used that celebrated phrase, in sending a wreath of primroses for the coffin of the dead statesman, she meant by "his" not Lord Beaconsfield, but her late husband, the Prince Consort. "Dizzy" rather sneered at prim- roses, as he sneered at most things. He wrote of them as good for a salad, and allowed his pea- fowl to eat them; he preferred peacocks, he said, to primroses. But, no matter; we shall hear again of "his favourite flower."

CADBURY'S caution the public against adulterated Cocoas, sold as pure Cocoa, to which about 4 per cent. of Alkali and other agents ,are add.d, to give appa- rent strength to Om liquor, by making it a dart cowur. This addition may be detected by the scent when a tin is freshly opened. No Coooa can be stronger than Cadbury's, which is guaranteed absolutely pure.—Advt. Two children, after taking shelter from Tuesday night's storm at Combo Abbey, Warwickshire, were pro- ceeding home, when they walked into the river and were , drowned. BRAVE RES= BY A MOTHER.—A little boy of three years of age fell into the canal at Grappenhall. near Stanny Lunt's Bridge, on Saturday, and was , bravely rescued from drowning by his mother. It appears that Mr T. Shakeshaft, a clerk in the goods ' department at Whines Railway Station, who resides at Runcorn, was, with his wife and family, staying for a few thys at the. house of relatives living near the bridge in question. On Saturday two of their children were playing near the canal when the little boy fell into the water. The other child, who is five years of age, ran to the house and told her mother, who went to the place indicated and in- stantly jumped into the water. She seized thechild, and with the assistance of one of her relatives, suc- ceeded in getting him safely out of the canal. When the alarm was given, the woman left her child of six weeks old in the house. It is to be hoped that she will be none the worse for her sudden immer- , sloth Mr. HENRY BUCK, Farmer, of Willow Farm, Ifempnall, Norfolk, writes to us saying :—Rackham's Liver Pills and Tonic Compound duly received, I have much pleasure in testifying to their value, the following are the facts of the ease I mentioned to you: My wife had been in a very weak state for more than two years, violent sickness in the morning, followed by utter prostration, no appetite ; all her friends said she could never get better, three Doctors were at different times called in, and although the medicine sent by them gave temporary relief, yet there was no prospect of cure, as In the spring of this year she was as bad and as weak as ever, since which time she has only taken Rackham's Liver Pills and Tonic Compound, and is now perfectly restored in health and spirits, and only taking occasional doses to keep her so.—Sold by all chemists, in boxes, Is. 10. and 25. 94.; and of the Pro- prietors, J. CHAPMAN St CO., St. Benedict's. Norwich.—Advt.

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

*** Our Readers will see from, a notice in our adver- tising columns that Mr. John Toulmin, of Pres- ton, has retired from the firm of "John Walker and Co.", proprietors of the Examiner series of newspapers. The newspaper and printing busi- ness will, however, be carried on, as heretofore, under the old style or title, by Mr. John Walker, who has for several years acted as editor and

managing partner. In announcing the change which has taken place, Nfr. Walker takes the op- portunity of cordially thanking his friends and patrons, and trusts to deserve and obtain a con- tinuance of the support which has hitherto been
so liberally accorded to the " Examiner."

MILTON CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH, WIDNES —Special services were conducted in this church on Sunday by the Rev. Benjamin Bond, of Skelmersdale. The attendance of worshippers was very good, and collections were made at each service. MOSS BANE WESLEYAN CHAPEL, WIDNES.—III connec- tion with this place of worship, special services were conducted on Sunday last. The preacher was Mr. Edgerley, of Newton-by-Frodsham, and he had large and attentive congregations both morning and evening. Collections were made in aid of the funds. HALTON CLOTHING CLUB.—TIIe 54th annual distribu- tion of clothing took place in the, Girls' 'School yesterday week. The value of the clothing distributed (including £55 4s) was £192 8s 10d, which really only represents ten months of the club year. The number of members has been—adults 100, children 76, total 176. Treasurer, Lady Brooke: secretaries, Miss Ward and Miss Short. STEALING PLUMS AT HALE.—On Thursday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, a youth named John Gaglian, of 42, Cromwell-st., Widnes, was charged with having, on the 26th August, stolen a quantity of plums from the garden of Ann Hitchmough, farmer, Hale. Walter Allen, a teamsman, deposed to finding the defendant in the gar- den plucking plums. The defendant ran away, and many plums fell from his pocket. He had done much damage to the hedge and trees. The defendant was fined 2s 6d and cost, 8s 6d, or in default seven days' hard labour. .....

DAMAGING GROWING CORN AT Winrms.—William Kelly (18) and James Rorke (14) were summoned to Widnes PAty Sessions, on Thursday, to answer a charge of hav- ing, on the 19th August, wilfully convnitted damage on the farm of Mr. Wm. Grace, at Upton Rocks by tramp- ling down the growing corn. In consequence of the damage Mr. Grace had sustained, P.C. Almond watched the field, and caught the defendants trampling down the corn and picking the heads off the wheat. Mr. Brock said it was a great shame that farmers' crops, should be damaged in this way, and other offenders of this kind would be severely dealt with. The defendants, were fined 2s 6d and costs, and damage is. INTER-WORKS FOOTBALL COMPETITION. The first round in this competition is still continued. On Satur- day afternoon the Widnes Alkali team met a team from the works of Messrs. Muspratt, on the Widnes Football Ground, and there was a fair number of spectators. The Alkali team proved by far the stronger and scored two goals, two tries, and six minors to their opponents one minor. Farrell ("Curley ") kicked both goals, Mr, W. Ireland was the referee. On Monday evening Ga.skell Deacon's team inet Mersey Copper Company, and the former earned a very easy victory. The scores were— Gaskell Deacon's one goal, three tries, and seven minors ; Copper Company, one try, one minor. Mr. J. Bingham was the referee.

BETHESDA CONGREGATIONAL SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN. —The anniversary of the establishment of this school was celebrated on Sunday last by special services. The morning and evening services wore conducted by the Rev. W. L. Roberts, of Liverpool, who alsc preached an eloquent and practical sermon on each occasion. The choir, assisted by the scholars, rendered specially selec- ted music. In the afternoon a service of song entitled "Whiter than Snow" was given by the scholars, con- ducted by Mr. W. Handley, the superintendent, and was much enjoyed by a good congregation. Miss Emily Ainsworth and Mists Heatherington sang several solos in good style. Mr. Joseph Hade officiated as reader. Mr. J. Clough presided at the organ in his usual able manner. The collections realised about £ll.

SERIOUS STABBING AFFRAY AT BOLD—Before Mr. H. Gaskell, junr., at Widnes Police Court, on Tuesday, a rough-looking man named Frank Dowd, a farm labourer, was charged with having wounded James Davies, at Bold, by stabbing him with a knife. It appeared that on Sunday night the prisoner was in the Tipping Arms, Bold, in company with four or five Irishmen. A quarrel arose amongst the men, and the prisoner was seen to stab Davies several times. It was evident that Davies was seriously injured, and several persons at once re- moved him to the surgery of Dr. O'Neil, at k'arnworth, where his wounds were dressed by Dr. Warke, who for- warded a certificate to the court, stating that Davies was in a very dangerous condition and was unable to appear. The prisoner was remanded for a week.

WESLEYAN PICNIC FROM WIDNES.—The teachers and a few friends in connection with Oakland-st. Wesleyan Sunday School had their annual picnic on Saturday afternoon. The party numbered about 38 persons, and the programme consisted of a pleasant drive to Lymm in a couple of waggonettes, supplied by Mr. J. H. Lee, and a ramble amongst the leafy hedgerows and picturesque places of the surrounding country. Much interest was also taken in the Ship Canal operations near Thelwall, and a stoppage was made there on the return journey. Ample provision had been made for the inner man, the party sitting down to an excellent repast served in the Wesleyan Schoolroom. Messis. William Hague, W. Jackson, and S. Jackson, thesuperintendents, had charge of the arrangements, which passed off satisfactorily, and Widnes was safely reached about 9 p.m. MERSEY MISSIONS TO SEAMEN (RUNCORN BRANCH).— The annual sermons in aid of these missions were held on Sunday. In the morning the scholars, headed by the band in uniform, walked in processional order from the Mission room to the Parish Church, where a sermon was preached by the Rev. J. Y. Reece, 8.A., Rector of Llanwrog. In the afternoon a service was conducted in the Public Hall, the scholars again walking in procession, and singing hymns en route. There was a large attend- ance, and the Rev. J. H. Wilcockson, incumbent of Weston Point, delivered an appropriate address. In the evening, service was again held in the Public Hall, and the Rev. J. F. Reece preached to a good congregation. The workers and scholars of the Mission met in Devon- shire Square, and, with the choir and missionary, Mr. Shaw, mached to the place of meeting. Special hymns were sung at each service. The afternoon and evening collections were in aid of the Runcorn branch, and realised £4 12s 60. TEMPERANCE DEMONSTRATION AT FARNWORTH.—The annual demonstration of the Farnworth Branch of the Church of England Temperance Society was held on. Saturday afternoon last, and was aided to a successful issue by fine weather. About a hundred members, headed by the Widnes Jubilee Brass Band, marched through the principal lanes and made stoppages at the residences of Mr. J. B. Imison, Mr. John Brock, J.P., and Mrs. Deacon, Appleton House. Afterwards they returned to the church, when the Rev. W. Edmondson, the curate, con- ducted a service, and the Rev. J. Holden, of Runcorn Parish Church, preached an appropriate sermon from the text Galatians VI, 12. The processionists now made their way to the school-room, where a substantial tea had been provided. The numbers were at least increased by a hundred friends; and their wants were attended to by the dames—Edmondson, Beatie, Williams. Carter, J. D. Davies, Abbott, W. Davies, and T. Carter: and Messrs. Fogg, Jameson, Stead, Hunter Jacks, and 11. Glover. The room was suitably decorated with flowers and mottoes. In the evening an entertainment was given and speeches were delivered by several local gen- tlemen. The Rev. W. Edmondson occupied the clriir. Mr. Brock urged the temperance party to take advan- tage of the opportunities they would have in the county councils for dealing with the liquor traffic. During the evening the proceedings were enlivened by a glee party rendering several glees in capital style, and the Parish Church hand-bell ringers gave an enjoyable performance. Songs were sung by Miss Fogg, Miss Stead, Miss. Flibbert, Messrs. U. Cowley, F. C. Davies, and A, G. Davies. Recitations were given by Mr. J. W. Davies and Mr. Harold Mercer. The customary votes of thanks brought the meeting to a close.

WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.-Mr. G. H. Hanby, clerk to the Widnes School Board, on Thursday summoned a number of persons for neglecting to send their children regularly to school. The usual fine of 5s was inflicted in each case. SHOCKING ACCUSATION AGAINST A FATHER.-At Run- corn Police Court, on Wednesday, John Conlon, a mid- dle-aged man, who lives at 4, St. John-A., was brought up on remand charged with attempting to commit a rape upon his daughter, Mary Conlon, 15 years of age. After hearing the evidence the magistrates discharged' the prisoner. FOUND DROWNED IN THE CANAL AT WESTON POINT.— An inquest was held on Tuesday. by Mr. J. E. WorSley, coroner of the honour and fee of Halton, at the Weaver Hotel, Weston Point, into the circumstances attending the death of a sailor named Robert Thompson, of Mont- rose, whose body was found in the Weston canal, on Saturday evening. The jury returned a verdict of "Found drowned." _

FOOTBALL AT Ruxcoftx.—On Thursday evening a friendly game between the Runcorn first team and Run- corn Recreation Club, assisted by members of the Run- corn seoend team, was played on the latter ground. Woods (at back), Crompton, Davies, W. Hughes, Faulk- ner, and Brazendale played a grand game on behalf of the Runcorn team, and S. Booth (at back) and the others for the Recreation placed a spirited game. However, the Runcorn team won the game by 2 goals and 1 try, to one goal and a touchdown. NEW CATHOLIC CHURCH AT RUNCORN.—To-morrow (Sunday) the new Church of St. Edward, Irwell-lane, will be opened by his Lordship the Bishop of Shrews- bury. The sacred edifice is commodious, comfortable, and handsome in its interior appointments, and also pre- sents a pleasing appearance on the exterior to the pa qspr by. It is a great improvement upon the old place of worship on Mill-brow, and is a monument to the ac- tivity and enPrgy of the priest, the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi. Full particulars of the opening services may be found in our announcement columns.

—.-- MARRIAGE AT RUNCORN.—On Tuesday, at St. Paul's Chapel, a marriage between Mary Ann Riley, grand- daughter of the late Mr. Peter Riley, of Rose Cottage, Higher Runcorn, and Mr. Robert Ceflinge, painter, &c., I Church-st., was solemnised by the Rev. A. P. Watson. The bride, who was attired in a dress of silver grey, was given away by her uncle, Mr. Arthur Riley, of Bridge- st., and she was attended by her si iters, Jessie and Edith, as bridesmaids. Mr. Richard Collinge officiated as best man. Mr. Peter Brereton supplied the coaches. The presents were numerous and valuable. SAD CASE AT WIDNES.—At Widees Police Court, on Monday, Mary Jane Riley, 17 years of age, who lives in Water-st., was eharged with being drunk and disorderly in Sankey-st.—P.S. Clarkson ...deposed that on Sunday morning the girl was very drunk, and was shouting and swearing in an awful manner.—Mr. Timmins said the last time the girl was in court Mr. Deacon paid the fine, and she was taken to the workhouse and had an op- portunity of leading a better life. lie (Mr. Titnmis) was sorry that ,Mr. Deacon's kindness was thrown away.— In default of paying a fine of 5s and costs the prisoner went to gaol for seven days. THEFT FROM A CLOTHES LINE AT WlDNES.—Catherine Doyle, a middle-aged woman, was brought before the Widnes magistrates on Thursday charged with having stolen a shirt, worth 2s, the property of John Owens, of 4, Caroline-st. On Monday, Mrs. Owens wastied the shirt, and placed it on a line to dry. Subsequently she missed it. On the same day the prisoner pawned the shirt for 2s. 3d. at the shop of Mr. F. Neil, Anne-st. West. The prisoner alleged that a boy had asked her to pawn the shirt, and sue had paid over to him the 2s. 3d. advanced. The Bench said they could not believe this statement in the absence of evidence, and sent the woman to gaol for 14 days. AN" OLD HAND" AT WIDNES.—John Ileyes, . a rough- looking fellow, who has an extensive acquaintance with the interior of Widnes Police Court, WAS brought before the magistrates charged with having stolen a shirt, value 2s, the property of Messrs. Calvert Bros. drapers, Vic- toria-road. On Saturday, at midnight, P.C. Field ap- prehended the prisoner on a charge of drunkentiesS, and Ihe was placed in the cells. On Monday morning he was found to be wearing a new shirt, and inquiry elicited that it had been stolen from the shop door of Messrs. I Calvert on Saturday night. The prisoner, when dharged, said" All right ;is there nothing else ?"—He was com- mitted to the Quarter Sessions for trial. RUNCORN POLICE COURT.—On Thursday, before Mr. G. Lloyd Wigg, William Forster, a Ship Canal navvy, was chaiged with obstructing the footpath in Church-st. on the previous evening. The prisoner refused to move on when requested by P.C. Taylor, and he was arrested. He said the police would be made civil.before the Ship Canal was completed. He was fined is and costs, 8s 4d. seaman named Edward Davies was fined lOs and costs for having been drunk and disorderly in Lowlands- on the previous night. His wife, who said she had " only been married a fortnight, asked the magistrate to grant a summons against her husband for assaulting her. She was referred to the magistrates' clerk's office. TREAT TO THE RUNCORN WORKHOUSE CHILDREN.—At ' the kind invitation of Mrs. J. H Hayes of Frodsham, the children from the Runcorn Union Workhouse, situate at Dutton, visited her residence on Wednesday, with others who have at some previous time been occupants of the house, altogether numbering nearly eighty. Under the charge of the schoolmaster (Mr. Stubbing) and school- mistress-(Mrs. Nuttall) the children arrived at Frodsham about noon, and after partaking of a substantial dinner went into the grounds, and heartily enjoyed the races and games which Mrs. Hayes had so generously and thoughtfully provided for their amusement until four o'clock, when tea was provided. Play was afterwards resumed until nearly 8 p.m., when, after a very pleasant afternoon, the children returned to ' Dutton, being con- veyed in a wagon which had been specially provided tor the return journey. A HOUSE STRUCK BY LIGHTENING n WIDNES. On' Wednesday at neon a very brief but violent thunder- storm broke over Widnes, the thunder and lightening be- ing accompanied by hailstorVe of large size. The post office at Appleton, occupied by Mr. Morris, was struck by the electric fluid, and considerable havoc was done. The lightning struck down the chimney stack, pierced through the roof of the back bedroom, and did consider- able damage. The iron cornice of the fire place was torn completely away from the wall, the small articles , in the room had been scattered about, and the place was covered with dust and mortar. The window frame was completely dislodged and the panes broken. The lightn- ing appeared to have made its exit through the front I door, as the counter was damaged, the fanlight smashed, and the window of an adjoining room broken. Mrs Mor- ris, who was in the house with her two children at the time, and received a shock but fortunately escaped with- out injuries. Tinier OF CORN AT At.PLETON.—At Widnes Petty Ses- sions, on Thursday, John Ford (15) and James Barrett (15) were charged with stealing three sheaves of corn, value is, the property of William Smith, farmer, Albert- road, Appleton.—Thontas Smith, farmer' stated that on Wednesday he was in his father's field, when he saw the prisoners drive up in a cart. One of them jumped from the cart and entered the field. He took up three sheaves of oats, and threw them into the cart, and both pri- soners crushed them into a hamper. Witness ran across the field and pursued the cart, and overtaking it, jumped in and drove the prisoners to the police station. —P.C. 1,162 deposed that he received the prisoners into custody and charged them. They replied" I did not take them." The cart and horse belonged to Mr. Frances, the fish dealer, who employed Barrett.—The prisoners now alleged that a boy whom they gave a ride took the sheaves and threw them into the cart.—Mr. Smith, re- called, said he did not see any third boy.—The Bench fined the prisoners 20s each, or fourteen days in de- fault. Tuts IMPROVEMENT OF WATERLOO BRIDGE. RUNCORN. —A special meeting of the Board of Commissioners was held on Morfday evening to consider a report of the Waterloo Bridge Committee with regard to the improve- ment of the thorougfare.of that name. There were pre- sent—Messrs. Pritchard, Taylor, White, Once, Speak- man, Hankinson, Imison, and Mellor, with Linaker (law clerk), and Marshall (secretary.) The representative of I this journal put in an appearance, but on the ground , that it 'was to the interests of the ratepayers that the subject should be discussed in private, Mr. Pritchard moved, and Mr. Taylor seconded that the meeting resolve into committee.—The motion was carried non con, and the reporter retired. Several of the members did not vote. Afterwards Mr. Lake and Mr. Smith attended the meeting and took part tn the deliberations. We understand that the proceedings occupied two hours, and that it was decided by 'a majority of one vote to purchase the coal yard at the corner of Waterloo-road, and also the Waterloo Hotel, at the sale on the following day, if necessary, in order to carry out the ideas of the committee in improving the bridge. The coal yard was purchased at a cost of £4lO, but the public-house went to Messrs. Greenall. unopposed by Mr. Linaker, who acted for the Commissioners. It is stated that an "un- written agreement" satisfactory to the Board has been, discussed with Messrs. Greenall. REVISION WORK AT RUNCORN.—Elections, it is said, are fought in the revision courts, and Mr. W. Handley, the secretary to the Northwich Division Liberal Association, is evidently a believer in the oft-repeated statement. For many weeks past he has been preparing for the approaching visit of the revising barrister, and the statement of claims and- objections show greatly in favour of the party of progress. The following figures may prove of interest. In Runcorn North the owners' register contains 208 names, owners' claims 12, occu- ' piers' list 2,200, occupiers' claims 30, old lodger claims 59, new lodger claims 22, total 2,529. Runcorn South : Owners' register 95, owners' claims 11, occupiers' list . 700, occupiers', claims 8, old lodger claims 17, new lodger claims 11, total 842. Taking both districts together the Liberals have made 14 owners' claims. 35 occupiers' claims, and 43 old lod- ger, and 20 hew lodger claims. They have also served 5 objectibns to owners' claim list, and two on the old owners' register ; also to two on the occupiers' list and four old lodgers. The Conservatives have made nine ownership, five occupiers, 33 old lodger, and 13 new lod- ger claims, and have served throe objections to the ownership claim list. A comparison of these figures shows very greatly in favour of the Liberals. It is an interesting fact that in Runcorn there are 313 women entitled to vote for members of the new County Councils under the recent Local Government Bill.

QUO/TB.—Marquis ( Warrington) v. Shannon: Having been disappointed two Saturdays in succession by a club in the neighbourhood of Liverpool, after hav- ing prepared for them, the Shannn club sent a team of nine men to Warrington on Saturday, when a friendly game was played, with the following re- sult 'MARQUIS; _ _ _
• SHANNON. M'Laine 25 Jackson Floyd 25 Leigh Isherwood 2SW. Catterall Wright. ... Miller Donohue 25 Bolton l4 Brown 2st. Catterall Pennington Prangleton 25 17. Jones 9 Total 225 Total

PROPERTY SALES AT RUNCORN.—On Tuesday, at the Waterloo Hotel, Top Locks, Mr. Thomas Sutton, auctioneer, of Warrington, offered for sale several valuable lots of property. There was a capital attendance, and the sale was very successful. On the same day, and at the same hotel, Mr. S. Yar- wood offered for sale two freehold dwelling-houses and shops, Nos. 58 and 60, Devonshire-place, Bridge-st., Runcorn, together with workshops, out offices, and land thereto belonging. The land, including sites, contains about 212 sq: yds. The com- petition was very keen, and the auctioneer received no fewer than 32 bids, the highest being 010, at which the property changerl. hands. Mr. Thomas Finegan, of the Boathouse Inn, was the purchaser. Mr. Robert Davies, of Warrington, was the solicitor. WESLEYAN CHANGES. The local ministerial changes in connection with the Wesleyan body, as 'annually fixed by the Conference, will take place after the present week. The Rev. T. Baine, of St. Helensouperintendent of the circuit, will go to Chorley. and his successor will be the Rev. W. Wood- ward Spencer, from Macclesfield. The Rev. J. Kent, of Earlestown, has been removed to Stockport, and he will be succeeded by the 11*rv. A. P. Watson, of Runcorn. The Rev. G. G. Brown, (St. Helens) removes to the Chelmsford circuit, and the Rev. C Hammond,' from Cornwall, will occupy his post. The Rev. T. Jackson (Prescot) remains at his present district. The Rev. T. Bailie preached his farewell sermon in the Corporation-st. Chapel (St. Helens) on Sunday night. Mrs. Baine, who has had charge of a mother's meeting, was recently the recipient of a handsome testimonial of respect in the form of a cruet stand.

TEE RENOWNED nuNeoax Raton is prepared from the choicest herbs, roots, and spices, which render it of most valuable assistance in the digestion of food.—Prepared and soli wholesale by Isoac Stubbs. Lowlands-road. Runcorn.— Ada.

div.head: I RUNCORN WATER WORKS COMPANY.
div.p: I RUNCORN WATER WORKS COMPANY.

The annual meeting of the shareholders of the Runcorn, IVeston, and Halton Water Works Com- pany was held at Runcorn Public Hall, on Monday afternoon. Mr. John Brundrit, J.P., chairman of the directors, presided, and there were present Messrs. Thomas Bankes, W. Whittaker, W. Hayes, E. Timmins, P. Smith, and W. F. Salkeld (secretary), with W. Jones (assistant), The directors' report stated that "the revenue account shows a balance of £879 lOs Bd, including £255 14s 2d brought from the previous half-yaar, out of which the directors recommend a dividend to be declared of 41 pounds per centum per annum free from income tax, payable on and after the Ist day of September. This will absorb £537 103, leaving a balance of £242 Os 8d to be carried forward. The water in the well continues to be abundant, the machinery and plant are in good working rder, and the buildings are in substantial . _

_ _ The Chairman moved the adoption of the report, and the payment of the dividend suggested. He remarked , that the revenue of the company was steadily increasing and had been for.the past two or three half-years, and they were thus enabled to &dare a dividend of 4i per cent same as last half-year. The number of honses sup- plied last half-year was 4,031; this half-year this num- ber was increased by about 40. The Ship Canal and the large works in the town were taking a larger quan- tity of water, which, of course, was a benefit to the funds of the company. The directors had found it necessary to prevent a petition to Parliament against the Frodsham Gas and Water Bill, as there were clauses in that bill prejudicial to the interests of the Company, and which were very much like the clause they opposed in the Liverpool Waterworks Bill.: The pro- moters of the Frodsham Bill were told that it would be strenuously opposed, and were shown just grounds for this course, and they agreed to insert a clause protecting the interests' of the Runcorn Waterworks Company with- out putting the shareholders to any further expense. The directors regretted that Mr. Richard Toft had re- signed his office as auditor owing to his continued Rimy's. He had been the auditor for a very long time, and had always efficiently carried out his duties, and they regret- ted his retirement. They suggested that Mr. James Col- lier, who was a shareholder, should be appointed to the vacant post.—Mr. W. Hayes seconded the motion, which was carried.

On the proposition of Mr. Bankes, seconded by Mr. Whittaker, Messrs. John Simpson and William Hayes, retiring distectors, were re-elected. Mr. James Collier was appointed auditor, on the mo- tion of Mr. Hayes, seconded by Mr. Timmins. The directors were thanked for their able and efficient services in the past, on the proposition of Mr. P. Smith.
IIIiNCORN BREWSTER SESSIONS.

The annual Brewster Sessions for the Runcorn Petty Sessional Division were held at Runcorn Police Court on Monday. The magistrates on the Bench were Messrs. J. Brundrit, A. Thomas, J. Handley, and G L. Wigg.
TiiiiqsrETts.

The license of the South Bank Hotel, Lord-st., was tranderred from Walter Jones to Thomas Jones; the Commercial Hotel, Bridge-st., from Thomas Jones to John James Linton; the Mersey Vaults, Mersev-st., from Thomas Blease to Alfred Bazley • the Clarendon Hotel, Church-st., from Mrs. Lea, deceased, to William Henry Lea; the Albion Inn, Peel-st.. from Sarah Little- wood to Jane Bradburn.

AN OBJECTION. Alfred Ellison applied for the transfer of the, license of the Man at the Wheel, from Thomas Williamson.—The applicant said he had permission to sell for three months. —Superintendent Hollingworth said he did not know whether he ought to obect to the application, but Ellison was convicted three weeks ago of permitting drunken- ness. The Bench adjourned the application for a month.

div.head: TUE TREA.TELR ROYAL.
div.p: TUE TREA.TELR ROYAL.

Mr. Wm. Richard Waldron, manager of the Theatre Royal, applied for a license to perform stage plays in that building.—Superintendent Hollingworth said he in- spected the Theatre on Saturday. There was no doubt that it was a tumble-down place, and it was constructed of such material that in case of fire it would be entirely consumed in twenty minutes if the flames got fairly ' hold. There, however, appeared to be a good supply of water.—Mr. Bnmdrit : What about the modes of ingress and egress—are they pretty good P—Superintendent Hollingworth Yes; I don't think there is anything to find fault with in that. He added that it would be better if a practical man were to inspect the structure ; but if their worships were satisfied he had no objection. Mr. Brundrit : Was it not surveyed last year by the ' County Surveyor.—The superintendent replied that it must have been three years ago. Mr. Waldron was asked for his old license, but he replied that he did not know what had become of it. He had removed his resi- dence, and the license had been mislaid. Superinten- dent Hollingworth: I don't like to say much about this thing, but there is a great responsibility if anything should happen.—Mr. Waldron: There are seven doors— or modes of egress—and all open outwards. Every pre- caution is taken to guard against fire.—The Bench ad- journed the application for a month; the county surveyor in the meantime would inspect the building. THE SUPERINTENDENT'S REPORT.-ORF.AT INCREASE OF

div.head: DRUNKENNESS.
div.p: DRUNKENNESS.

Superintendent Hollingworth read the following re- port : I have the honour to submit my annual repor with reference to the conduct of the licensed victualler and beer retailers in this division during the past year There are 45 licensed victuallers, 53 beersellers, and 5 others who sell off the premises, total 103 ; which gives an average of 185 of the population to each license. Five licensed victuallers have been proceeded against during the year, all of whom were convicted, as compared with Ithree proceeded against and two convicted in the pre- ceding year. Five beersellers have been proceeded against and convicted, as compared with two proceeded 'against and one convicted in the previous year. 344 persons have been convicted of drunkenness during the lyear as compared with 175 in the preceding year. The following is a list of the publicans and beersellers pro- ceeded against :—Richard Heap. Swan Inn, permitting drunkenness on 6th August, lBB7, fined 20s, and costs 12. s 6d; William Fitton, Waterman's Arms, Weston, selling to drunken person on 3rd September, 1887, fined 10s, and costs 18s 6d ; John Coxhill, Greenway Vaults, keeping open during, prohibited hours on the 12th De- cember, 1887, fined 2013, and costs lOs 6d ; Henry Kelly, Holy-head Harbour, keeping open during prohibited hours, Bth Feb., 1888, Is, and costs 8s 6d ; Geo. Linch, Friendship Inn, permitting drunkenness on the 18th of February, 1888, fined 20s, and costs 18s 6d; Joseph Grundy, Masonic Inn, selling to drunken persons on 16th June, fined 20s and costs 16s 6d; Sinclair Arm- strong, Bull's Head, supplying beer to police constables on 16th June, fined is, and costs 12s 6d; John Done, Royal Oak, permitting drunkenness on the 16th July, fined 20s, and costs 17s 6d ; Alf. Ellison, Man at the Wheel, permitting drunkenness on 28th July, fined 20s, and costs 17s 6d; David Snell, Blue Bell, harbouring prostitutes, fined £4, and costs 25s 6d.—Mr. Brundrit said the report showed a had state of affairs. There was a great increase in the number of licensed victuallers and beersellers proceeded' against and convicted, and the number of persons convicted of drunkenness was nearly doubled. This showed a very bad state of affairs, and whether it proceeded from extra vigilance on the part of the -police, or through the licensed vie-. • , .

uallers not keeping their houses as they might do; was an open question. The magistrates hoped there would be an improvement next year.—Superintendent Holling- worth said he had served a notice upon David Snell that he should object to the renewal of the license to the Blue Ball Inn, Fryer-st.—Mr. Brundrit said consideration of the renewal of the licenses against which convictions had been recorded would be held at an adjourned ses- sions in a month.

THINGS HEARD AND SEEN. That the public of Runcorn will be required to wade through the slush and mire of Waterloo Bridge and dodge the dangers of the lurries and the carts for yet another winter. That Mr. Timmis says the widening of the Bridge was talked of about 25 years ago to his knowledge. That the Commissioners after showing "how not to do it" for many years, have wakened up, but it is only to spend £4lO upon the purchase of a cor- ner plot, which will of as little use as the corner plot they acquired years ago on the opposite side, unless more pro;gress is made in coming to an arrangement with the Ship Canal Company, for carrying out the work. What a pity it is that the approaching election does not give the ratepayers an opportunity of " heck- ling " the retiring members on the question. That it is said that the Ship Canal navvies are respon- sible for the great increase in the number of persons con- victed of drunkenness in Runcorn during the past year. No doubt they are the cause of a portion of the increase, but a reference to the "Black List" would show that they are far from being responsible for the whole. No doubt the figures altogether indicate a spread of the drinking habit that is extensive enough already. The more probable explanation is that the police have ex- ercised greater vigilance and been more fortunate ix meeting with the inebriates "rolling home in the morn- ing:"

'That Mr. D. H. Jones has a grievance with regard to. the contracts at Dutton Workhouse, and is prepared to fight on in the face of very great odds. Not a guardian would so much as second his proposition at the meeting on Tuesday, and the matter consequently had to drop, but he immediately returned to the charge by giving notice that he would ask the Master certain questions at the next meeting. In the course of his remarks, Mr. Jones made a grave charge, and in justice both to the contractor and to the Master it ought to be inquired into.

That it is hoped that at the election of Commissioners on Thursday five gentlemen who are in favour of public baths will be returned; then, perhaps, Mr. P. Smith would bring his scheme into the light of day, as it is evident he regards the case as hopeless with the present constitution of the Board. That the Rev. R. Burdon left Widnes for his new cir- cuit with the best wishes of the numerous followers of Wesley in the town. He has done much uhostentatious yet earnest work during his three years stay, and he was appreciated accordingly.

RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton. on Tuesday. Present Colonel Ashton (chairman), Rev. J. W. I. Tanner, Messrs Mclntyre, Weir, Heywood, Lewis, Stokes, Aaron, D. H. Jones, T. Hewitt, W. Hewitt, E. A. Wallington, Brandreth, Parr, Smith, Jackson.

THE APPOINTMENT OF CHAPLAIN.-THE CATHOLIC INMATES. The Committee appointed to consider the applications for the chaplaincy of the house reported t hat letters were read from the Rev. L. D. Lyon Bennett, of Little Leigh, and the Rev. W. Preston, M.A.. vicar of Holy Trinity, Runcorn. It was resolved on the motion of Mr. Aaron, seconded by Mr. Brandreth, that the chaplain visit the house at least once a week, in addition to the ordinary duties mentioned in the consolidated orders. It was resolved on the motion of Mr. Aaron, seconded by Mr. Wallington, that Mr. Bennett be recommended for the appointment of chaplain, at a salary of £4O a year. The attention of the Committee had been called to the fact that there were a number of inmates in the House- belonging to the Catholic faith and that at present there was no arrangement for these having spiritual consola- tion.—Mr. Speakman moved the confirmation of these minutes. The Assistant Clerk said the chaplain would be required to make 118 visits to the Workhouse in addition to any special time he may be sent for. A salary of £4O a year gave an average of B.s 9d per visit.—Mr. Mclntyre seconded the motion.— Mr. Grice moved that Mr. Preston have the appointment. —Mr. Parr seconded the motion.—The voting took place by ballot, and Mr. Bennett received 14 votes, and Mr. Preston three votes. Mr. Bennett was therefore declared appointed.—Mr. Speakman pointed out that there were 15 Catholics in the house at the present time, and when any of these required spiritual comfort a priest was sent. for from NVarrington, and he had to pay his own ex- penses. In justice something ought to be done in this matter, and he moved the appointment of a committee to consider the payment of some small remuneration to a priest.—Mr. Mclntyre said this would open a very wide question. Were there no other inmates but of the Catholic and Church persuasion ?—The Clerk said there were 178 inmates, 15 were Catholic, 48 of other denomina- tion, and remainder were Church-Mr. G rice said UN Guar- dians represented all denominations, and they ought to con- sider this question. He seconded Mr. Speakman's motion.- Mr. Parr asked if the priests who had visited the House had ever asked for remuneration ?—Mr. Speakman: I don't think the 7 have.—ln answer to questions, the Chairman said toe Board would not be bound by the re- port of the committee, and the motion was passed.

MR. JONES AND THE CONTRACTS-. The next business was the following notice of which Mr. D. H. Jones had given notice:—" I will introduce a scheme for the more tradesman-like and better identifi- cation of the drapery and clothing samples, and which will simplify the duties of the master, minimise the labour and save the time of the Guardians when the question of these contracts is before the Board."—The. Chairman read a communication he hadreceived from Mr. Jones, who said he had reason to believe that because he had been a former contractor his motion would be. rejected. He pointed out that his presence at the Board would debar him from participating in these con- tracts, and he further informed the chairman that it was not his intention, except at the special request of the Board, to again take up these contracts, and should he forget this promise at any time he gave the officiating chairman full and unconditional power to reject the same at all times.—Mr. Jones complained that an application of his to the master for specimens of samples of drapery and clothing kept in the house had been treated with a want of courtesy and due assistance, and that it should have been considered by a meeting of the whole Board. Ordinarily he should have treated this matter with silence, but he had good reason to suppose that there was undue opposition and prejudice, inasmuch as a similarity of names led him to suppose that there was one present who was working energeti- cally at the last election of Guardians on Savage's Bridge trying to influence the workingmen to vote-against his return for the simple reason that "lie didna want that rnon on the Board."—The Clerk: Mr. Jones complains of something that took place at the last meeting, but there was nothing took place here.—Mr. Jones: It was at a private meeting . I think it should have come before the Beard.—The Chairman : Do you say that owing to this conduct you are not able to go on with your mo- tion.—Mr. Jones said it had prevented him dealing with certain things.—Mr, Grice explained that the matter came before the Visiting Committee of which he was the Chairman. It was an application for samples of the different goods that had been supplied to the house, and it appeared to the Committee to be a very extraordinary proceeding, and that it was not competent for them to grant the request.—The Clerk said Mr. Jones had asked for something the master had no right to comply with.—Mr. Jones said he had no motive but to serve the cause of justice and right, and to suggest a scheme by which the contracts would give the best possible results.—The Chairman: I think it would be very much better if you made a speech, and not read one.—Mr. Jones said he had written it purposely to take less time—ten minutes will do it.—Mr. Parr: There is nothing in it—it will be _ all the same 20 year hence.—Mr. Jones argued that the principle upon which the contracts were now accepted was right, but it was not carried out.—Mr. Stokes: Have you any complaints to make about the goods now supplied ?—Mr. Jones: Yes, I have. He produced two pieces of linen, and asked "Which is the best of those two." The samples were examined by several guardians.—Mr. Stokes: Has the master brought any complaints about the goods supplied not being equal to sample.—The Clerk: There have been no complaints brought before the Board.—Mr. Jones said the Board now advertised one thing and did another.—The Master said the present contractor supplied goods equal to the standard samples. He was satisfied of that.—Mr. Jones: I say they are not.—There was no seconder to Mr. Jones' scheme, and the matter dropped —Subsequently Mr. Jones gave notice that at the next Board meeting he should ask the master certain questions with regard to the contract supplies which, in the interests of the Board, ought to be satisfactorily answered —The Chairman pointed out that Mr. Jones must let the master know the questions before the meeting.

THE COM.ITY PRECEPT. Mr. Brandreth, as Chairman of the Finance Committee, reported that the County precept, demanding £1,154 7s Bd, had been received. This was a decrease,of £319 18s 4d on the corresponding period of last year. (Hear. hear.)—A cheque forithe amount was ordered to be drawn.

div.head: ESTIMATE.
div.p: THE ESTIMATE.

The Finance Committee submitted the estimate of ex- penditure for the half-year ending Lady Day, 1889, and it was recommended that a call of 6d in the £ be made upon the overseers, being an increase of id in the £ more than the call made for the corresponding period of last year. It had been arranged that the appeal of the Manchester Ship Canal Company is to be heard at Chester ia October next.—The estimate was adopted on the motion of Mr. Brandreth, and it 'was decided to make the call recommended.

John Wardle admitted having been drunk, in Ir- laps-st., at the same time. It appeared that he came to the Police Station and enquired whether it was not "the station for the housing of the poor." As he had £6 3s 10d and a watch and chain upon him at the time he was loeked up for safety. Prisoner now stated that he had lost a spirit-level the previous night, but could not de- scribe it. ILLTREATING A Hons.—Henry Burton, the captain of a canal boat, was summoned for having on the 19th inst., at Walton Superior, illtreated a horse by working it while it was in an unfir state.—Sergeant Booth deposed that the animal was suffering from a large sore on the near shoulder.—Defendant, who denied the offence, was fined lOs and costs.

EATING PART OF A RAW TlNlKEY.—Patrick Coleman, a labourer, was charred with stealing a turkey, the pro- perty of John Camiikin, farmer, Dutton.—The prosecutor said he missed the turkey at twelve o'clock on the pre- vious day, and he subsequently found that it had been stolen by the prisoner, who had plucked and eaten the greater part of it. After the prisoner had eaten some oi the bird raw he went to sbeep in a field, and the remains of the turkey were found by his side.—On the ap- plication of the police, the case was adjourned for a week.

BEER BUT NO BENT.—Martin Grady, of 28, Water-st., was charged with committing a breach of the peace in Water-st. by fighting with a man named John Ditch- field.—lnspector Keighley said it was discovered that Ditchfield was acting in self-defence, and he was libe- rated.—The defendant said Ditchfield wanted his rent, and because he could not have it he struck him. Defen- dant then struck him back.—Mr. Timmis : Why didn't you pay your rent with the money you got the beer with 2—Defendant: I had the beet given to me. sir.— The defendant was bound over to be of good behaviour for two months in the usual sureties.

A MASTER AND SERVANT CASE.—Edward Brocklehurst farmer, Stretton, was summoned for having on the 30th July, at Stretton, assaulted James Wilkinson, his teams- man. A cross-summons was heard, Wilkinso being charged with assaulting Mr. Brocklehurst. Wilkinson also complained that his employer had 'wrongfully dis- missed him contrary to the terms of his contract, and claimed the sum of £4 lOs as compensation."—Mr. Robt. Davies appeared for Mr. Brocklehurst, and Mr. Jenkins ' for Mr. Wilkinson.—Complainant Wilkinson said that on the day in question he commenced work at three o'clock in the morning, and in the afternoon went to Warring- ton with some potatoes. He returned about 9 o'clock at night. He had a " small whisky" at Warrington, and a beer at Stockton Heath. When he got back Mrs. Brockle burst reproached him for having been away so long- and he told her why he had been detained, when she said he was "not tit to look after donkeys." When Mr. Brocklehurst saw him the same night he caught hold of him by the thrbat and pushed him on some iron rails with sharp points. He said nothing to his master, who after- wards kicked him.—Witnesses having been called by Mr. Jenkins. it was stated for the other side that when Wil- kinson returned and went to the house for the horse's

- provender some words took place between him and Mr. Brocklehurst as to his delay, and Wilkinson, picking up some articles belonging to him, said he would go, and would not feed the horses for anybody. In passing through the yard he met Mr. Brocklehurst, and after a few words he " clawed " the latter's whiskers. Mr. • Brocklehurst in consequence gave him a push and he fell to the ground.—All the cases were dismissed. Don CASES.—The following persons were fined is and costs for allowing their dogs to be at large contrary to the Rabies Order :—Frederick Dean, Mary Cornish, William Hands, Charles Harold Broadbent, and Mary

Tompkins. SLEEPY CARTERS.—Frederick Higginson was charged with being asleep in his lurry on the highway at Apple- ton on the 28th July. Defendant said he had had a• fit a few minutes before the policeman saw him.. The officer who proved the case said the defendant appeared to be under the influence of drink, and he did not think he had had a fit. Fined 2s 6d and costs.—John Smith, of Iffersey-st., Warrington, was charged with a similar offence at Appleton, on the lith August, and was fined 55 and costs.
A despatch from Natal states that the revolt in Zulu- land is practically suppressed. It is generally believed that Dinizulu is a prisoner either to the Transvaal Boers or the British troops. .

DISTRESSING FATALITY.—At Myrtleville, near Cork, OR Wednesday, a young married lady named O'Conner was carried out to sea when bathing, and her husband went out to her rescue. Just as Mr. O'Conner was about to bring his wife ashore she was dashed against a rock by a wave and rendered unconscious. She died about an hour afterwards.

THE Srcum.—Considerable damage was done through- out the country bythe storm of Tuesday night. The Salvation Army barracks at Bishops Stortford were de- molished by the gale The crops in the southern coun- ties were greatly damaged, and the rivers in Wales overflowed their ba.nk.s. Several shipping casualties were also reported. Two CHILDREN DEOWNED.—On Wednesday morning two children named Makepeace, aged respectively thir- teen and seven, were found drowned in the Oxford Canal, at Brinklow, Warwickshire. The children were sent .on Tuesday night to meet a carrier about a mile from their home, and on their return journey at about nine o'clock took the way of the canal towing-path. According- to Present arrangements, the Queen, with the Prince and Princess Henry of Battenberg will leave Scotland on November 22, arriving at Windsor the fol- lowing morning. Extensive alterations are being made at the Castle.

A boy named Parsons was attempting to walk across the parapet of the Great Western Railway bridge at Crosskeys, Carinarthenshire, when he fell a great height, alighting on spiked railings below, where he was transfixed. He died shortly afterwards.

THE MANCH' ESTE It SHIP CANAL. A BOY KILLED AT EASTHAM. Benjamin Atkins. a lad of fourteen, who was employed as a waggon oiler on the Eastham section of the works, died on Saturday, at the hospital at Ellesmere Port, from injuries that he ad sustained a few days previously by being run over by an engine. mooRE AND ACTON GRANGE. , On these sections, especially on the former, operations are impeded by the water which collects along the bot- tom of the cutting. The heavy rain of the last few days has caused considerable increase in the quantity which had before collected in the Moore portion of the cutting, so that the bottom of thei e,xcavation there is now covered with a lake two or three feet deep in parts. The powerful 16 inch pump whick is being, laid down there to deal with this obstacle is not yet completed, but it is expected to commence work very shortly, and will no doubt do much to remove the water from the cutting. The work has not otherwise been seriously impeded by the wet weather. Very little blasting Is being done at present on these sections, the rock being so soft that nearly all along the section it can be removed with spade and pick. The railway embankment is rapidly progress- ing, most of the soft sand-stone being used for its con- struction. Morley Common, up to the Old Quay Canal, is now crossed by a line of zails and a double row of tall posts indicating the course of the canal. Visitors to the works are becoming rare, probably swing to the quantity of mud to be found in this vicinity. STOCKTON HEATH AND WALTON. On this part of the canal the work of filling up the Latchford and Runcorn Canal, and of clearing the way for the steam navvies, is proceeding in such a.taanner as quickly alters the appearance of the landscape. At Walton Arches the canal is crossed by a line of rails, con- necting the Twenty Step Bridge operations with the Acton Grange section, which is in constant , use. The steam navvy at Tom Payne's Bridge has not yet com- menced work, but may be expected to do so daily. Wherever the scene of operations is visible from the Chester and Northwich-roads, there is always a group of interested spectators.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 1,1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 1,1888.
BARTON.

_ Preparations continue to be made for the construction of the track bridge and railway which is to col:wattle ballast lines east of Barton Jocks with those in the mea- dows west of Barton Bridge. The contractor proposes, it is stated, as soon as the harvest has been gathered, to cover 44 acres of land in the meadows at Bronlyhurst with the spoil from the cutting of the Ship Canal. These meadows, which belong to Sir Humphrey de Trafford, lie very low and slope towards the river, and adjoin those wbich the Manchester Corporation propose to ac- ,quire for the construction of sewage disposal works. It is proposed to raise the meadows level with the highway running from Barton to Stretford. They have often been flooded through the overflow of the Irwell. At Stickins Island, where the locks will be situate, the required depth of the canal has been reached at a small portion of the cutting. On the Weaste section a boundky wall is being erected to separate Trafford Park from the Ship Canal. Recently several distinguished persons have visited this section from Trafford Hall, in- cluding Lord Charles Beresford, R.N., Lord Saye and Sole, Captain and the Hon. Mrs Allfrey, and Sir H. and Lady de Trafford. It is confidently asserted that the idea has been abandoned of erecting a swing bridge at Barton for the traffic between Barton and Stretford, and that a high-level bridge will now be erected in- stead. IRLAM.

The second bridge across the river on the section be- tween Warburton and Barton is now completed, and a third is just being commenced near Partington. The buildings at Irlam are progressing favourably, and the offices have been transferred from Cadishead to the new buildings on the works at Irlam. A large engine shed is being added to the buildings already erected here. The two steam navvies have got fairly to work, and have al- ready made a cutting over 100 yards long and close on 20 feet deep. MODE WHEEL.

The Frendh navvy in the cutting on Stickin's Island has almost completed the first cutting, and, we under- stand, is about to be removed to the Trafford sub-section, near Mode Wheel. The second and lower lifts on this cutting are through rock, the blasting of which has al- ready commenced. A new cutting is just being started at Mode Wheel, where one of Ruston and Proctor's steam navvies, which has been brought from the Preston Dock contract, is being built, ready to commence operations as soon as the cutting is ready for it. and another cutting has been commenced and a steam navvy inserted in it, On the south side of the river near Trafford Bridge.

THE MANCFMSTER SHIP CANAL COMPANY. The sixth ordinary general meeting of the Ship Canal Company was held on Wednesday in St. James's Hall, Oxford-st., Manchester. There was a attendance of sharehclders. Lord Egerton of m, chairman of the directors, presided, and amongst those on the platform were Sir J. C. Lee (deputy-chairman), Mr. W. 11. Bailey, Mr. J. K. Isythell, Mr. W. J. Crossley, Mr. C. J. Galloway, Sir E. G. Jenkinson,X,C.B., Mr. Joseph Leigh. Mr. E. Leader Williams (engineer), Mr. W. J. Saxon (solici- tor), Mr. A. H. Whitworth (secretary), Mr. B. T. Leech. Mr. E. Guthrie, Mr. A. A. Gillies, Mr. W. H. Collier, Mr. R. Spencer, Mr. G. A. Haworth, and Dr. Lund.
large ; Tattoi

The secretary read the report of the directors, which stated that the affairs of the company were in a very satisfactory condition. Not only have the calls payable been promptly met, but a considerable sum has been re- ceived in advance, and the directors were able to delay making a further call payable until September 12. The share capital remains practically as it stood in December 31, 1887, the whole of the shares having been allotted, with the exception of 61,356 ordinary shares, of which the company has the right to allot 50,000, fully paid, to the contractor, in lieu of cash, leaving a balance of 11,356 shares. The total amount of share capi- tal allotted to June 30, 1888, was £7,386,440 £4,000,000 being preference and £3386,440 ordi- nary. The total amount resolved from the formation of the company to the end of the half-year was £3,513,769 7s id, and the total expenditure £3,401,244 6s sd. leav- ing a balance to the credit of capital account of £112,525 Os Bd. The expenditure charged to capital during the half-year was £991,880 lOs 2d, against the estimate of £1,230,000. The directors' estimate of further expendi- ture on capital account for the current half-year is as follows :—Purchase of land and compensation, £400,000; construction of works £BOO,OOO •, interest, engineering, and general expenses;£lo4,67s—total, £1,304,675. The balance to credit of revenue account, representing the net profit of the Bridgewater Canal undertaking for the half-year, after providing for depreciation of craft, &c. (£4,488) and an insurance fund to cover risks on the river Mersey £900), is £30,546 Os 10d. Cash in hand and at the banker's amounted to £325,310 12s 2d. Traffic ac- ' counts owing to the company amounted to £66,893 5s 9d, and sundry outstanding accounts t0£155,309 19s 10d. The interest payable out of capital, in accordance with the company's Act of 1886, was duly paid on the let of July to all shareholders who were entitled to receive the same. After long negotiations with the Inland Revenue Department, the directors have made an arrangement under which income-tax will be deducted by the com- pany from interest warrants amounting to £2 108 and upwards only. The directors have acquired possession of nearly the whole of the land necessary for the con- struction of the canal, docks, and other works, and have handed it over to the contractor. The directors feel con- fident that the canal will be completed in the specified time.

The Chairman, in moving the adoption of the report, said he was glad the directors were able to give so satis- factory an account of the affairs of the company as that which was contained in the report. There was an old saving that a work well begun was half ended---(hear, hear)—and although he could not say that this was liter- ally the case with regard to the canal, yet it was so to a greater extent than appeared at first sight, because the success of such an undertaking, its steady progress to- , wards completion within the specified time, must depend in a large measure on the systematic way in which the work was begun. He was glad to say that the contrac- tor had, b 7 his dnergy, foresight, and powers of organiza- tion, inspired them with the hope that he would be able to continue the work he had so well begun. Tor the efficient carrying on of the work there had been brought together perhaps the largest amount of mechanical assis- tance that had ever been brought together for such work. So far as the directors could see at present, there would be no difficulty in carrying out the canal within the time contemplated. At the present moment there were employed on the canal 8,568 men and boys,' 161 horses, 98 locomotives, 3,221 wagons, 51 steam navvies 449 steam cranes, and 104 pumping and other steam engines. Those figures, he thought, furnished the best proof that everything possible was being done to have the work finished in good time. The directors were devoting a great deal of their time to the undertaking, and he trus- ted that what they had done and were doing was to the satisfaction of the shareholders. (Applause). Sir J. C. Lee, deputy chairman, in seconding the adop- tion of the report, referred to various points connected with the finances of the company. The report, he pointed out, stated that after deducting the 50,000 shares which the contractor would take in lieu of cash, there remained unallotted 11,356 shares. Since the first of July, he was happy to say, some few hundreds of shares had been ap- plied for and had been allotted. (Applause.) There were 40,000 shareholders in the company, and the direc- tors hoped that the shareholders would make application for the shares still unallotted, so that those shares might be written off the boxes. With regard to the future financial requirements of the company, he explained that , the call which was to be made next month would not be sufficient to carry them on till the time of the next call in the spring of next year, and it was therefore proposed to call the shareholders together on an early data to gat their sanction to the issue of L 1,000,000 of debentures. Their Acts gave them power to issue £1,812,000 of deben- tures. The excellence of the security ought to warrant the company in issuing this stock at 3 per cent. In its issue a preference would be given to those who already held shares.
The motion was unanimously adopted. Thanks to Mr. Reilly for the use of the hall, and to
Lord Egerton and the other directors for their services, concluded the proceedings.

OUTRAGE BY SHIP CANAL NAVVIES NEAR RUNCORN. RAID ON A GROCER'S SHOP. At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Messrs. Bkundrit, Thomas, and IN igg, six powerful- looking .navvies named Wm. Paul, John Birchall, Chas. Watson. Wm. Atkin, Geo. Day, and Benjamin Bush were charged with having, on Sunday, the 26th August, at the township of Clifton, felo- niously stolen, taken, and carried away 61bs. of bread, 31bs. of haddock, 10 bloaters, 24 bottles of ginger beer, and two cucumbers, valued altogether at 68 4d, the property of John Williams. Watson, Atkins, Day, and Bush were further charged with having resisted P.C. Brew in the execution of his duty.— From the evidence adduced it appeared that Wil- liams is a labourer at Weston Chemical Works, and keeps a small .grocer's shop in the village of Clifton. On ~so.nplay afternoon, about three o'clock, eleven INiviries entered the shop, and called for al 'bottle of ginger beer each. Williams supplied them as last as he could, but several of the men did not wait to be served, but helped themselves, and the contents of the bottles quickly disappeared down their capacious throats. Upon Williams demandingyayment he was referred to a ganger, who was present, and stated that he would settle for the lot "just now." Several of the men said they had come a long way, and asked if they could have something to eat, and Mrs Williams at once set about to provide for them. She Cooked nearly three pounds of haddock and ten bloaters, and made a largo quantity cif bread and butter; and whilst this was being prepared Birchall cheekily walked through into the back kitchen and inquired ." Isn't it ready yet ?' The provisions were set upon the table, and the eleven navvies quickly crowded round and commenced their repast, wash- ing it down with more ginger beer. It was apparently so much to their liking that more than one could not help exclaiming "Well done mother;' and set upon it with a will, and aeon there was not a scrap left. Mrs. Williams mentioned her modest charge, and was told to "go to-- for it," the men at Op same time leaving the house two by two. She called to her husband, but he was of no avail against so many, and they made their exit. He, however, seized hold of the last man and locked the door, but his companions returned, and ;with many frightful oaths, demanded his release. They enforced their threats by violently kicking the door, and Williams becoming alarmed for his own safety, opened the door and allowed his prisoner to escape. He at once conveyed information of the occurrence to the police, and about six o'clock was with Constables Brew and Taylor in Heath road when a gang of navvies approached. He re- cognised several of them and the officers seized Bir- chall and Bush. The former acted with such vio- lence that Taylor allowed Bush his liberty and went to aid Brew in retaining Birchall, when Watson, Atkin, Day, and Bush set upon them and attempted to release their comrade. They were about to suc- ceed in their object when Inspector O'Donnell ap- peared on the scene in plain clothes. The inspector took his snaps in his hand and sprang amongst the group, threatening to smash the face of the first man who set a hand upon the constables. The nav- vies were taken aback and walked away, but the inspector kept them in view, and several more con- stables arriving he gave them into custody. At an early part of the proceedings Superintendent Hol- lingworth pointed out t'hat the men were well able to pay for what they had. One man had £3 in his possession, and others sums of 278, 245, and so on. Atkin denied that he was ever in the shop, but the other prisoners admitted having a bottle of ginger beer. The men charged with resisting the constables denied the charge.—Mr. Brundrit said with regard to stealing the provisions, the Bench considered there was no proof against Atkin, and he would be discharged. As to the others, the case was properly proved. This was not an ordinary larceny, it was levying black mail, and such a thing would not be allowed. Strangers must not come into the neigh- bourhood and think they could act as they pleased and defy the law. Each prisoner was sentenced to a month's hard labour. The four charged with re- sisting the police were further fined 20s and costs, or a month's hard labour. WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT TEACHERS' ASSOCIATION. On Saturday an ordinary meeting of this associa- tion was held in the Southworth-with-Croft Board School. Mr A Brimelow (vice-president) took the chair and, after the usual routine business was disposed of, briefly introduced the subject of the report of tile Royal Commission on Education for discussion.— Mr. HopoiNs (the secretary) took up the majority re- port and dwelt chiefly upon those clauses which most affect teachers in this district. The general tone of the recommendations was considered favourable to volun- tary schools, but exception was taken to the clause upon school accommodation, which requires ten square feet of space for each child, instead of eight as hero tofore, as that would press very heavily upon all the schools in this district. Upon the question of supply of teachers it was felt that there was no doubt the market vrasgreatly over- stocked; and the remark upon the code requirements as to staff was fully endorsed. The leaving of the ques- tion of superannuation to managdrs was not looked upon favourably, as it was felt that the subject should be taken up by the 'Government, and contribution to the fund should be compulsory upon all teachers. With re- gard to pupil teachers, the recommendation of 5 years' apprenticeship instead of 4 was favourably looked upon. With the remarks of the Commission upon religious and moral training the teachers were in full sympathy; and the prospect of liberty of classification seemed almost too good to be true. Upon the subject of manual and tech- nical instruction, it was agreed that these matters cannot be touched upon effectually under the present system. The last subject discussed was that of Government in- spection. The project of not recording individual passes below' Standard HI. was looked upon as a great conces- sion, although it was thought Standard 111. might have been included, as it was felt much of the existing over- pressure would thus be avoided, as the duller children could be thoroughly grounded in the three lower stan- dards before proceeding to the fourth, and thus, though a little less work would be done, a far more complete and accurate knowledge of what was done would be attained. With the remarks upon payment, by results the meeting was fully, in sympathy. All were pleased to find the merit grant condemned, as it has utterly failed in its object, and really fostered the system of cram which it was intended to check. The prospective abolition of the 170 6d limit to the Govern- ment grant was looked upon as a great boon to struggling schools, while the recommendation that the cost per head should not exceed 45s was thought to be a very wise provision for the pockets of the ratepayers.-At the close of the discussion the Secretary read the memo- rial presented to Parliament by the Executive of the Union, and it was decided that a letter should be written to the Secretary of the Union approving of the peti- tion. The business part of the meeting being ended, a hearty vote of thanks was tendered—through Mr. W. H. Ball, the master—to the chairman and members for granting the use of the school.—All then separated until tea time, in the meantime visiting the many attractions of the pleasant gardens and grounds of the neighbouring hos- telry, the. General Elliott. Mr. R. Owen did the catering for the excellent knife and fork tea, which was laid out in the schoolroom. After tea the room was cleared, and a social evening was indulged in until half-past eight o'clock.

The strike of coalminers in New South Wales is caus- ing serious inconvenience and loss. Steamers are laid by and factories closing for want of coal. TEE SUGAR CONVENTION.—The text i 3 published of the Convention signed by the Plenipotentiaries on the sugar bounties question at their final meeting at the Foreign Office in London on Thursday. The signatory Powers are Great Britain, Germany, Austria-Hungary, Belgium, Spain, Italy, the Netherlands, and Russia. The French and Swedish representatives did not sign, but made declarations reserving the right to adhere to the Conven- tion later. Among other provisions connected with the constitution of "an absolute and complete guaran- tee that no open or disguised bounty shall be granted on the manufacture or exportation of sugar," the treaty will bring about the establishment of a permanent inter- national commission charged with watching the execu- tion of the provisions of the Convention, and a bureau for collecting and circulating information. It is provi- ded that the Convention shall come into force on the Ist September, 1891, and remain in force for ten years.

THE "WELLS LIGHT," which is being put on the mar- ket by A. C. Wells and Co., of Manchester, is just now creating some stir, and it appears to be one of the most important inventions of modern times. The patents are owned by Messrs. Wallwork and Wells, who have worked several years to bring this lamp to perfection. By its use an immense white light'is obtained from common mineral oils, at a cost many times less than coal gas or the electric light. Not the least remarkable feature is its portability, and a lamp giving out the gigantic light of 5,000 candle power, can be carried about by two men from place to place. Its use in large out of door works can scarcely be over estimated, and we understand that it is the only light in use through the extensive workings of the Manchester Ship Canal, and that it has been sup- plied for the most varied purposes to some of the largest firms. With the extensive supplies of oil which are being opened up in all parts of the globe, such a simple ap- pargus for burning them must have a very large sale in the future.

WARRINGTON SAILING CLUB. On Saturday afternoon a sailing match was held on the Mersey, under the auspices of this club. The starting point was Atherton's Quay—at which a considerable number of persons had gathered at the time of starting—and the course lay to New Ferry.. The following boats competed :—Siesta, Captain Jackson; Gipsy, Captain S. Lee; Doctor, Captain Jefferson; Primrose, Captain Spencer; and Maggie, Captain F. Monks. The start was made at a quarter-past three, but on reaching Fidler's Ferry, the Gipsy grounded, and was, consequently, unable to compete further. The remaining boats, however, succeeded in getting to Runcorn, at which time the Maggie was taking the lead, followed by the Siesta. Fram Runcorn the boats proceeded in safety until the Duke's Docks had been reached, where the course lay between two buoys. Unfortunately, the Siesta got out of the course and had to turn back, but as she was endeavouring to get into place she grounded, and, like the Gipsy, was thrown out of the race. The Maggie sailed on until within five or six miles of the finish ingpoint,when all furtherracing was put to an end owing to the darkness. As none of the boats were able to sail the required distance, another match will have to take place, probably on this day (Saturday) week. The Sailing Committee consists of the following :—Messrs Thomas Jackson, John Fairhurst, jun., A. W. Howard, F. W. Monks, John Bertham, M. Nosworthy (Dunham Massey), J. Simeock, T. Doraville, J. Harris, W. Bodle, and W. Jackson. Messrs J T. Higginson and T. Hall acted as starters and judges, and followed the boats in a steam launch belonging to th a club.

- - WARRINGTON V. BROUGHTON. -- Played on the ground of the Warrington Club on Saturday, and resulted hr a decisive victory for the home team by 101 runs. War- rington were without Tinsley and J J Crosfield, and Broughton only put ten men in the field. The hone team winning the toss, elected to bat, and Lawton and Reynolds played splendid eAcket. When Broughton went in so well did Fleetwood and Irving bowl that the Broughtonians were dismissed for the insignificant total of 39. The fielding of the Warrington men was very good, and both bowlers were almost unplayable, as will be seen from the analysis. It will be remembered that the Warringtonians defeated the Broughton team in the the first match by 29 runs, this being chiefly due to the fine batting of Tinsley, who scored 46, and the splendid bowling of Fleetwood, who took eight wickets Score :

div.head: NOTES BY TITE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY TITE WAY.

The contest between Middlesex and Gloucestershire terminated on Saturday ift a defeat for the western county by an innings and 33 runs. Lancashire brought thelr season to a close on Satur- day, when the contest at Old Trafford with Nottingham ended in a very even draw. It must be admitted that the Lancashire season has not beettquite so successful as was generally expected. In fact it is not so good as that of last season. Including all matches Lancashtre has won 11, lost 5, drawn 5, total 21. Kent brought their season to a close on Saturday with a defeat by Yorkshire. The match between the Australians and the Past and Present of Oxford and Cambridge Universities of Ports- mouth ended on Wednesday in a draw. The county cricket season ended on Wednesday, the matches between Surrey and Gloucestershire and Notts and Middlesex being drawn, while Yorkshire beat Sussex by three wickets. This leaves Surrey champion county for the year, with twelve victories, one defeat, and one drawn game. Kent and Yorkshire must be bracketed second, the latter's record standing at six wins, four de- feats, and four draws, while Kent won seven times, lost five times, and drew thrice. The others follow in this order—Gloucestershire fourth, Lancashire fifth, Notts sixth, Middlesex seventh, and Sussex last.

Herbert Synyer, of Nottingham; the amateur bicycle champion, still continues his winning career. On Satur- day he had very little difficulty in placing the 50 guinea challenge cup, given to the winner of the two miles bicycle scratch race at Lincoln, to his credit. Synyer won the cup last year, beating Wareham. This year he had very little trouble in securing it, being opposed by only B. Hinchcliffe, of Derby, and G. R. Adcock, pf Lon- don, whom he beat easily.

The annual sessions for the renewal of existing licenses in Warrington was held on Monday morn- ing at the Sessions-room in lrlam-st. The Mayor (Alderman T. Sutton) presided, and the other magistrates present were Alderman Pickmere and Harrison, Councillor Francomb, Major Litton, and Mr. E. J. Guest. Amongst those of the public in court were the Revs. John Yonge, E. H. Jackson, and G. D. Wray. Mr. Jenkins, solicitor, represented theinterestsof the Warrington and District Licensed Victuallers' Association. The following report of the Chief Constable (Mr. S. Hunt), in regard to DRUNKENNESS IN THE BOROUGH and the number of licensed houses, had been submitted for the consideration of the magistrates :—" The number of license holders are-87 licensed victuallers, 48 beer- house keepers, and 70 shopkeepers. The transfers dur- ing the year were-15 licensed victuallers, 8 beerhouse keepers, and 10 shopkeepers. Two licensed victuallers, 2 beerhouse keepers, and two shopkeepers were sum- moned for offences against their licenses, four being dis- missed, one fined lOs, and the other 5s 6d.
