The first business for consideration was the renewal of existing licenses of full-licensed alehouses, and,•in answer to a question from the magistrates' clerk, the Chief Con- stable saidthat no notices of objection had been served in respect to such houses. There had been no conviction against any licensed victuallers, but two had been sum- moned and dismissed. The whole of these licenses were then renewed, and the beerhouse licenses were next con- sidered. The Chief Constable intimated that no objec- tions had been made in regard to these licenses. On be- half of Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co., Wilderspool Brewery, Mr. Robert Davies made an application con- cerning the beerhouse known as the

_ GUN INN, SCOTLAND-ROAD, A summons against the landlord had, he said, been taken out and dismissed, and there was no conviction against the house. Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Company, to whom the house belonged, had for some time felt that there was not the accommodation at the Gun that they would desire, and that it was not a house that could easily be carried on respectably oa account of the con- fined and intricate passages and rooms that there were in it. They had, therefore, made up their minds to re- build the house in a proper manner so as to afford access to the police or anyone else, and to have it well conduc- ted. The situation of the house was very low, and he had in his lifetime seen floods there. It was intended to build a proper house, and he was instructed to ask the magistrates to sanction the proposed alterations. Hav- ing quoted law on the subject, Mr. Davies said it had been laid down that where a house was not so com- pletely changed in site as to be a new house, the magi- strates had power to sanction the alterations, and must license the new premises as far as they were bound to license anywhere. It must not be an entirely new site, but must be a sufficient renova- tion of old premises to enable the magistrates to decide that it was a bona-fide extension, and not the building of new premises. In the present case it was proposed not to entirely build on the old site. It was desired to throw the house back, and to take in a portion of an adjoining cottage. The plans that he was about to submit would show that a very great improvement was intended. As he had on a former occasion said to their worships, his idea would be to lessen the number of licenses and in- crease the accommodation of the houses, but, of course, there were vested interests and so on to be considered. Messrs. Greenall and Co. were taking this step because they wished to improve the premises that they held. Mr. Mumford, architect, was then called to depose to the correctness of the plans, and, after a little discussion had taken plhce on the matter the Mayor said that the Bench were glad to learn that 'the present house was to be pulled down, because they did not con- sider that it was a proper place to have as a public-house in that neighbourhood. They were of opinion that a new building, well conducted, would very much im- prove the morality of the neighbourhood, and therefore they were disposed to grant the request. At this stage of the proceedings the Rev. E. H. Jackson asked the Bench if he should be in order if he asked a question.— Mr. Jenkins, on behalf of the Association he represented, MADE AN OBJECTION

to any ex-parte statement being made by gentlemen who had no locus standi. He stibmitted that Mr. Jackson had no right to ask a question, and should certainly ob- jectl—Mr. Jackson said that he thought that as a rate- payer he had a right to ask a question.—The Mayor: may at once say that the Bench is quite disposed to listen to every case on its merits, and they do not think that any statement, by either one party or another outside, will influence them in any way whatever. I do not think it is necessary, in that case, to take up any time. —Mr. Jackson: I simply wanted to ask a question.— The Mayor: If we allow one question to be asked we may sit here all day having questions asked. Theßench have already decided that they are not disposed to be in- fluenced in the slightest degree by any opinions or re- marks of outsiders. Ido not think it would aid you at all in asking the question. I am not now sneaking on behalf of myself, but lain expressing the feelings of the 'Bench generally.—Mr. Jackson: I pay deference to the Bench but at the same time I believe lam quite in order, and that it is quite legal for me to ask a question as a ratepayer.—The Mayor Ido not say that we can go so far as to absolutely refuse you asking a question. Perhaps you will let us know what it is P—Mr. Jackson: The question is this. Certain "'statements have been made in the papers about rooms being habitually used, in beershops, as

A RUNCORN BRICKLAYER'S PROTEST. Sir,—ln your issue of August 25th, I find a report of a police case headed "A Bricklayer's Brawl at Runcorn," in which a Mr. Lawrence Mullarney played a sort of double-barrelled role as plaintiff and defendant. Per- sonally, I have not the slightest objection to Mr. Mullar- ney punching his opponent's head, or, if the fates so willed, having his head punched, as he said he had, but what I very gravely demur to is this, that without any more plausible claim to the distinction than the fact of having for so many years carried a hod on his shoulder, this war-like Mullarney, and ea-hod carrier, should, perhaps, to vamp up his battered respectability, dub himself a bricklayer. He is no such thing. For the sake of the craft of which lam a humble practitioner, I would a.-1 you, of your courtesy, to find space for this repudiation of the claims of this gentleman, who, for all I know to the contrary, may be a very good " braw- ler," but is certainly no " bricklayer.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, A BRICKLAYER.

THE LICENSING QUESTION AT WARRINGTON. Sir,—As Monday next is the day appointed for the granting of new licenses, I trust the borough magistrates will follow the precedents of previous years and refuse every application. No substantial reason can be ad- vanced in favour of a change. The town has not grown to any extent, and there is no crying injustice done by the present arrangement. Indeed, if any change is to be made, it ought to be in the direction of curtailing the existing facilities for the supply of drink, and thus re- ducing the awful amount of drunkenness which now attains in the borough. Just fancy an increase of 30 per cent, in the amount of drunkenness in a year! Truly our town is a besotted place, and I fear it will remain so, so long as we are dominated by wealthy brewers. But we. as ratepayers, have rights, and these rights enable us to protest against any increased facilities for drinking being granted. No doubt renewed attempts will be made to get sanction for the erection of palatial houses in the populous districts of Battersby-lane and Bewsey ; but it is to be hoped that, no matter what tempting baits are held out by the brewers, the magistrates will be proof against them. Even now the districts swarm with beerhouses, while off licenses are held by almost every corner shop, and it would be an undoubted blessing if these could all be suppressed. Certain it is that no necessity exists for any extension of licenses, and the magistrates will do well on Monday to continue in the path they some years ago marked out for themselves.— lam, kc.,

div.head: August 29th, 1888.
div.p: August 29th, 1888.

SUNDAY OPENING AT THE WOOL PACK INN. Sir,—For months past I have been grieved to see the Wool Pack Inn, Sankey-st., open for business on Sun- days. How this has come about lam at a loss to say, siuccept it be by the supineness of the Temperance Asso- eatitn; and the total indifference of the Wesleyan Methodits.ts. wea rezmber when the old tumble-down building which did duty M inn was pulled down, and the landlords had erected the present strl;,:ure., they were in fear and trembling lest they should be Unable to get the license transferred. The opposition thereto was strong, and particularly so by the members of the powerful Methodist Church in Bold-st. Special remark was made as to the scenes resulting from Sunday trading, and the dreadful examples of- fered to the young people as they left the chapel. In deference to the Methodists, Messrs. P. Walker and Sons said they would be content with a six days' license, and would willingly close the house on Sundays. They got the license and matters progressed quietly for a few years; but directly the local Temperance Society was disorganised, and a number of ministers came to Bold- at. who understood not the state of thinzs, the brewers quietly asked for and obtained a full license. Conse- quently on Sundays the Wool Pack is open as usual, and in the evening casts its alluring lights in the pathway of the young. It is singular the Wesleyans have not previously dis- covered and taken action in this matter, and as there is now an opportunity for them to do so, at the approach- ing Brewster Sessions, I call attention to the subject. This casein itself shows how eager brewers are to take advantage, and it behoves all who are opposed to the least extension of the facilities for dispensing a debasing and destroying liquor to be equally on the alert. I trust that by calling public attention to this house, the owners will be compelled to revert to their original compact.— Yours truly, Warrington, August 29th, 1888.
SOLDIERS AND CIVILIANS.

div.head: ONE INTERESTED,
div.p: ONE INTERESTED,
A RESIDENT.

Sir,—l trust you will allow me to protest against the last paragraph of the letter in your issue of 25th instant, signed "Morality." Your correspondent goes out of his way to cast inuendoes at the military regarding their alleged ruffianly propensities. I should like to see the result of a report from the civic authorities showing the per c,entage of crimes of the above nature by the mili- tary and civilian populations of Warrington respectively for the past year. I think it would be found that few, if any, such charges have been made against soldiers, whilst with regard to those recorded against the civilians their name is legion. Now, where is the ruffianism of Warrington located, and who are the constituents? It is not so long ago since the magistrates sent to durance vile some of these rascals for an aggravated assault upon military sergeants in Buttermarket-st. of a quite unprovoked description; and, owing to the frequent assaults committed by civilian roughs upon soldier recruits, the latter have been prohibited from visiting certain portions of "down town "which lend themselves to the undetected perpe- tration of such offences. Perhaps your correspondent is not aware that ruffians are not retained in the army, as, in the event of a soldier being convicted of felony or serious military offences, he is invariably discharged as unfit for the members of the army to associate with, and relegated to the place from whence he was derived—the civilian population. The above facts, in conjunction with a visit, any night, to the foot of Orford-lane and neighbourhood would convince any impartial individual who are the "ruffians" of Warrington, and where they most do con- gregate, and show conclusively that the neighbourhood of the Barracks is not their rendezvous.

The character of the public-houses adjacent to the Barracks, in the neighbouring lane to that mentioned, entirely confutes the prophecy that "close proximity to the Barracks" would contribute to the results specified in such choice diction by "Morality," as the " Haw- thorne " and "Wheat Sheaf" amply exemplify. I trust the above facts will prevent your moral corres- pondent from attempting, in future, to cast a slur upon a body of men who are honestly serving in the defence of their native land and the lives and property of their co- patriots—" Morality" included. His is the old cry of "Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth ?" or may it simply be ruse de guerre of a total abstainer ? Allow me, sir, to subscribe myself, yours, TUEBOR. Warrington, 27th August, 1888.

Sir,—ln your issue of Saturday's "Examiner," " Morality," a writer (evidently a tax-payer) who writes so charitably of soldiers, perhaps is not aware that the bar- racks in this town is but a training school: and that the misbehaviour of men wearing Her Majesty's uniform meriting the title of ruffians are not soldiers, but are youths fresh from home, hav- ing had the benefit of a School Board educa- tion, and the refining influence of their fathers and mothers. To the army is left the work of training these lads, and it is no easy work, endeavouring to do what their parents failed in doing—viz., making them good soldiers and respectable citizens. Warrington, 25/8/88.
COMO.
"THE TROUBLES OF A TRICYCLING TOUR."

Sir,—l was much amused by the account of the Tricycle Tour in your last Saturday's issue, by "Towns- man," and I think the gentlemen of the, party are very much to blame for all the troubles which befell them. With the ladies I can sympathise, for any cyclist knows that to the novice the first few days means down-right hard work; and for any one to go and hire three tri- cycles on the Saturday evening, and early on the Mon- day morning to mount three lady novices on them with- out any regard to size or weight, and without giving them the slightest opportunity for a little private prac- tice, or of adjusting the machines to their requirements, is, to say the least of it, hardly the thing.

Nothing looks worse than to see a lady attired in an ordinary walking costume, with all the appurtenances thereto, mounted on a tricycle several sizes too large for her, with the handles up to her elbows, the seat two or three inches too low, and cranks two or three inches too long, so that at every revolution the knees come into close proximity to the chin. It is such sights as these which deter many of our lady friends from parti- cipating in this most healthful and pleasant pastime. There can be nothing prettier or more graceful than a lady suitably attired and mounted on a nice light tri- cycle adjusted to her requirements, and I am only sorry there are not more lady riders in our ranks than there are at present. Our tourists seem to have started ent without any in- formation as to the roads, or where they should stop for the might, but have simply pushed on until compelled by fatigue and hunger to come to a halt—which has general- ly been in some thinly populated district. No wonder the inhabitants were scared by the sight of six travel stained hungry looking cyclists, and refused to 'admit them. Why did not they have their meals when oppor- tunity offered, at some respectable hotel? Their consi- deration for the ladies ought to have been sufficient to remind them that they could not ride a whole day with- out a proper meal; and then to make matters worse, to refuse a glass of wine when generously offered, because they wanted bread, is most absurd. Why not have made sure of the wine, and then looked after the bread ?

It seems to me that what ought to have been a most enjoyable trip, was spoiled through the want of ordinary care and forethought. Why did not they consult some experienced cyclists in town, of whom there are many, who would have been pleased to give them all the in- formation in their power; or better still why not have joined the Cyclist Touring Club and called upon the local consuls en route? Then their troubles would never have arisen.—Yours truly, A CYCLIST. [Perhaps it will be a relief to our correspondent to learn that there is a silver lining to the cloud. Next week we shall furnish our readers with a sketch by" Towns- man" entitled "The Pleasures of a Tricycling Tour." —En. Er.]

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. (Continued from page 6.) RUNCORN. WIGG'S WORKS STOPPED. THE WORKMEN UNDER NOTICE.
div.p: THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. (Continued from page 6.) RUNCORN. WIGG'S WORKS STOPPED. THE WORKMEN UNDER NOTICE.

In connection with the Ship Canal operations at Run- corn the past week has proved very eventful. As is now well:known, the course of the Shin Canal cuts across the Old Quay Canal at several places between Warrington and Runcorn, and the smaller waterway will eventually be absorbed into the greater undertaking. Near the Depot at the Big Field, Norton, the Old Quay Canal is crossed, and about a fortnight ago it was deemed necessary, in order that the operations might be carried out as designed to construct a dam across the canal about a quarter of a mile below the trestle bridge erected by Mr. Kirkham. That the supply of water might be kept up in the lower reaches of the canal, a culvert was constructed through the dam. As the sequel proves the quantity of water passing through the cul- vert was altogether inadequate to requirements. On Tuesday the water had sunk so low that flats grounded on the bottom, and could not proceed to their destination, while Messrs. Wigg, Brothel's, and Steele, which draws their supply from the canal, were compelled to suspend operations at their 'ex- tensive chemical works for want on the precious, if very dirty, fluid. This was a very serious matter, as 'nearly five hundred men depend upon the firm for daily sustenance. Although the chemical operations were stopped, the men were kept on the premises "doing odd jobs," but on Wednesday considerable consternation ' was caused through the fact that each man received a week's notice. On Wednesday the flow of water into ' the canal was increased by enlarging the culverts, but in the afternoon the water was not deeper than two feet. Mr. Loader Williams, the engineer; Mr. Walker, the contractor; and several engineers arrived on the scene and held a consulta- tion on the state of affairs, with the result that water was run into the canal from the Bridge- water canal by means of a culvert laid from a point op- posite Mr. Lello's tan yard. On Thursday morning the flats were able to make progress and the works resumed part of the customary operations, while by evening the men were at work as usual, and we understand that the notices have been withdrawn. In order to prevent any such serious catastrophe in the future, Mr. Walker has decided to fix two pumping engines on the river side to pump water from the Mersey into the canal each day at high tide. Already one of the engines has arrived and men are engaged fixing and fitting it up with all de- spatch. Permission having been given to proceed in the river, greater activity is being displayed on the Runcorn sec- tion. A vast quantity of timber has been unshipped at the o';L: D(.x.'/Cs: whict P. 97 vpsent wiiiiettya,nce much like Canada, nocir, Liverpool. Hundreds of pil2s are stacked on the quay, and, in view of the river ope- rations, two pile drivers are being constructed. The railway lines from the cutting have been laid to within a short distance of Mersey-st., and they will shortly be continued along the foreshore and streets to Runcorn Bridge. Another step in the way of progress was taken on Wednesday, when, in accordance with instructions received from the Manchester Ship Canal Company, Mr. T. Whitehead, of Warrington, offered for sale the Old Quay Pottery and the Old Quay Flour Mill, the site of each being required tor the Ship Canal. The pottery was first put up. The machinery comprised one hori- zontal steam enOne, a nearly new steel Cornish boiler, clay grinding mill. Whitehead's No. 8 vertical pug mill, Doulton's patent pipe prees,&c. The buildings are of brick. Mr. F. J. Norman secured the lot at £325. The ma- chinery at the Flour Mill, which has been closed for several years, comprised horizontal tandem compound engine, Lancashire boiler by Galloway and Sons, five pairs of 48-inch mill stones, and driving gear, grain ele- vators, automatic weighing machines, &c., &c. The buildings of brick contained 80 tons of cast iron columns and girders, ten wrought iron folding and fire sliding doors, eight iron staircases, 600 superficial yards of 2-inch York flags, corrugated iron stone 45 feet long, 38 feet wide of tin stores, &c. Mr. Ebenezer Timmins, of Run- corn, was the highest bidder at £BOO, and the lot was knocked down to him. The work of demolition com- menced immediately after the sale, and in a few days , the buildings Ntill have entirely ,disappeared.

div.head: THELIVILL.
div.p: THELIVILL.

There is little that is fresh to add with regard to this section. At Morris Brook the steam navvies are, during the day time at all events, constantly at work on the site of the intended Latchford locks, and the cutting is now of very great width and depth. Nearer Thelwall another long row of navvies' huts is in course of erection.

div.head: BURIED OAK.
div.p: THE BURIED OAK.

The uninjured parts of the large tree which, as we mentioned last week, was disclosed by a steam navvy at Statham, and which turns out to be a fine specimen of black oak, have been removed by Messrs. Garnett, cabinet makers, Warrington. The timber, after being cut up at Mr. Mounfield's saw-mill, will be made into a suite of dining-room furniture by Messrs. Garnett for Mr. H. Stanton, J.P., of Thelwall. DIVERSION OF THE RIVER AT IRLAM. On the Irlarn and Cadishead section of the Ship Canal, which, owing to the difficulty experienced by Mr. T. A. Walker, the contractor, in the purchase of land, was the last to be commenced, great activity now prevails. All along the route the work of excavation is being carried on at high pressure, a depth of nearly fifty feet having been reached at Skeer Rock, Cadishead, and one more " graft "of fifteen feet yet remains to be cut. At Bird- haw Point and Knowe Rock wooden constructions have been built across the river to facilitate the workings be- tween these points and the "Great Wette," which is the largest meadow in Cheshire being 100 statute acres in extent. Between Hollins Green and the " Great Wette " the course of the Ship Canal crosses the river no less than seven times, and after leaving the " Wette," within a space of 400 yards. three more times, " Sandywalk's Island" being thus formed. The third wooden bridge has been erected across the river, some 400 yaris below Irlam rail wav:station , and a ballast line runs over and has connection with a new siding that has been made on the Cheshire Lines Rail- way. In consequence of the river again taking a very zig-zag course, at this point a new cutting has been made, in which the course of the river will be diverted next week. By this diversion the contractor (Mr. Wal- ker) will have another large " tip " at his Command ; already one formed in a similar manner at Sticken's Island being utilised in the circuitous old river bed. Three steam navvies arrived in the earlier part of the week, and after being fitted up will be set to work between Partington and the point where the diversion takes place.

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 1, 1888.

made their acquaintance, it was pregnant with I happy recollections, and when he arrived at his destination his thoughts would often revert to the pleasant associations he had left behind, while their present gift would be a powerful stimulus in the great work he had so much at heart. He produced &gold watch, value 80 guineas, which had been presented to his father by his church during his 15 years labour in the West Indies. The watch had been handed to him in consequence of his being the only surviving missionary in the family. He also thanked the people who had shown so much respect on the day of his father's funeral, and said it was a consolation to his family to think they had left his remains on the hill side where loving hands would tend the grave.— Mr. Rowe, Sunday School superintenpent, was then called upon to make the presentation to Miss Hor- nabrook, and the incident occasioned another mani- festation of kindly feeling. Mr. Rowe, in his remarks, said he had been connected with the school over 39 years. and during the last four years he was thankful to say he Had been able to fill his attendances without recording an absence. Conse- quently, he could say from experience that Miss Ilornabrook was most interested in her class, the school, and all other duties which had devolved upon her in connection with the church, so it was with thegreatest pleasure that he made the presen- tation.—Mr. Hornabrook, kindly acknowledged on behalf of his sister.—Addresses were afterwards delivered by the Revs. G. Wood and A. P. Watson, Mr. Gamon, and Mr. llancock. The pleasure of the evening was very much enhanced by the rendering of three anthems by the choir. Votes of thanks were passed to the chairman, the ladies for presid- ing at the tables, the choir, and to Mr. Johnston for the loan of his flowers. The singing of the doxology brought a pleasant evening to a close.

MARRIA GE 4IF MISS CRESSWELL REYNOLDS, AT FRODSHAM. The marriage of Miss Mary C. Creswell Reynolds, daughter of Mr. William Reynolds, of Melbourne, Vic- toria, to Dr. Albert Vaughan Stieglitz, of Berlin, was celebrated at Frodsham Parish Church on Wednesday. Some time before the hour fixed for the ceremony, the church was filled to its utmost capacity with sightseers from Frodsham and neighbouring hamlets, and outside also a large number of spectators had assembled to wit- ness the arrival and departure of the bridal party. ShKtly after half-past twelve the equipages—seven in number—were driven up to the south gate, and the wedding party alighting, passed down the flagged path, which had been carpeted for the occasion, into the church, and proceeding up the aisle, took up their sta? tions at the communion rails. The bride, who looked charming, wore a dress of white moire, with a tulle veil and wreath of orange blossoms. Her ornaments were a pearl and diamond brooch, the gift of the bride- groom, and a pearl and diamond necklace (a heirloom). She carried a beautiful bouquet, composed of stepha.no- tis, gardenias, lilies, and other choice hothouse flowers. The bridesmaids were Miss Ada Reynolds and Miss May Reynolds (Latchford), Miss Dolly Hutchings and Miss Daisy Hutchings (Frodsham). They carried bouquets of red and white roses, and were dressed in white nun's veiling, with hats to match, and wore gold bangles, the gift of the bridegroom. Mr. Alphonse L. Stieglitz, brother of the bridegroom, acted as best man, and Messrs. Frank Brocklehurst and Sylvanus Reynolds as groomsmen. The marriage service was at once pro- ceeded with, the officiating clergymen being the Vicar of Frodsham, the Rev. Hy. Birchwood Blogg, and the Rev. Frederick Reynolds, cousin of the bride. The ceremony was a brief but impressive one, and at the conclusion the parties repaired to the vestry for the purpose of signing the registry. This necessary formality over, the bells rang out a merry peal to signalize the joyous event and as the bride and bridegroom left the church the sun burst from behind a cloud and beamed its genial rays upon them. The time-honoured but, to the targets, de- cidedly uncomfortable practice of rice-throwing was vigorously indulged in by many of the spectators, and the bridesmaids also received a portion of the shower. On reaching their carriages, which, it may be remarked in passing, were supplied by Mr. Edward Connor, of Sankey-st., Warrington, the party returned to Foxhill. About 30 guests sat down to the wedding breakfast, at the close of which the health of the happy pair was heartily drunk and suitably acknowledged. A garden party was afterwards held, and between 70 and 80 friends of the family were present. Unfortunately, the weather, to some extent, marred the afternoon's enjoy- ment, but nevertheless everything passed off successfully, and all assembled about five o'clock to bid "God speed" to the newly-wedded couple, whii left Chester by the 5.25 p.m. train for London, where the honeymoon will be spent. The gifts to the bride and bridegroom were numerous and costly, and betokened the high esteem in which the parties are held by a large circle of friends and well-wishers. PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians was held on Thursday afternoon. There were present Mr. J. Kenwright (chairman), the Rev. S. A. K. Sylvester, Messrs. W. Paine, C. B. Johnson, W. Middle- hurst, J. Elli.;on, .T. Leatherbarrow, J. Ranson, W. Burchall, J. Fisher, J. Birchall, E. Syder, R. Tuson, T. F. Hill, R. A. Graves, W. B. Longton, J. Matthews, and Mr. S. H. Hartley (clerk.) WORKHOUSE INMATES.—Mr. Hale, master of the Work- .house, reported that there were in the Workhouse this week 524 inmates. against 531 in the previous week, and 477 in the corresponding week last year. There had been 78 vagrants relieved during the week, against 104 in the corresponding week last year. THE GUARDIAN FOR RORY.—The Clerk reported that for the vacancy caused by the death of Mr. W. G. Ash- ton, the Rev. S. A. K. Sylvester, vicar of Roby, was the only candidate nominated, and he had been declared elected as the Guardian for that township. RELIEF RETURNS.—The Clerk submitted a duplicate of the annual poor rate return for the year ending Lady Day, 1888, which had been sent to the Local Government Board. It showed the gross receipts from all sources for the year were £58,179, and the expenditure £58,270. He had also forwarded to the Local Government Board the statement of the number ot persons in receipt of re- lief on the Ist July of this year. This indoor, which meant persons in the workhouse, or schools in Liver- pool, Pantasaph, or West Derby Orphanage, was 661, including 8 vagrants relieved in the workhouse. In 1887 the total was 696. whilst the outdoor in 1888 was 3,524, and in 1887. 3,198. AN INDISPOSED OFFICIAL.—In accordance with notice of motion Mr. Hill moved that Mr. R. G. Waterman be appointed a temporary substitute for Mr. Henry Kay, school attendance officer for Woolton, during that offi- cer's illness, at a salary of £1 per week.—Mr. Leather- barrow seconded the motion, which was carried unani- mously. THE PRESCOT UNION AND THE NEW LOCAL GOVERN- MENT BILL.—The Clerk reported the receipt of a com- munication from the Local Government Board, stating that under the new Local Government Act the number of county councillors for the county of Lan- caster would be 105, of which 85 were to be elected by the County, exclusive of boroughs. He was asked to at- tend a meeting in Liverpool on Tuesday, for the purpose of conferring upon the best manner of obtaining a due representation of the rural and urban authori- ties in the Prescot Union. He attended the meeting and found a scheme had been drafted which would give to the Prescot Union 'exclusive of the borough of St. Helens, four rearesentative,s, and of these four—out of 85—it was intended to give two to Widnes Local Board district; and Little Woolton, Much Woolton, with Huyton and Prescot Local Boards, were to form another district, having one representative. The district of the Rural Sanitary Authority, containing twelve townships and parts of townships, together with the Rainford Local Board, should form another dis- trict, having one representative. In the absence of any direction from the Guardians, he felt justified in drawing attention to the injustice which the rural portion of the Union would suffer if the scheme as contemplated were carried out. As things arelin the Prescot Union, Widnes would not be fairly entitled to two representatives, as there were only 29,000 inhabitants, while a population of over 30,000 was necessary before they could be entitled to two repre- sentatives. It was not finally settled that there should be five representatives for the Prescot Union. If they would only give them five out of the 85 there would be no difficulty with respect to Widnes, as Widnes then would fairly be entitled to two. The Rural Sanitary Authority, with Rainford added or Prescot, would then havS;two, and the four Local Boards joined would have one, which would be a fair division. Mr. Hulton appeared to be positive they could not have more than four. A proposal was made that Cronton and Ditt,on, and a portion of Hale- wood, should be taken from the sanitary district, and merged in the Widnes district. He opposed that very much indeed, and contended it would be quite unfair and contrary to the intention in the Act of Parliament, and was altogether outside the instructions which had been received by the Clerk of the Peace in one of the circulars. It was then suggested that a part of the Widnes district should be taken (rom them and given to the Rural Sanitary Authority. But he failed to see there would be any great advantage in that. The Wid- nes Authority would be quite satisfied with the scheme as originally proposed by the county officials.— Mr. Hill : Because it gives them two representatives.— The Clerk : Yes. The representatives of the Local Boirds of Little Woolton, Much Woolton, and Prescot were scarcely in a position to offer any strong opposition to the scheme inasmuch as none of them, or even three of them, would be able to claim a representative on ac- count of their population,,so that they were prepared to fall in with the views of the county authorities. It only rested for that Board to say whether he should press in a fair and legitimate manner the claims of the Guardians for two representatives for the rural portion of the dis- trict being joined with one Local Board. The Widnes Local Board had a population of 29,000, with an area of only 3,039 acres. The Rural Sanitary District, with Rainford joined, had an average of 37,000 for which

div.head: HOUSE ROBBERY BY A BOY AT SPEKE.
div.p: HOUSE ROBBERY BY A BOY AT SPEKE.

At the Widnes Police Court, on Monday, before Messrs. T. S. Timmis and 11. Gaskell, jun., a boy named John Thomas Guest (9), living at Speke, was charged with stealing -CS 6s 6d from the house of William Ireland, Hale-road, Speke. Ann Ireland, wife of the prosecutor, said that on Saturday last she left her house about seven o'clock to go to Liverpool market. She returned home about ten o'clock. When she went out she left a purse in a chest of drawers up- stairs, which contained the mentioned sum. The drawers were not locked, and in her absence the money was stolen. Prisoner had been to her house on previous oc- casions begging. P.C. Walker said from information received he went to Wm. Ireland's house on Sunday night, and found footprints in the garden. He had sus- picion, and apprehended the boy. The boy had been in Spoke churchyard in the morning, and witness went there and found £7 19s 6d and one ounce of tobacco on the wall in the porch. He showed the boy a piece of briarwood, which the prisoner had left in the house, and when asked where he left it he said he did not know. The prisoner afterwards admitted that he had entered the house by the window, and had taken the money from the drawers. He had spent some of it in tobacco, sweets, and a pipe, at shops in Garston. The boy was ordered to receive six strokes with the birch rod.

div.head: BREAKING INTO OFFICES AT WIDNES
div.p: BREAKING INTO OFFICES AT WIDNES
DOCK.

At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, before Mr. John Brock, a rough looking fellow named Thomas Hart was charged with having, sometime between Saturday at noon and Monday morning, broken into and entered the office of Messrs. Clarke and Goulder, West Bank Dock, and stolen three coats, a muffler, a vest, a handkerchief, and a knife, value .£2, 3s, the property of Wm. Clarke, sen., and Wm. Clarke, junr.—Wm Clarke, junr., said he was a clerk in the employ of Messrs. Clarke and Goulder, ship- ping agents, West Bank Dock, Widnes, and lived at the HoHies, Hough Green, On Saturday, the 25th August, he left the office safe and secure. On Monday morning, at half-past eight he found that the office had been broken open and an entrance effected by forcing open the door. The clothing and knife produced were missing. —James Stringer, tool maker, of 6, Oliver-st., Warring- ton, deposed that on Sunday might, the 26th August, he was driving from Hale to Warrington with a number of friends. They picked up the prisoner, and gave him a ride to Farnworth. On the way the prisoner offered to 591.1 the coat produced for 2s, and witness purchased it for a shilling. He afterwards handed the coat to P.C. Thompson.—P.C. Thompson deposed to finding the pri- soner in the pawnbroker's shop of Mr. Syred, Waterloo- road, on Monday morning. The prisoner was in posses- sion of a bundle of the stolen clothing, and stated that they were given him at Ditton on Sunday. At the police station the pocket knife was found in his trousers pocket. In answer to the charge prisoner replied "All right."—The prisoner was then charged with having, sometime between Saturday at noon and Monday morn- ing, broken into the office of Messrs. Clarke and Goulder. Joseph James Rutledge, dockmaster at West Bank Dock, left the office securely fastened, and on Monday morning he found that the door had been broken open. A coat that had been stolen from the office of Messrs. Clarke and Goulder was lying on the desk. The drawers had been tampered with and there were marks of a knife which corresponded with the blade in the knife stolen from Messrs. Clarke. There had, however, been nothing taken away from the place. The blade of the knife had been broken, and the broken piece was found embedded in the frame of a drawer. The prisoner was committed to the quarter sessions for trial.

BRUTAL ASSAULT ON AN OLD WOMAN AT WIDNES. At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, before Messrs T. Sutton Timmis and H. Gaskell, junr., a young man named John Killslin, of 2, Sankey-st., was charged with haying maliciously and feloniously caused grievous bodily harm to Bridget Glynn, of 23, Sankey-st.—The prosecutrix deposed that on the 29th July she was having some words with Mrs Johnson about her daughter Annie Johnson, who was a friend of the prisoner's. The prisoner came to her in the backyard, and without saying a word, struck her on the head with his fist, and knocked her against the door. She ran into the house and locked the door. The prisoner then threw a bucket filled with water through the kitchen window, and entered the house through the aperture he had thus made. Seizing a low wooden stool (produced), he aimed it at her (witness), and struck her on the right side. The violence of the blow was such that the ntoc: Was broken. She was seri9usly injured, and still suffered paid. She was 63 years of age. She never gave the prisoner any provocation.—Mary Ann Glynn, daughter, and Margaret Ann Pearson, wife of Jonathan Pearson, of 19, Sankey-st., c .rrobo- rated.—Dr. Hutchinson stated that the woman's sixth rib was fractured, and she had bruises on the I head, body, arms, and legs. She was confined to her ' bed until the 23rd August, during which time she suffered great pain. Her life was in danger from the injuries in consequence of her age. She was now slowly improving. A blow from the stool pro- duced would cause the injuries, but it must have been thrown with great violence.—P.S. Robinson deposed to apprehending the prisoner, who said that he would reply to the charge before the magistrates. He now said "I am not guilty of using the stool. Mary Glynn and I got drunk together. Bridget Glynn threatened me with a poker, and I don't re- member any more." The prisoner was committed to take his trial at the next Liverpool Assizes.

div.head: TRINITY WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL,
div.p: TRINITY WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL,

HALTON. A congregational tea meeting was held in the above school on Monday. The assembly was called to do honour to the Rev. R. F. Hornabrook, the resident minister, in consequence of his removal from Halton. occasioned by a call trom the Wesleyan Missionary Committee, to labour in South Africa, the land where he has already spent seven years of his earlier life as a missionary of the Gospel. The occasion was in every way a thorough success. On it becoming known that his connection was to be severed so abruply it was suggested that it was an admirable opportunity for his people and friends to show their appreciation of his kindness, of which they had so often been the recipients, and to recog- nize the services of his aged mother. who has, when able, gladly given help and counsel when visiting from house to house, also to Miss Hornabrook, who has manifested the greatest interest in all connec- ted with the Sunday school and church. It is a matter of congratulation to note that the suggestion was acted upon with the greatest enthusiasm, and the liberality of the neople soori proved more than sufficient to enable tile Committee to present to the rev, gentleman a pedestal oak writing desk. and Miss Hornabrook with a writing desk. Tea was on the table at 645, when about 170 sat down. Presid- ing at the tables were Mesdames Brereton, W. Nixon, R Nixon, Jno Barrow, Faulkner, Snape, Rowe, Misses Lea and Hornabrook. The tables were beautifully decorated with plants kindly lent by Mr. Johnstone and friends. After tea, which was thoroughly enjoyed, a public meeting was held. The room was crowded to excess. Mr. John Bagu- ley presided, and was supported on the platform by the Revs. G. Wood, superintendent, and A. P. Wat- son, who are also leaving the Runcorn circuit, their three years' itinerancy having expired. The Chair- man having briefly addressed the meeting, called upon Messrs. S. Barrow, R. Hughes, and J. Looker, Each gentleman in turn spoke in the highest terms of the services rendered by Mrs Hornabrook and family, frequently eliciting applause when speaking of their past association and friendship, evidencing they were expressing the sentiments of the audi- ence. Mr. Lea (chapel steward) then rose amidst loud applause to make the presentation, the hand- some table, bearing the following inscription "Presented to the Rev. R. F. Hornabrook, in recog- nition of his valuable services, and as an expression of the affectionate regard by the Wesleyan S. S. and congregation, Halton, Cheshire, August 27th, 1888." Mr. Lea ob.erved that although their society had been of so short a duration, he had on no occasion felt the severance of a minister more keenly than he did the present one, and while it afforded him the greatest pleasure in making the presentation, he should have been better pleased to have done so if Mr. Hornabrook had been staying at Halton. But as he believes it was the call of God, and the ex- press wish of the church that he should again labour in a foreign land, lie hoped the small me- mento which carried with it the kind wishes of the Halton people, might be made a blessing and a plea- sure when on his lonely mission and weary with his arduous toil, when separated from his family and friends who contributed so much to make life happy.—Mr. Hornabrook, in rising to acknowledge the presentation, was re- ceived with applause, and said there were times in the history of most men when their emotional nature was ungovernable, and if he were to attempt to express his feelings his utterances would be at an end. It was for this reason, since he had heard of their intentions, that he had been very much humbled by the thought of how little he deserved so much Christian sympathy, and that he had dreaded the approach of the meeting. He thanked the public for their kindness, and said although it was only two years ago since he had

they were to have one member. Heithought they would see there the injustice of the spirit of the instructions of the Local Crovernrnent Board, if they were to be carried out.— Mr. Johnson considered it would be unfair if Widnes had two representatives and the whole of the district only ithe same number.—Mr. Birchall thought they should press the scheme laid down by the clerk, and moved a motion to that effect.—Mr. Matthews thought if they had two representatives from Widnes there would be no- thing detrimental to the Union, and they would be as safe in the hands of the Widnes division as any other part of the Union. Mr. Middlehurst thought the clerk's idea a very reasonable one, and seconded Mr. Burchall's proposition. The Clerk said he hoped they would not think he was fighting against Widnes. He was anxious to have five members He suggested that the following districts be made :—No. 1 district, Huyton, Little Woolton, Much Woolton, and Rainford ; acreage, 11,321; population, 14,958. No. 2 district, Prescot,-Ec,cleston (rural), Windle (rural), and Knowsley; acreage, 10,816; population, 12,543. No. 3 district, Rural Sanitary district, Whiston, Rainhill, Bold, Cronton, Ditton, Tarbock. Halewood, and Speke ; acre- age' 21,378 ; population, 12,144. The rateable value of the first division is £102,924; second, £52,682; and third division, £109,352. That seemed a fair way of dividing the union, with regard to area and pursuits of the population.—The motion was afterwards carried unanimously. This was all the business.

MANCHESTER HAY AND STRAW, FRIDAY.—HRy (OW). 9/d to 104; ditto (new), Od. to 04; clover (old), 9fd. to 101 d. ; ditto (new), 61d to 84; wheat straw, 7d to 7d; ditto oat. 74 per stone of 14tt. LONDON PRODUCE. FRIDAY.—Sugar market very quiet; beetroot quoted 14s 6d September and 138 414 less 1 per cent October. Coffee quiet but steady. Tea : No sales to- day. Riee firm but inactive. Cotton market steady. Jute continues firm. Tallow without change. Rape oil. 25s ; lin- seed, 188 114 to 188 3d. Turpentine. 28s 6d to 28s 74d. Petro- -1 leum ; American, 744 spot. LIVERPOOL PROVISIONS, FRIDAY.—For beef holders are very firm, and asking full prices. Pork remains steady at recent rates. Bacon: From America the quotations for hog I products come rather dearer, but they are without effect upon our market, which is firm but quiet. Hams rule slightly easier. Shoulders are firmer. Cheese arid butter continue steady at previous prices. Cable advices from America re- ceived to-day quote no change in the value of lard and bacon.

div.head: MEETING OF CHESHIRE LIBERAIS.
div.p: MEETING OF CHESHIRE LIBERAIS.

Mr. and Mrs Tomkinson, of Willington Hall, on Thursday entertained about 80 members of the Council of the Eddisbury Liberal Association at their residence. In the course of an address, Mr. Tomkinson alluded to the Irish question and his experience of a study of the situation on the spot. He claimed that Ireland, notwithstanding all that was said to the contrary, was about the best rent paying country in the world. A certain nobleman told a friend of his that his gross rental was £27,000 a year in Ireland, and out of that he received £26,000 every year, without one shilling reduction, the remaining one thou- sand pounds representing agent's commission. He (Mr. Tomkinson) had also a Cheshire friend who had large property in Cork and Tipperary, and another in Huntingdonshire. This gentleman told a friend last year that he got his rent from his Tipperary and Cork property very well, but hardly got enough from Huntingdonshire to pay tithe. (Laughter and cheers) Though condemning boycotting, Mr. Tomkin- son said that it came with very bad grace from the Tories to denounce it, seeing that they had for years adopted it as one of their weapons. He expressed confidence in Mr. Parnell's ability to clear himself entirely from the charges preferred against him in the " Times," and said it was almost universally accepted now as a fact that the letters which appeared in that journal were wicked forgeries. Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., who also spoke, said from personal knowledge of Mr. Mandeville, that no charge could have less foundation than the impudent one of drunkenness which had been insinuated against him. He (Mr. Brunner) had sat at his hospitable table, and was convinced that there was no symptom, either in Mr. Mandeville or in his surroundings, of excess of any kind. Mr. Brunner 'went on to say that it was right at times even to break the law, and that it was wrong at times to enforce the law. (Cheers.) This was amply illus- trated by recent events in Ireland, and he believed that right, justice, and mercy would prevail before long. (Cheers.)
FRODSHAM. POLICE NEWS.
At Eddisbury Petty Sessions on Monday, the following cases were heard by Messrs. S. Woodhouse, J. Higson, and R. Wilbraham.

ASSAULTS.—James Goodall summoned Thomas Spen- cer for assault at Frodsham on the 11th August.—Seve- ral witnesses were called, and the defendant, who em- phatically denied the offence, was fined 5s and costs...

STRAY' ANIMALS.—Robert 'Walker was summoned for allowing a cow to stray on the highway at Kingsley on the Bth August. Constable Marshall proved the case. Defendant's wife appeared, and stated that the cow was a very unlucky animal, as she was constantly straying on to other people's fields. Fined Is and 4s costs.—Wm. Blanc was summoned for allowing a horse to stray on the highway at Kingsley at 1 a.m. on the Ist August. The same defendant was also charged with allowing a cow to stray on the highway in Kingsley. Fined 13 and 4s costs in each case. ALLEGED ILLEGAL POSSESSION OF RABBITS.—EIIen Gar- ner was charged with being in unlawful possession of six rabbits on the highway at Overton on the 14th August. —P.C. Pearson stated that on the day in question he was onputy in Overton with Sergeant Waller and Constable Brewster, when he saw the defendant come from her house in Mersey-view with a basket which they (the officers) had reason to suspect contained game. They accordingly intercepted the woman, who, in reply to an inquiry as to the contents of the basket, said, "Well, it's no use trying to deceive you; they are six rabbits." She added that she obtained them from her house, but would not say who brought them there. The rabbits were warm and unpaunched.—Sergeant Waller gave corrobo- rative evidence.—Defendant denied that she had come by the rabbits illegally, and averred that her husband hacl leave to catch rabbits over a number of acres in the neighbourhood of Mersey-view. She called Mrs. Parker, wife of William Parker, who stated that she held four acres of land, and had given the defendant's husband, who was her sin-in-law, permission to catch rabbits on it. He had also permission to take rabbits on other land. —The Chairman: The magistrates look upon this as a case of suspicion, but there is not sufficient evidence to justify a conviction. The case will' be dismissed.

God has established no equality among men in practice or theory, but a moral equality. The giant has a natural right to his stature of eight feet, and his strength equal to five hundred pounds, and the dwarf to his three feet, and his strength equal to fifty pounds.

THE BAPTIST AGITATION.-It is reported that the mem- bers of the Metropolitan Tabernacle congregation have followed the action of their pastor, the Rev. C. H. Spur- geon, and retired from the London Baptist Association, in consequence of the want of decision displayed by the body with regard to qnestions concerned in what is known as the "down-grade controversy."

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

An explosion took place on Friday afternoon in sink- ing a shaft at Chester Moor Colliery, Chester-le-street, by which five men were seriously injured. Some consternation prevails in the iron trade circles in the North of England owing to the stoppage of the works of Messrs. Jones Bros. and Co., at Middlesbro. The alarming intelligence has reached St. Asaph that Dr. Hughes, Bishop of the diocese, who is now in his eighty-second year, has been stricken with paraly*s. Mr. Carvill, J.P.. of Newry, visited Mr. Dillon, M.P., in Dundalk Gaol, yesterday, and states that the prisoner is growing daily weaker from the effects of imprison- ment.

Over a thousand flax workers, employed at Chapel Flax Spinning Works, Montrose, struck work on Friday owing to the refusal of their employers to grant an in- crease of 10 per cent, in their wages. SUICIDE OF A MINISTER. —A Primitive Methodist minister, named W`: Dunham, committed suicide on Thursday night in the schoolroom attached to his church at Dartford, by suspending himself to the stove- pipe- THE REPRFSENTATION OF MERTHYR TYDVIL. - It was stated on Friday morning that in the event of a labour candidate being brought forward and accepted by a fair proportion of workin,gmen Mr. Pritchard Morgan, "the Gold King," will withdraw his own candidature.

THE EVICTIONS ON LORD ~CLANRICARD—Ecs..E'S.TATE. Serious resistance was offered by only one out of the five tenants of Lord Clanricarde, who were evicted at Wood- ford on Thursday. At the house of Thomas Porter, hot water and reddened turf were thrown at the bailiffs by three young men, who were eventually arrested. ANOTHER CARBOLIC ACID POISONING CASE—Another death from carbolic acid poisoning occurred in Liverpool on Friday. The police were called to the house of a man named Mealey, who said his wife had taken carbolic acid. The woman, who was in a state of collapse, was re- moved to the hospital, where, in spite overy attention, she died in a short time.

ADVANCE OF WAGES.—The boilermakers, angle iron- smiths, rivetters, and holders-up in the employ of Messrs Adamson, of Hyde Junction, Messrs. Taylor and Shen- ton, of Hyde, and Mr. Joseph Adamson, of Hyde, all near Ashton-under-Lyne, have been granted an advance bf the ten per cent, recently asked for by the boiler- makers in the Mancheste4district. A FIREMAN KILLED OR THE RAILWAY.—On Friday morning, a ystung man named Samuel Eaton, fireman in the employ of the North-Western Railway Company, and who lived at 248, Inch Green-lane, Wigan, was spragging the wheels of his train near Winsford siding, when he was knocked down and the engine passed over his body. He was taken to the company's hospital at Crewe, and died soon afterwards. FACTORY DESTROYED By FlRE.—Patterson's large match factory, in Dublin, was destroyed by fire on Fri- day morning. A n,umber of people are thrown out of employment. Some of the operatives were burned—one girl, it is feared, fatally. A panic occurred when the outbreak was discovered, the gates of the factory being closed. The girls rushed about heedlessly, and finally, after a dangerous crush, they escaped through a small wicket.

HORRIBLE MURDER IN LONDON. Another brutal murder was committed in Whitechapel, London, on Friday morning, when a constable found a woman, aged about 35, lying dead with her throat cut and her body cut open, in Bucks-row, Thomas-st. There were evidences of a desperate struggle. The murderer is unknown. The brutality of the crime leads the police to believe that the perpetrator must be a ferocious maniac. This is the third crime of the kind which has occurred in the neighbourhood recently. The deceased wore a rough brown ulster, with large buttons in front. Her clothes are torn and cut up in several places, bearing evidence of the ferocity with which the murder was committed. The only way by which the police can prosecute an inquiry at present is by find- ing someone who can identify the body, and then if pos- sible to trace those in whose company she was last seen. The greatest excitement prevails in the locality, and several persons in the neighbourhood state that an affray occurred shortly after midnight, but no screams were heard, nor anything beyond what might have been con- sidered evidence of an ordinary brawl. The brutality of the murder is beyond conception or description. Not only was the unfortunate woman's throat cut in two gashes with a sharp instrument, but the knife was stabbed into the lower part of the abdomen and sav- agely drawn upwards twice, one cut cutting left of the groin and hip, and the other slitting the body as high as the breast bone.

Later details show that the clothing of the woman was not torn and cut as at first stated, 'nor where there in- dications of a struggle. Part of the underclothing-shows that the deceased was recently an inmate of the Lambeth Workhouse. The police, who are making a most careful investigation into the matter, express an opinion that the deceased was killed by a left-handed person, judging from the nature of the injuries. No one has yet come forward to identify the body. Bucks-row, says another correspondent, is a narrow passage running out of Thomas-st., and contains about a dozen of 'a very low class. It would appear as if the murder were committed in a house and the body I afterwards removed to the place where it was found, the nature of the wounds being such that it would be hardly possible for them to be inflicted whilst the deceased was dressed. The body was warmly clad. The workhouse stamp was on one of the undergarments. The body has not yet been identified, though a large number of per- sons have visited the Whitechapel mortuary. The date of the inquest has not been fixed.
LATEST.

The doctor who examined the body calls attention to the fact that hardly half a pint of blood was on the ground at the spot, yet the wounds, especially that in the throat, must have bled profusely. Blood marks have been found leading to a place some three hundred yards distant, but have not enabled anyone to establish the scene of the murder. A woman living in Brody-st., adjoining the thoroughfare, heard screams of " Police " and " Murder " in the small hours, but this informant can add nothing else. Up to a late hour last night the matter remained as unsolved as at the hour when the body was found.

ANOTHER GREAT FIRE. 200 FAMILIES HOMELESS. Another terrible fire is reported from Tarnobezeg, in Galicia, where 150 houses have been burnt, causing 1,000,0005. damage. More than 200 families are home- less, and several persons have been seriously injured. The houses in small polish towns are largely built of wood, and the water supply is always bad, so that when a fire breaks out it spreads with great rapidity.

NTOTICE IS lIEREBY GIVEN that a GENERAL .1.11 MEETING of the Ratepayers within the District of the Frodsham and Helsby Drainage Board will be held in the TOWN HALL, FRODSHAM, on MONDAY. THE 3RD DAY OF .BEP- TEMBER, 1888, at half-past seven o'clock in the evening, ' for the purpose of electing new members of the Board. The number of members to be elected is 15, and the qualifi- cations are as follows :—The proprietor of not less than 20 statute acres within the District : The heir apparent of the proprietor of an estate of not less than 20 statute acres within the District; The occupier, yearly or otherwise, of not less than 30 statute acres within the District; The Agent of a pro- prietor of an estate of not less than 20 statute acres within the Distrk-t, such Agent acting under a written appointment. HENRY BESWICK, Returning Officer. Clerk's Office, Frodsham, 21st August, 1888.

GUY'S HO6PIT AL MEDICAL SCIICOL. THE WINTER SESSION COMMENCES ON MONDAY, OCTOBER IST. The Hospital contains 695 beds, of which 500 are inconstant occupation. There are Wards for Obstetric and Opthalmie cases, an,' other special Departments. Special classes are held in the Hospital for Students preparing for the Examinations of the University of London, and other Higher Exardlina- time. APPOINTMENTS.—The House-qurgeoncies, HouseaThy- siciancies, Dresserships, and all other Appointments, arernade strictly in accordance with the merits of the Candidates, and without extra payment. There are also a large number of Junior Appointments, every part of the Hospital practice be- ing systematically employed for instruction, so that Students who have completed their preliminary studies elsewhere may enter at once upon the practice of the Hospital. ENTRANCE SCHOLARSHIPS—Open Scholarship of 125 guineas In Clas- sics, Mathematics, and Modern Languages. Open Scholar- ship of 125 guineas in Chemistry. Physics, and Biology. PRIZES are open to Students in their various years amount- ing in the aggregate to more than £3OO. During the past year the accommodation in the PHYSIOLOGICAL.'AND PATHOLOGICAL Departments has been greatly increased, and a STUDENTS' CLUB has been opened in the Hospital, containing a Dining-room, Reading-rooms and a large Gym- nasium. COLLEGE.—A residential College is in the course ,of erec- tion upon a site immediately contiguous to the Hospital to accommodate about 50 Students in addition to the Resident' Staff of the Hospital. for -Prospectus and further information apply to the Dean, Dr. PERRY, Guy's Hospital, London, S.E.
